div.p: *Mr..

SUCH A BOY. Little Willie Sunny-head, Only quiet when in bed! Other times he tumbling, dancing, Or like a restive pony prancing: Such a boy ! Such a bov ! Yet he's mother's darling joy— . 'Mother's precious Willie! Up and and down, now here, now there, Sunny-head is everywhere— Peering into dishes, hampers, Or with kitty wildly scampers; Such .a boy, such a boy! Yet he's father's darling joy— Father's precious Willie! Sometimes on an old tin pan; Making ail the nolo he can; Sometimes en the parlour mat, %ailing stories to the eat; Clutching poker by the middle, Scraping bellows for a Iddle : Such a boy, such a boy! Yet he's everybody's joy— Sunny-hearted Willie!

IN MEMORIAM. Menai 28-ra, 1884. Lo! in the flush of youth, when hope was high, And her sweet light like sunshine tonch'd the years, Beath comes, when not a cloud was in the sky, And smiles a Royal household into tears. And all the people standing from afar Can only watch, with pity-breathing breath, A queenly mother that has seen his star Shoot down into the night of early death. 0 mateless one I In this dark hour of hope, A nation sorrows for thy child and thee, The widow of him who had for horoscope Our second Albert--that was not to be. Prince of the people, at one with all their aims, Who saw the life around them with their eyes; royal lowly heart to all their claims, And quick to catch the wisdom of the wise. Our hopes were high; the seeming gracious years Bent towards him and flower'd upon his way— One touch shook all their blossoms, and, in tears, His England mourns beside his grave to-day. No more "the untravelled traveller"—he stands In that high realm where souls to souls outflow; And shapes to perfect orb, with holier hands, • The incompleted life he left below. Bereaf ter, there shall be on England's page This picture for our children as they read, A young Prince full of courtesy, and sage, Loved by the people and a Prince indeed. And in their eyes, as in our own to-day, There shall be tears for her who, late a bride, A wife and mother, now walks her widow'd way, A nation's love and sorrow at her side. .--14 Good Words" for May. ALExammta Atengasorr.

The cry of Teetotallism—" All hands to the pump!" Why is the world like a piano 2—Because it is fall of sharps and flats. "Duty before pleasure," as the Custom House officer said 'when he lighted on some smuggled tobacco. An Irishman says he can see no earthly reason why women should not be allowed to become medical men. A handbill has been put forth at Exeter, headed— "Wanted, a few healthy members to complete a sick so- ciety." Teacher (severely) : "John, why is it that boys' hands are always dirtier than girls' ?"—John (hesitatingly) : "Please, sir, the girls washes the diehes." "All the world's a stage, and all the men and women merely players." And it may be added, without irreverence $o Shakspere, very poor players most of them. "Doctor," said a gentleman to his pastor, "how can I best train up my boy in the way he should go ?" By going that way yourself," blandly replied the pastor. "Do you drink?" said a Temperance reformer to a beggar who had implored alms of him. "Yes, thank you," re- turned the candid pauper. "Where shall we go 2" "Do you know a good way of curing hams?" asked a man of his neighbour. "Oh, yea," was the reply; "but the trouble with me is, I have no way of pro-curing them." "It is a shame, John, that I have to sit here mending your old clothes I" exclaimed a wife the other day. "Don't say a word about it, my dear." rejoined the husband; "the least said the soonest mended." A bookinder said to his wife at their wedding, "It seems that now we are bound together, two volumes in one, with clasps." "Yes," observed one of the guests; "one side highly ornamental Turkey morocco, the other plain calf." Cultivate the physical exclusively, and you have an ath- lete or a savage; the moral only, and you have an enthusiast Or a maniac; the intellectual only, and you have a diseased oddity—it may be a monster. It is only by wisely training all of them together that the complete man can be found.- Bmdes. A young man in a railway carriage was making fan .of a lady's hat to an elderly gentleman on the seat with hint. "Yes," said the elderly gent, "that's my wife, and I told her that if she wore that bonnet some fool would make fan of her." The young man was silent for the remainder of the journey. There are ten things for which no one has ever yet been sorry—for doing good to all, for speaking evil of none, for hearing before judging, for thinking before speaking, for bolding an angry tongue, for being kind to the distressed, ' for asking pardon for all wrongs, for being patient towards everybody, for stopping the ears of a tale-bearer, for dis- believing ill reports. At the Pont des Arts, in Paris, is a blind man who carries a board around his neck with this singular sign—" Blind by Birth and by Accident." "See here, my good man," said a passer-by, "your sign is positively distracting. Can you tell us-how you happen to be blind by birth and by accident! ,at the same time ?' 'Easy enough," said the old man. "You see, I'm blind by birth myself, and I've bought out a blind man who did business at the other end of the bridge. Ee was blind by accident." A farmer in a remote district of the Yorkshire Wolds met a country rector who had been two years absent on travel.— "Mr. Rector," said the farmer, "you've been to the Holy Land, I hear?"—" I have, John, and got safe back, you see. —" Well," said John," I often thou% I'd like to hear aboot that spot. It's a fine country, I lay "—" Well," said the lector, I saw Lebanon, and Jerusalem, and the Twelve Palm Trees, and the wells of water in the Great Desert ; and we went across the Jordan, and up Mount—"—" Ex- cuse Me interruntin' you, Mr. Rector, noo," said the farmer, "but if it be fair question, boo was turmet (turnips) looking out yonder ? " One of the best stories of social presents is this. Some Sweaty or thirty years ago lived and flourished a young lady. She was always young, always unmarried, and always a "leader of fashion." She had, like humbler mortals, every year a birthday, although she never grew older, and on these birthdays all her acquaintances were expected to give her a • present. These votive offerings were arranged on a table in an ante-chamber. Lord Brougham called upon her on one of these rent-days. He had forgotten his present. With ready presence of mind he seized upon the best in the ante. . chamber, wrapped it carefully up in paper, and then pre- seated It to the young lady. She was "so much obliged" to him, and never discovered that it had already been given to her by seine one else. Are you going to kiss me, sir ?" If someone had offered to lend me ten dollars I could not have been more surprised, and hardly knowing what to say, and in order to gain a little time, I gasped out, "Pardon, Miss, what did • you ask ?" HIGH PRICE FOR A CLYDESDALE FILLY.—The other ciaF Mr. Smith, Pittengardner-by-Ferdoun, sold to the Marquis of Einntley a fine pure Clydesdale filly rising three years old (sire Prince Charlie). The price was 200 guineas. MANORS FROM SLAG.—A process has been recently in- troduced for making phosphoric acid and mineral phosphates from slag—especially by the slags produced by the Besse- mer and Siemens processes. These phosphate are of course valuable as manure, especially as guano is said to be be- coming scarcer. EARLY POTATOES:ALI amateur gardener, determined to try the autumn planting of potatoes, sowed some last autumn. In the beginning of March they were above ground, and presented such a flourishing appearance that they were chirstened "First Early Wonderfuls." At the end of March it was considered appropriate to re-name them, and "First Early Anxieties" was the name chosen. In the second week in April the potatoes were described as "First Early Doubtfuls," and in the third week of the month, after the frosts, "First Early Done-fors." FAIRY Ituros.—The dark green circles of grass known as " fairy rings" have long attracted the notice of scientists, but Messrs. Lewes, Gilbert, and Wallington, of Rothamstead, have probably given us the true explanation of the pheno- menon at last. The luxuriance of the grass is due to nitro- gen, that potent fertiliser, which is abstracted from the sur- rounding soil by the fungus plants in the ring. The grass in turn feeds on the minerals collected by the fungi, thus obeying the principles of the rotation of crops. It was not proved before that any kind of plant could feed directly on the organic nitrogen of the soil; and the explanation of the fairy ring may lead to advances in agricultural chemistry. LismiNG IN LA.NCASHIRE.—North-east winds have steadily prevailed, still growth is far from being at a stand- still, as is evidenced by a slight scour in sheep on old pas- tures, arising from the new grass shoots. We have all but finished lambing. Including losses the Leicesters have given 150 per cent, of lambs. The losses of lambs for the heavy Leicester ewes were greater than in ordinary years, probably arising from the wet season leading up to difficult births. The Cheviots have returned 175 per cent, of living lambs, several having brought three each. I never remem- ber a season where the lambs looked better. Once on their feet, they have "never looked behind them." It is a treat to see them Budding over the pastures, and playing "cock off my midden" on every piece of rising ground. The great secret of sheep farming is undoubtedly in frequent change of pastures, and not having them too numerous on the land. On dry, sound pasture you may keep a lot in health, with supplementary food if you have frequent change, so as to allow the land to become sweetened as it were. If the land is inclined to dampness then the more need for dry food and for more frequent change. For a few hours during the middle of the clay milch cattle and young stock go out on the pas- tures, and this saves one meal per day in the house. Once out in the sunshine it is difficult to get them to return ere the evening's chill air sets in.—R. STRAW AS FOOD.—There is no doubt that the question as to the best use of straw—whether it should be given to stock for food, or trodden down in the yard or stable for the purpose of manure—is one of much interest and importance to the British farmer. As a general rule it may be said that its value as food is one-half to two-thirds that of average meadow hay. In winter straw there are, says Wolff, 356 per cent, of digestible elements in the shape of carbo- hydrates and only 8-10 per cent, of albuminoids and 4.10 of fat: the rest, being of no use for the purposes of diges- tion, passes away in the solid droppings. The only vain- able elements as manure are the albarainoids. of which there would be 161bs. in a ton, or lib. of nitrogen, the whole of the other elements having no such value. Animal heat is created and fat put on by the carbon contained in the straw, and in this respect it has an important food value, and may be used without materially diminishing its value as manure. No doubt the soil of heavy arable land is im- proved by putting in straw manure in its whole state; but farmers, with whom economy is the principle or a neces- sity, will not care to make use of it in this way when it is possible for them to purchase artificial manures by selling their straw, and then leaving a balance in their favour. Several years ago when a gentleman very well known in the agricultural world stated his belief in the value of and ad- vised the use of straw as food, he was laughed at by his audience although he supported his view by experiments conducted by himself. He said it was of half the value of hay, and equal in manure value to straw used as litter. If a ton of straw is used simply as manure, it is not more than half the value of straw given as food and afterwards used as manure. No one will think of feeding with straw alone. It should be given in combination with cake or meal, wheat bran, oats, or other highly nitrogenous foods. STATE CONTROL OF FERTILISERS.—The State of North Carolina has very stringent laws respecting the sale and Purity of artificial manures, these laws being enforced by a board of officers known as "The Fertilisers' Control," the regulations of which require a guarantee of the composition and grade of the article sold, and provide for an examina- -1 Con of all goods to see that this guarantee is sustained. 1 Manufacturers are required to take out an annual license, ! and to file their stamp or brand, which the law requires shall include the guaranteed analysis of the article, and i must be uniform upon all packages. The following manures are free from taxation :—Ground bone, bone ash, ground bone black, ground phosphate rock, or other mineral phos- phate, nitrogenous organic matter commercially free from phosphoric acid and potash, nitrate of soda, nitrate of potash (saltpetre), sulphate of ammonia, chloride of am- monia, kainite, sulphate of magnesia, sulphate of potash, sulphate of soda, chlorate of potash, lime, plaster, ground cracklings, ground tankage, salt, and oil of vitriol. Any of the foregoing articles, or others, sold for fertilising material under any trade mark or proprietary brand, are chargeable with the license tax, this impost being apparently directed against the concoctions of manures narrated to be particu- larly beneficial in the case of some specified crop. The tax is also exacted upon dissolved bone, dissolved bone black, dissolved mineral phosphates (all acid phosphates or super- phosphates), and upon any two or more of the articles, already mentioned as free of tax, if combined either me- chanically or chemically. Government agents are em- powered to collect samples of fertilisers, much in the same way as the police in this country take samples of milk or groceries under the Adulteration Act. The sample, bearing a number placed on it by the officers, is sent to the chemist of the State Agricultural Experiment Station, who is thus left without any information as to the source and descrip- tion of the manure. The result of his analysis is sent to the Commissioner's office, and is then compared with the composition guaranteed or branded on the bag from which the sample was procured. Should it appear that the article is deficient in any respect, the manufacturer or agent is given an opportunity of correcting the error, but unless the law is promptly satisfied, its penalties are exacted. Some of my friends who have gone southward tell me that they continue the time of sowing, as in the North, and they secure heavy crops of roots. I may mention that last year we had reserved a piece of land for cabbage; but as the weather was so dry, we thought it useless to plant them, and swedes were oat in. Now, although we hail a capital growing autumn and a mild winter, and those roots were not taken off until February, they did not make half a crop, the roots not being much bigger than a man's fist, showing that late sowing does not answer here, even in the most favourable seasons. As the subsequent weather turned out, if we had only put in cabbage, we should have had a capital crop.—R.

THE LATE MR. M. T. Bass.—The funeral of the late Mr. Michael Thomas Bass took place at Rangemoor Church on Monday. Upwards of 20,000 persons travelled from Derby and Buxton to witness the interment. IRISH MURDER CONSPIRACY.—ARREST IN OLDHAM —lt is expected that John Casey, arrested, on Tuesday, in Old- ham, by two Irish constables, on a charge of murder con- spiracy three years ago, will be taken to Sligo, and will then be formally remanded until Monday, when be will be brought up with other eleven prisoners. Casey used to drill the Tubbercurry Fenians, and instruct them in the use of fire-arms, but he occupied a rather non-important position in the organisation. Patrick N. Fitzgerald and the eleven men charged with being concerned in the alleged conspi- racy to murder landlords and others at Tubbercurry, County Sligo, were brought before two special resident magistrates at Sligo, on Monday. The prisoners were represented by counsel. The Crown prosecutor opened the case of the pro- secution. The first witness to be examined is John Moran, a native of Tubbercurry, and at one time a companion of P.J. Sheridan. He is a young man, 26 years of age, very intelligent, and has been a member of the inner circle of the Irish Republican Brotherhood. DUTCH BABIES.—When the childaen of a family are told that they have a new brother or sister they are not always willing to welcome it as they should. The youngest espe- cially, who has been "baby"hitherto, feels rather aggrieved, and considers the new-comer in the light of a usurper who deserves to be pinched rather than kissed. Now, the good parents of Holland, who are very fond of their children, and •try to spare them all unnecessary pain, have hit upon an excellent plan to make baby welcome. As he lies in his cradle, which is like the English one, they fill his little arms with trumpet-shaped bags brimful of comfits, and these are distributed among the children as baby's presents. Baby continues to present these tiny comfits—which the children eat on bread and butter, and are very fond of—for the space of six weeks, when he is supposed to have established his right to exist. Babies are dressed very much as in Eng- land, except that, in some cases, an old custom is adhered to of wrapping up their heads in three caps—one of cambric, another of silk, and the third of lace. The christening al- ways takes place on a Sunday, and after the christening there is a grand dinner, to which all the relations are in- vited.—‘' Little Folks Magazine" for May. 'Ma SECRET OF ENGLAND'S POWEIR.—But whence comes all the boundless wealth of England? To what cause is due her undisputed supremacy in commerce? How did her Empire come to encircle the globe? These are the questions which present themselves for solution, which are always fresh, and which can never lose their interest. When we come down to what gold miners call the "hard pan," it appears to me that we reach the mental, physical, and reli- gions character of the Anglo-Saxon race. This is the true basis of England's wealth and greatness. There is some truth in what the physical geographers tell us of the effect of the natural conformation of a country on the character of its inhabitants. The British Islands would appear to have been designed to produce a nation of sea-kings and colonisers; their insular position and inhospitable climate have developed a race of men such as the unclouded skies and perpetual summer of the tropics has never yet produced: men who, scorning hardship, knowing and loving the free- dom of the ocean, could not brook slavery on shore. Who bat Englishmen would have ventured to cross the stormy Atlantic in a crazy craft like the Mayflower, and to brave the dangers and hardships of settling in an unknown land among savages cruel as tigers, for conscience-sake, and love of liberty ?-77ze Hon. CORRESPONDENCE WITH GENERAL GO/MON.—Further correspondence between General Gordon and the Govern- ment is published. General Gordon considers himself free to act according to circumstances, that he should hold on to Khartoum as long as he can, and will endeavour to suppress the rebellion, and that if he cannot do so, he will retire to the equator. General Gordon has informed Colonel Stewart and Mr. Power that they should go to Berber as soon as it is possible to send steamers down. Colonel Stewart and Mr. Power, however, both elect to follow General Gordon on to the equator. Sir E. Baring says that it is most unfortunate that of all the telegrams which he has sent to General Gor- don since March 10th, only one very short one of the 23rd appeared to have reached him. General Gordon appears to think he is to be abandoned, and is very indignant. Major- General Gordon wrote to Sir E. Waring from Khartoum on April Bth :—" Zebebr is at Korosko, so you did not tell me this important fact. Scarcely a day passes without our in- flicting losses on the rebels, which losses are quite unneces- sary if eventually we are to succumb. I have telegraphed to Baker to make an appeal to British and American mil- lionaires to give me £300,000 to engage 3,000 Turkish troops from the Sultan and send them here. This would settle the Soudan and the Mandi for ever. For my part I think you would agree with use. Ido not see the fun of be- ing caught here to walk about the streets for years as a dervish with sandalled feet ; not that (Dm) I will ever be taken alive. It would be the climax of meanness after I had borrowed money from the people here, had called on them to sell their grain for a low price, etc., to go and abandon them without aging every effort to relieve them, whether those efforts are diplomatically cerrect or not; and I feel sure, whatever you may feel deplomatically, I have your support, and that of every man professing himself a go Aleman in private. Nothing could be more meagre than your telegram, 'Osman Digma's followers are dispersed.' Surely something more than this was required by me." General Gordon having contemplated a visit to the Matadi in February, Sir E. Baring was authorised to inform him that he is not to put himself voluntarily in the Mandi's power. General Gordon afterwards disclaimed any further intention of visiting the Mandi. On February Ist General Gordon asked Sir E. Baring to mention to the British Vol eign Office that the King of Belgium was willing to take two provinces around Korosko. The, General Gordon said, would meth the slave trade.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING

FRUIT Paoensers.—With 11 degrees of frost on the 18th and seven degrees on the 25th of the past month, and minor frosts at intervals, fruit prospects might be expected to be reduced to a minimum. This is the case in the vicinity of London, along the Valley of the Thames, and in the Mid- lands. What trees we have seen in the neighbourhood of Preston slightly injured, promise an abundant crop, all of them looking healthy. Some Pear treea are a sheet of blossom, and the shoots of Black Currants are clothed from base to summit. Other Currant and Gooseberry trees are equally well furnished. Plums appear to be better flowered than they have been for some years, and as for Cherry trees we have seen on some of them very little else visible but flowers, so that if one flower in every hundred sets there should be a prodigious crop. We dare not prophesy any- thing respecting any other kind of fruit trees, for there is time yet for Jack Frost to destroy the whole. So far we . have escaped in consequence of the exceptional dryness of the atmosphere, as well as a fair amount of sunshine to warm the earth and surrounding objects, so that the maxi- mum cold has only been of short duration. BEETROOT succeeds more or less in moist soils, but the best results are obtained from a rich light one which has been well manured for a previous crop. Beetroot are bad because they are badly grown, or sown on land unsuitable for the particular variety. For strong or heavy soils, Dell's Black-leaved and Henderson's Pine Apple; in light soils, Cattell's Blood-red will suffice, and for soils of intermediate character, Troughton's Superb Crimson is in every way suitable. The ground, of whatever nature, should be well worked so as to secure a fine surface; when that has been satisfactorily obtained, drills may be drawn one inch deep and 12in. to 15in, distant, and the seeds, instead of being sown in a continuous line, may be dropped in patches three or four inches apart, so that less seed will be required. When the ground is free from slugs the distance between the patches may be eight inches, so that when the crop is thinned the best plant in each group must be left. Persons who have tasted beetroot for the first time have been astonished when informed that they were eating an esculent that could be grown in any garden. It is rarely one meets with anyone that dislikes it, either sliced with vinegar with or without a little salad oil, or in the shape of a pickle. PEAS.—We frequently hear the query—When should I sow peas to be ready for such and such show or such a date? In these matters the most experienced will sometimes have his calculations upset. He may be well acquainted with the character of the variety he sows. and he may sow at the right time, according to previous reckonings, but, owing to adverse circumstances, the seeds are ten days later coming up, and when the pods are swelling, cold, sunless weather occurs, and another week is lost, so that by the show day he has not a score of pods fit to look at. Chagrined at this, he takes a different course another year, and sows his favourite sort a week sooner, and from the time the seeds are deposited in the soil they are forced along by the con- tinuous fine weather, so that they are well nigh over by the required date. The best safeguard against such contingen- cies is to make two sowings a fortnight apart. Both together need only be the extent of an ordinary one, for the proba- bilities are that there will be some ready on each, and more good pods than if both sowings had been made as one. Second, early Peas, such as Advancer, Laxton's Alpha, and Fillbaaket, sown now, should be ready from the first to the end of the second week in August, and another week or ten days must be allowed for such as Lancashire Hero, Omega, and Telegraph, or about fifteen weeks from the time of sowing. THE FRONT GARDEN.—Where the grass has been al- lowed to grow to an undue length advantage should be taken of moist weather to cut it, for if performed on a dry sunny day it will assume sundry colours before it is green again. To maintain a nice green plot the grass should be cut every week or ten days. When allowed to grow several inches high, the weakest and finer grasses perish in the struggle for existence. Now, that the weather is warmer, various classes of plants may be planted in the beds or borders. The first that should be dealt with are the Violas of various hues, Which should be arranged in the front row, so as not to be hidden by others of more robust growth. Many cottagers are in possession of Echeveria Glanca, a near relative of the Houseleek ; both of them are useful in setting off the beds. The cottager's stock may not be suf- ficient to make a great shoby having a row or more round his beds, but to make the nalist of what he has he can plant them in his rockery, or he can raise a mound of earth in the most sunny spot, and partially unbed a few rough stones in it, and fix the plants amongst them with their flat surface facing the spectator. To effect this the roots mast be placed obliquely. Like all thick fleshy leaved plants, they require very little soil and water to maintain them in good health. When the Echeverias are scattered indiscriminately amongst other plants, their beauty is lost, hence the de- sirability of making some more suitable provision for them. THE WINDOW.—The green-fly wilP now be very trouble- some on window plants. Much may be done to keep them down by daily pressing every insect between the finger and thumb; but if they should get the upper hand there is nothing so effectual as the fumes of tobacco carefully admi- nistered. This, however, mast not be applied to such flowers as Geraniums and Fuchsias when in flower, or all the ex- panded blossoms will fall off in a few hours. Callas, or Arum Lilies, must be well supplied with water, and if some of the inert soil is moved from the surface and replaced with fresh and an equal portion of decayed manure, it will assist them to throw up their spathes, as the trumpet-shaped flower is termed. These plants are frequently attacked with green-fly, but as they are rather large to fumigate they may be laid on their sides and the vermin removed with a soft brush.

VENETIAN VISITING CARDS.—The etiquette of visiting was always a serious duty in the social life of the Venetian nobility. On every conceivable occasion, on departure from the city, on return, on birthdays, saints' days, New Year's Day, a family was expected to leave cards on all its acquaintances, and these visits had to be returned. And as the vigour of the Venetians slowly dwindled away and lost its force in the inanities, the luxury, and effeminacy of an enervated and corrupt society, more and more time and thought were bestowed upon the formalities of life; it be. came a matter of pride to invent a design, and the dandies of Venice piqued themselves on the elegance of the cards they left upon their friends. And hence a trade arose in card-making to meet the demand. Those who were careless , in such matters would go to their stationer and buy the de- sign that happened to be in fashion. At one time it was a picture of the Rialto, at another the favourite pattern was a sketch of some of the statues round the Pra dells Valle at Padna ; but the more modish and testhetic were not content with cards cast off by the hundred and used by any one and every one; and so they either designed their cards for them- selves, bestowing much labour and ingenuity on the work, or they employed some distinguished artist to furnish them with a design. Even Canova did not refuse to put his genius to this service for Ms friend Capello ; and one of the most beautiful of these Venetian visiting cards is that drawn and printed in London for Alvise Pisani, by Henry Tresham, the English painter.-11 L. Brown in "The Magazine of Art."

div.p: A militiaman at Ely shot at and wounded one of his officers on Thursday morning. It is stated that Mr. Charles Dalrymple will oppose Mr. Gladstone in Midlothian at the next election. A statue of William Tyndale, erected on the Thames Embankment, was unveiled on Wednesday by Lord Shaftes- bury.

The Home Secretary has advised Her Majesty to respite the sentence of death recently passed upon Thomas Smith, 21. puddler, for murdering his wife at Stockton-on-Tees. Mr. Chamberlain had a third interview on Thursday is private, at the Board of Trade Offices, with a number of shipowners and underwriters on the subject of the Merchant shipping Bill. It is stated that the Conservative candidates for North- East Lancashire will be Mr. Ralph Assheton, formerly member for Chitheroe, and Mr. Arthur B. Forwood, of Liver- pool. The Liberal candidates will be the present members, I Lord Hartington and Mr. Grafton. A meeting was held in St. James's Hall, London, 01 Thursday evening, "to protest against the abandonment of General Gordon." Among those who took part in the Igo' ceedings were Earl Cadogan, wha presided, Mr. ChaPlll39 Ashmead-Bartlett, and Mr. E. Clarke, M.F. At Brentford, on Thursday, Lord St. Leonards (standwilf of the great lawyer) was committed for trial on a charge o having unlawfully assaulted a young woman who was i2l service at the house of an acquaintance. His Lordship vnle, according to the statement of the prosecutrix, drunk at the time.

FIRE IN A Crecus.—Early on Thursday morning, a Ir° broke out in the stable-tent of Mr. George Ginnett's circus, now visiting Luton. An elephant, which was in the tent, tore down half of it; and one pony was so badly bran, that it had to be shot, while several others were severel scorched. Fly MEN DROWNED.—While a small boat was return* ing from the fishing in the Dornoch Firth, Sutherlandshirep on Wednesday night, it was struck by a squall and eaP" sized. Two of the men were afterwards observed on the keel waving their hands, but the sea was so rough that nn assistance could be rendered from the shore and the enell' pants of the boat, five in number, were drowned. RETURN OF THE QUEEN.—The Queen, with Prineeee Beatrice, the Grand Duke of Hesse, and the Princess Elle, arrived at Sheerness from Flushing on Wednesday evening, on board the Royal yacht Osborne, after a rough passage* The Queen and other members of the party disetnbis at Pert Victoria Pier, and proceeded thence to Windsorl train. The vessels in Sheerness harbour were dressed with masthead flags in honour of ner Majesty's arrival. WEST LANCASHIRE RAILWAY (EXTENSION) EILL.--"013 Wednesday this bill was before the Committee of the Eloneed of Commons on unopposed bills, the Chairman of Wayne° Means presiding. The bill authorises an extension of tbe West Lancashire Railway from its present terminus at Ffet ton to the new dock to be constructed by the Corporation et Preston. The preamble was proved, and the clauses having been adjusted the bill was ordered to be repotted to the House.

The deceased, who has, recently been depressed in consequence of some Mimeo," was found hanging in the stable of his residence. The der were fastened by means of chains. The deceased had be pendent means, and no family. His wife hearing of th", occurrence was rendered unconscious, and is in a precariou• state. ROUSE O 1 LORDS—MONDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4-15. Lord GaereviLLe, replying to a question from Lord Salis- IMrYe said that no intelligence as to General Gordon had teached the Government within the previous four hours. Tme LUNACY LAws.—Lord MILLTOWN, having called at- tention to observations of Mr. Baron Huddleston in the case of "Weldon v. Winslow," pointed out various defects in the ,e_l4lttate.Y Laws, He moved that in the opinion of the House orta state of those laws was eminently unsatisfactory, and constituted a serious danger to the liberty of the subject.— Lord SHAFTESBURY, who is chairman of the Lunacy Com- Mission, explained that there were precautions required en- der the Lunacy Acts which afforded to persons against Whom lunacy was alleged far greater protection than the words used by Mr. Baron Huddleston would seem to imply. Re did not allege that there were no abuses, but he said that there was much exaggeration in thie rnatter.—Lord COLERIDGE, while bearing testimony to the great improve- Ment that had been effected by the Lunacy Act of 1855, fer Which the country was indebted to Lord Shaftesbury, said his experience as a judge had shown him that our system Of dealing with allegations of lunacy, though perfect on Paper, broke down in practice.—The LORD CHANCELLOR by flo means contended that there were not points in which the ' existiug Lunacy Laws required amendment; but he could not accept the motion because he regarded its terms as ex- travagant.—Lord SALISBURY thought that the debate had been a useful one, and that after the statement made by the , Lord Chancellor he recommended Lord Milltown not to press his motion. He himself was of opinion that the present state of the Lunacy Laws was very unsatisfactory.—The !notion was withdrawn. Flamm Coervtors —Lord ROSRBERRY bad given notice that he would call attention to the proposed deportation of Eicidivists from France to the Western Pacific, and move for papers, but at the request of Lord Granville he post- POned the matter. Lord MORLEY, in answer to Lord Enfield, stated that af- ter a full consideration of the matter and a reference to pre-, cedents, her Majesty's Government did not intend to move formal vote of thanks to the forces engaged in the opera- tions near Snakim. Several bills having been advanced a stage, Their Lordships rose at 7 35. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair at 4-0. EoYor AND THE SOIMAN.—In the House of Commons lir W. Lawsom gave notice of an amendment to the Vote Censure declaring that the House declines to censure Her najesty's Government for not taking stops that would in- 'Give military operations in connection with an expedition I distinctly and avowedly of a pacific nature.—Sabsequently fair A. GORDON, amid same laughter from the Conservative tenches, gave notice of an amendment affirming that the ',louse continues to place confidence in the general conduct Of business by the Government-1n reply to Mr. Onslow, Lord RARTINGTON said the Goverement had carefully con- sidered pree!dents bearing upon the question of the pro- Posed vote of thanks to officers and men engaged in the '3ouclan expedition, and they found that to move a formal rote of thanks for an expedition which could not be regarded ae an independent operation, but rather as an incident in Poo military occupation of Egypt, evoteld extend the practice , !Critic' former precedent.—ln reply to Sir M. Hicks-Beach, GLADSTONE briefly answered that the Government lied considered the matter of furnishing facilities for discussing the Vote of Censure, and were desirous to give the earliest °,,,Pen day. Monday next would be such day but looking (o the limited scope of the motion, he trusted that the de- bate would finish on that night. If it did not, the Govern- rlent would reluctantly give Tuesday morning, leaving the eaders of the Opposition to consider whether they could I get Tuesday night from the private members. THE ARMY ESTIMATES.—The House went into Committee I on the Army Estimates, and on the vote'to complete the rOto of £57,448 for Divine service, a general discussion be place as to the order in which the several votes should ce taken.—On the vote for £303,000 for Medical Establish- ? Cents and Services, Mr. GUI DAWNAY complained that dur- Mg the late Egyptian expedition a considerable amount of Dreventible disease existed at Cairo and lamella. This, he eaid, was due to the inefficient organisation of the medical Service.—After some remarks from Dr. LYONS, who thought I the charges against the administration of the medical staff „4, Egypt had not been sustained, the Marquis of HARTING- -4.',..°14, replying on behalf of the War Department, contended °Oat nothing like a breakdown had been shown to have taken Place in the medical arrangements —The discussion was Continued by Colonel MILNE HORN—After a few remarks from Col. ALEXANDER, the vote was agreed to 911 the vote of £568,000 for the Volunteer force. Mr. BRAND, iI answer to questions by Mr. Egerton and others, stated that the general question of the issue of rifles to the army had been under consideration, and would shortly be before the Secretary of State for decision. Mr. 'Tommesore made an appeal on behalf of the Lance- Shire Volunteers, who stood at the head of the Volunteer corps of the country, to increase the camp allowance in Lancashire. The Marquis of HARTlNcercoe recognised the strength of feeling which existed on this subject, and said it was clear that before another year elapsed the subject must be con- dared either with the view of increasing the provision now blade for camp allowance or else of devising some less ob- Lectionable method of controlling the expenditure. He could „Qt, however, undertake to bring in a supplementary estimate eor the Purpose in the present year. It should be borne in 1,5,1_15 that the volunteer force bad bean popular because it "ae, been economical. The vote was agreed to. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY. Their Lordships met at 5-15. The Fisheries (Ireland) Bill was read a first time. tORE REDISTRIBUTION OF SEATS.—Lord Waveney had on l'Osooe Paper a resolution that all boroughs of not more than ;SONO registered voters, at the time of passing any Act for L'Oe redistribution of seats in Ireland, should be incorporated the representation of the counties wherein they are Situatedee by the addition of so many members to the county p,resentation as those boroughs should have previously ii7rned. lie was about to speak in support of this propo- b:Son, when Lord REDESDALE objected to the resolution e, log Put, as the redistribution of seats was the subject of a Zeasure before the other House.—Earl GRANVILLE con- rreed in thinking that the resolution was out of order.:— irrd WAVENEY persisted in proceeding, and the Marquis of ektlslttney asked that the question that the noble lord be eot heard shoald be put to the House.—The Lord CwAte- jriketeLote then put the question, and declared that the ayes .BIL it, whereupon Lord WAVENEY gave notice that on an ettlY day he will call attention to the municipal proportions tlf the Irish boroughs. Lord Edmond Fitzmaurice, declining to be 4,drawn into premature debate," referred the questioners to "ae DaperS before the House. TRE FRANCHISE Min.—The House early got into Corn- teittee on the Franchise Bill. The first clause, simply con- !Cuing the title' was agreed to. Clause 2, which provides "a uniform household and lodger franchise in counties ehd boroughs," Sir R. A. Cress proposed to preface by the !ells " subject to the provisions of this Act hereinafter ,Tlotained," Mr. G'adstone refusing to accede to the proposi- no, the mover disclosed its meaning by complaining that the clause passed as it stood it would be impossible there- ‘fter to introduce provisione dealing with the time when the tneasure should come into operation.—Mr. GLADsTONE said to Government admitted that a Redistribution Bill was the toner complement of the Franchise Bill. It was urgent iinat such a Bill should be passed, and the Government had of 4,°llleced their intention to pass it before the dissolution ett OOe present Parliament. That, he said amid cheers, was eht`Oat coald be askel.—The amendment, which found ex- B's• support on the Conservative side, was upon a divi- joL;l rejected by 263 votes against 149, a substantial ma- -00 the first joining of issue between the two parties, was loudly cheered from the Liberal benches.—Mr. freost.rr next proposed to leave out the word " uniform " eoo7„r,he definition of the household and lodger franchise in reetZtes and boroughs.--After some discussion the amend- eider F,as Withdrawn. The House then entered upon con- eft, 4,th01l of an amendment by Mr. Stanley Leighton to add Nal' lodger the words "and freehold." Upon this the House DOrl„e4llgaged when at 10 minutes to seven progress was re- The Report of Supply was brought up and. agreed Tod at five minutes to seven the sitting was suspended. DECEASED WIFE'S SISTER QUESTION.—On resuen• atte„,,t nine o'clock, Mr. WARTON made an ineffectual soiPt to count the House.—Mr. BROADHURST moved a re- floe '°ll declaring that, in view of the painful and unneces- thi; hardships inflicted upon large numbers of people of ' decea"tintry by the law prohibiting marriage with a teem Bed wife's sieter; it is the opinion of the House that a of th:re of relief is urgently called for. The common sense I::ae.%ii,:estrltorty, he urged, regarded the prohibition of these 7 Ret es as absurd. and it was the duty' of Parliament to public opinion in the matter as soon as possi- wh. °oh amusement was created by his reading a circular. 511 ch the Secretary of "the Church of England Work- liddr "'a Sbciety" directed members of the society to, " Sth • • Vete their Parliamentary representatives urging them ,tO. that arcest the resolution; but above all not to mention littiNesY had been asked to do so by the society' "Write e•S w thing men" was the secretary's instruction,

rhailed with renewed laughter on both sides of the House.— Mr. HENEAGE seconded the resolution, declaring that mar- riage with a deceased wife's sister was neither agaivat the Divine law nor the natural interests of mankind. —Colonel MAICINS moved an amendment ref,rring the matter to a Royal Commission. "If it is a shame to obstruct this proposal," he said, "I glory in the shame." Colonel Mrues Home contended that it was in the interests of the great body of the people that the law should remain as it is. Mr. Edward Clarke, in an earnest and eloquent speech, beard with much attention in a House now crowded, declared himself in favour of the resolution, although, as he said, he had been warned that such a course might be fatal to his political prospects. The debate was continued by Mr. Thomasson, Earl Percy, and Mr. H. Fowler, who protested that his indignation deepened into disgust at the prurient insinuations that defiled the controversy. The minority in the House of Lords might be out-voted again by a clerical caste, but he trusted the House of Commons would by an overwhelming majority declare against the impolicy, the injustice, and the cruelty of the law. Mr. Beresford Hope, rising at half-past twelve, was greeted with loud cries for the division. The right hon. member, nevertheless, delivered at some length a speech against the resolution. Sir Patrick O'Brien renewed the flagging interest of the debate,delivering towards one o'clock in the morning a humorous and much-applauded speech, in which he traced back the history of the controversy to the matrimonial proclivities of Henry VIII. At five minutes past one the House divided, and the motion was carried by 238 against 127. Mr. Gladstone, who had been present during the greater part of the debate, left at midnight. Sir S. Northcote, Sir R. A. Cross, Mr. W. H. Smith, Lord John Manners, and the great body of the Conservative party voted against the resolution. It was supported amongst other Liberals, by Sir Charles Mike, Mr. Chamberlain, Mr. G. Russell, Mr. Trevelyan, Mr. Childers, Mr. Courtney, Mr. Fawcett, and Sir W. Harcourt. There was much cross- voting, but the vast majority of the supporters of the 13il1 were Liberals. The House rose at ten minutes past one. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at 12-40. THE SCOTCH LIQUOR TRAFFIC.

Mr. M'LesLaw moved the second reading of the Liquor Traffic Local Veto (Scotland) Bill, which he stated was framed very much upon the lines of Sir W. Lawson's Per- missive Prohibitory Bill. Public opinion on tha question, he said, was far more advanced in Scotland than in England or Ireland, and what was proposed by this bill WAS to give power to a majority of the ratepayers in any parish or borough to prevent the sale of intoxicating liquors within those areas. He left it to the committee to determine what that majority should be, and he was quite prepared to make lit a large one. What he considered one of the great merits of the bill was thatit would allow a small community num- bering not less than 300 inhabitants to take advantage of its provisions, and there was also a clause to reimburse a man who bad laia out money in structural arrangements t) meet the requirements of the visiting justices —Mr. PARKER moved as an amendment that the House, while fully recog- nising the urgent call far legislation to give to local com- munities effectual control over the drink traffic, did not deem it expedient to proceed with a bill which offered to the ratepayers no other other remedy than total prohibition.— Mr. BAXTER, in seconding the amendment, abstained from making a long speech, because he understood the supporters of the bill desired that it should be. talked out, in order te avoid a division. The measure was impracticable and un- workable, and but for Mr. Parker's amendment he should have moved it rejection.—Mr. Oren-Emma believed that temperance might be promoted by persuasion or example, but not by legislative prohibition. The present bill was open to the additional objection that it made no provision for compensation.—Dr. CAMERON, in supporting the bill, remarked that the compensation it provided was for unex- hausted improvements, precisely on the basis of the com- pensation secured to agricultural tenants.—Mr. COCHRANE- PATRICK said one of his principal objections to the measure was that it introduced a large number of new crimes.—Mr. A. GRANT said the provisions of the bill were far too arbi- trary, and if they became law would defeat their object by their stringency.—Mr. J. A. CAMPBELL could not support the bill. He thought a great deal of good might be done by a reduction in the number of licensed houses.— The LORD ADVOCATE admitted the necessity for legislation on the subject, and that the fact that Scotland had had for thirty years a Sunday Closing Act, which had worked well, was favourable to the prospects of such legislation. The Government must be satisfied that that was the best method of carrying out the object in view. They were not able to assent to a bill which proposed to deal with the question by total prohibition without alternative, and they would, there- fore, give their support to the amendment.—Mr. ANDERSON said he believed the bill would do great harm to the tem- perance cause in Scotland.—Mr. Noel said he would vote for the second reading, but would be content with any bill which would give effectual local control over the liquor traffic.—Sir G. CAMPBELL apprehended that if the local authority were armed with the force of total prohitition, liquor politics would run so high as to overwhelm every- thing else. He intended, however, to vote for the second reading.—Mr. Warton denounced the bill as supremely ridiculous. —Sir W. LAWSON thought that the country, after having waited patiently for so long a time to have effect given to the resolutions which the House had passed on this subject, would feel Some surprise that the Lord Advo- cate had declined to support the principle of a bill which only carried out those resolutions.—Sir A. Gordon opposed the bill.—The House divided, and the numbers were—for the second reading, 85 ; against, 148; majority, 83.

On Mr. Parker's resolution being pet as a substantive motion, Mr, T. Collins moved the adjournment of the debate. —The motion for adjournment was negatived by 113 to 64, but the division having carried the time beyond a quarter to six, and Mr. Warten objecting te. the resolution being taken, the debate was adjourned in accordance with the standing orders._ _ .
The Bankruptcy Frauds and Disabilities (Scotland) Bill was read a second tires, and the House adjourned at six o'clock.
HOUSE OF LORDS.—Twasspey.

The Lord Chancellor took his seat shortly after four o'clock. QUESTIONS.—EarI GRANVILLE, replying to the Earl of Rosebery, said the Government had received no confirmation of the report that a convention had been concluded for the cession of the fortress of Sarakhs to Russia by the Persian Government, and he thought it very likely that some con- fusion had arisen between two Sarakhs. His Lordship told Earl de la Warr that the Government had no further information to give than they had alt-eady given with respect to the position of General Gordon. THE SCOTCH SECRETARY.—The Earl Of DALHOUSIE brought in a bill providing for the appointment of a Secre- tary for Scotland with a seat in Parliament.—The Marquis of SALMI:TRY, while not unfriendly to the object of theUill, thought it would be necessary to scrutinise its details very carefally.—The bill was read a first time. Their Lordships adjourned at half-past five o'clopk. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Thousney.

The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. MiscELLAxitous.—Mr. MUNDELLA announced that the bill on the sale of poisons and patent medicines would be intro- duced in the House of Lords.—Lord E. FITZ MAURICE in- formed Mr. Arnold that the Government were in communi- cation with the Government of Portugal as to the beat means of obtaining the assent of other Powers to the treaty between this country and Portugal with respect to the Cengo.—The PRIME MINISTER repeated the assurance that the House would have full opportunity for discussing the treaty before it was ratified. The right hon. gentleman also stated that the Government did not intend to introduce any subject at tha Conference on Egyptian affairs ex- cept that described in the invitation addressed to the Powers.—Lord E. FITZHAURICE, referring to our commer- cial relations with Spain, said the current session of the Cortes would, owing to the elections' be so short that the agreement with Spain, mentioned in Her Majesty's Speech in February, could not be discussed until the next session of the Cortes. In the meantime the duties on English goods imported either into Spain or her colonies would re- main as at present. The noble lord, replying to Mr. Bourke, stated that the Foreign Office had no confirmation of the re- port that Sarakhs had been acquired by Russia.—The AT- TORNEY-GENERAL explained that orders made at quarter sessions respecting polling districts would be effective until the new register comes into operation on the let of January next. TER NAVY ESTIMATES.—The House went into Committee of Supply on the Navy Estimates, and on the vote of £870,400 for the victualling and clothing of the seamen and marines, M. W. H. &mu referred at considerable length to the changes that were constantly made in a ship during con- struction, and urged in the interest of efficiency and economy that when once the design of a vessel had been settled nothing but a revolution should alter it.—Sir E. REED urged that shins should be built more rapidly than had hitherto been done.—Captain Price, Mr. Macliver, Mr. Gourley, Mr. Rylands and others continued the discussion. —The vote for wages to seamen and marines, and some ether votes, were agreed to.—Progress was reported and the House resumed. CONTAGIOUS DISEASES (ANIMALS) BILL.—OR the Order of the Day for the third reading of this bill, Mr. A. ARNOLD pretested against useless and irritating legislation, and he moved that the bill be read a third time on that day six months.—Mr. BROADHURST declared that if this bill passed at all its title should be a landowner's relief bill.—Mr. CHAPLIN said that in a few years the prices of meat instead of being increased would be lowered.—Mr. SLAG° protested against this most objectionable measure.—Mr. W. JAMES also protested against the third reading of the bill.—The House divided—For the second reading, 124; against, 21- 103. The bill was read a third time. The House adjourned at 1-30.

The party desirous of legalising marriage with a de- ceased wife's sister will, it is stated, forthwith bring a Bill in the House of Lords, which it is hoped will be got back in time to pass through the Commons this session. ALLEGED HOUSEBREAKING AT SUTTON.—At the St. Helens Police Court, on Tuesday, a middle-aged man named John Toner was charged with breaking and entering a dwelling-house at Sutton-heath, occupied by Win. Hewitt, colliery underlooker, and stealing therefrom a silver lever watch, a pair of boots, and a tin cashbox containing £7 odd in money.—lt was stated that the house was entered some- time between Saturday night and Sunday morning, and the articles and money named carried off. The matter was placed in the hands of the police, and the prisoner was on Monday apprehended in Wigan by Police-constable Kendal. He was then wearing the stolen boots, though the missing monoy was not in his possession.—On the application of Superintendent Johnston. the prisoner was remanded for a week.

T. Burgess, Crosfield, Greening, Elutchinson, Franconth, Barker, Ashton, Tinsley, Caldwell, Bolton, Dixon, Litton, Marsti, Tailor; the Clerk (Mr. W. H. Brook), the Deputy Clerk (Mr. .1. L. Whittle), the Borough Surveyor (Mr. Longdin), and the Borough Treasurer (Mr. Chorle7).
THE NEW COUNCILLOR. The Towle CLERK said he had to give notice to the Coun- cil that Mr. Wm. Tinsley had been duly elected Councillor for Latchford Word. THE DEATH OF COUNCILLOR WOOLFALL.

, The MAYOR said that since their last meeting what he might call the remorseless band of death, that never seemed weary of inflicting blows upon them, had removed from their midst one who, up to a very short time ago was ap- parently full of life and activity, and doing his duty as a member of that Council solidly, silently, and efficiently, and without ostentation, and it was their duty that night—ful- filling a custom which had become an old one—of publicly noticing it, and of passing a resolution of condolence with his friends on the loss that they had sustained. He alluded to the late Mr. Councillor Woolfall, who, notwithstanding some ef his personal idiosnycracies, which were, perhaps, sometimes perplexing to understand, he still firmly believed was a living illustration of what Pope meant to convey in that somewhat hackneyed lino of his- - - -

Councillor Buttortss seconded the amendment. ,Councillor GREENING remarked that he had no desire whatever to be deputy-chairruan of the Sanitary Committee. fie had been asked to accept the position, and lie thought,. that Mr. Francomb would not attribute to him any motive of taking the position to prevent any ether gentleman Bitting. In fact, he was not at the time aware of the motion of Mr. Broadbent. If the Council thought fit to appoint Mr. Sutton deputy-chairman he was sure that he should have great pleasure in giving way. Alderman CHANDLEY, in speaking to the minutes, said that it was a very gratifying thing to most of them that the sanitary question had come to the issue that it had. The deputation appeared to have given that matter very great and careful thought and attention, and he thought that the question in regard to the machine proposed to be purchased resolved itself entirely into one of confidence or no con- fidence in the committee.

Alderman BURGESS then amended his proposition, with Councillor Francomb's approval, to the effect that" the minutes of the Sanitary committee be confirmed with the exception of the one under date July 30th, which resolved that Mr. Greening be appointed deputy-chairman of the com- mittee," remarking that the appointment would then rest with the committee.
Councillor GHERICING regretted that this matter had not been mentioned at the meeting of the committee. Councillor Sutton was present and he regretted that he, or some one else, did not mention it.

The Mayon: Of their own merits modest men are dumb. Councillor GRBENING seconded the amended proposition. Alderman CHANDLEY supported the proposition. • Refer- ring to the recommendation re the depot at Longford, that was, he said, so entirely a question of a practical nature that the Council could not be supposed to enter into its mechani- cal merits. It was a question of confidence or no confidence in the judgment of the committee. Councillor BOLTON wished to know what had been the cost of sending deputations to London. He understood that the first deputation cost £24 and sundries. Why was there any need of sending an expensive deputation a second time? He understood that the total amount would come to about £7O, and the machine would cost £220, and he asked if that I was economy? What was the machine, and what was it for? To carry out another series of experiments. ("No.") It said in the report that the deputation recommended the machine so that further experiments might be tried.— (Alderman Burgess: You are wrong.)—Then why was it put In the report? • He thought that before the Council ex- pended any more money at Longford they should provide further particulars about the machine, and that they should have something MOND satisfactory than a further series of experiments. It was all very well to talk about an income el £3,000. Ile should move that the recommendation be withdrawn from the minutes, as, with the present rate, he thought it was time they began to think before they ex- pended any more money in experiments. Councillor BARKER seconded the amendment, and re- marked that he should like to include the withdrawal of the recommendation of the purchase of land also. Councillor BOLTON: I BM take that in too, then. (Laugh- ter.) Anything in connection with the Sanitary Committee

. - I have great doubts about. Councillor BARKER did net think that the field proposed to be purchased was required. It was to cost £3OO, and then there was the elevation and p tving of the road. After two deputations had been at Lon-don three or four days each week—(a voice: "Question.")—he thought they should have a better description et the machine than was the case. He would suggest that the Borough Surveyor be invited to try before the committee a plan of a drying machine which would meet the requirements at Longford. Councillor PLATT, referring to the working of the ma- chine proposed to be purchased, said that it would deal with 12 tons of crude manure in a week, whereas they had 130 tons to deal with in that time, so that they would really require 11 machines. Alderman BURGESS explained that Councillor Platt had somewhat misunderstood the report, and Councillor PLATT remarked that he thought the report was apt to mislead the Council.

Councillor CROSFIELD : The experiment was one really to see what the effect would be on the material in its crude state. Councillor FRANCOMB said that the machine was so simple i and seemed to do the work so satisfactorily that he had no hesitation in supporting its purchase. It was to try to gain information that they had gone to London and other places, and a body of gentlemen who had to conduct the affairs of the town should not sit there to grumble. It was not right to waste the time of the Sanitary Committee by a sort of dog in the manger style, for it was nothing less. Those who knew nothing about it blackguarded them, and would not try to find it out. Councillor BOLTON : That is not correct ; we have tried to find it out. Councillor BARKER: I must ask Mr. Francomb to recall those words. I have been to several places my- self. Councillor FRANCOMB said that he would withdraw any word that was objected to, but he thought that it was wrong lobe continually grumbling at a thing without offering anything better iu its stead. With the stove they had no means of keeping the smell within reasonable bounds, but if they had the machine they would certainly have some- thing that would enable them to get rid of the smell with- out it being a nuisance to anyone. Councillor BURGESS said that he was not surprised that Mr. Bolton and Mr. Platt should make some mistakes, but he was certainly surprised that Mr. Barker, who was a mem- ber of the committee, and who knew, he supposed, what the deputations went for, should have made the remarks that he did. It seemed to him (Councillor Burgess) from the printed reports that the committee never dreamt in the first instance of trying whether the dryer would be useful in dealing with the raw material. He though that it would be well to have the machine and see if it would not de the work required at Longford. Alderman PICEMERE observed that Councillor Bolton evi- dently knew more about the matter than the members of the committee did themselves, and that they had better make him (Councillor Balton) a member of the committee. He (Alderman Pickmere) wished to see whether the expendi- ture of the town could not be reduced by a machine which would do more and better work than the one they had at Longford. The machine was cheap, easily put up, and the application simple. The stove was done away with, and the , material well dried and made into a marketable commodity. ' He was certain that the Council and the town would ue in- debted to the committee if they would allow them to ' have one of those machines and to make experiments with it. Alderman WEBSTER said that the Council had appointed the committee to do certain work, and he thought that the thanks of the Coancil were due to the Committee for the time and trouble that they had spent in trying to solve this sanitary question. He did not understand the machinery himself, but according to the statements made by the com- mittee, in whom he trad every confidence, it would ac- complish what was desired ,with the preparation of the manure. They must also hear iR mind that the whole thing was an experiment, without which they could not get infor- mation. The committee did the best that they could, and he thought that if the Council had confidence in the commit- tee they were hound to support the recommendrions. Councillor Cnosrmn said that in the first place he ' would like to say he objected to Councillor Bolton's remarks about the deputation. He (Mr. Crosfield) thought the Council ad the town were very much indebted to the gentlemen who went on a deputation on such business as that. He knew he would have given a good deal of money rather than have gone, and he did not think it was kind or Proper to find fault with the deputation when they did their duty by going on disagreeable business. Ile could under stand Mr. Councillor Barker's reasons for objecting, because they knew that he had a pet scheme of his own. He (Mr. Barker) believed in hot air rather than steam. Councillor BARKER: I have no pet scheme of my own. The scheme I propose is not my own invention at all. Councillor CROSFIELD: I think I may say that you be- lieve in hot air rather than in steam? Councillor BARKER: I do not oppose this scheme for the sake of that. Councillor CROSFIELD, continuing, said the machine in question did its work by means of hot steam, and that he believed to be decidedly the best. The first interest con- nected with Longford was the getting rid of the naisance, because the place was liable to be stopped almost at any time. They had no business to make a nuisance, and the great advantage of that machine of Johnson's was that it secured the object that the committee had in view of doing away with the nuisance. Re did hope that the Council would have confidence in their committee in what they had done, and that they would allow them without hesitation to i try that machine. The expense was not great compara- tively, and without an experiment was made Rothing would I ever be known. - _ - _

Alderman HotarEs said it seemed to him entirely out of the question to discuss the merits of the mlchinery, and it w.is simply a question of whether or not they had confidence in the committee. From a rough examination of the accounts he thought there would be a saving of at least £l,OOO a year, and advocated the carrying out of the scheme. Councillor CALDwELL also supported the original motion. Councillor GREENING did not think that Mr. Bolton or Mr. Barker had any desire to thwart the success of the busi- ness, but he did think that on this occasion they were mis- taken. He did not think that anything would be gained if ' the amendment were passed. Alderman Kean and Councillor Hutchinson having spoken in favour of the purchase, Alderman BURCH'S% referring to the remarks of Councillor , Bolton, said that he wished Mr. Bolton to understand that he (Alderman Burgess) expected to be of as much service to the town in the saving of money as Mr. Bolton. He bad a great aversion to spending the ratepayers money upon himself, and it had been no treat to him'to go to London. He thought that the efforts of the Sanitary Committee should have been spoken of in a different manner. The amendment was then put as follows and lost, viz.: —'That the minutes of the Sanitary Committee be con- firmed with the exception of the minute of the 30th April, having reference to the purchase of one ef Johnson's patent drying machines; and the minute of the '24th March, hav- ing reference to the purchase of a plot of land from Mr. Samuel Broadhurst. The motion for the confirmation of the minutes was then put and carried, the one relating to the appointment of Councillor Greening as deputy-chairman being withdrawn. TOWN HALL, PARE, AND RATES COMMITTEE. The MAYOR moved, and Alderman PIONMSRE seconded, the confirmation of the minutes of this committee. he Councillor LITTON moved as an amendment that the minutes be accepted with the exception of the following resolution 1—" That the borough surveyor be requested to

'mewl., a plan and estimate of an extension of the present carriageway at the front of the Town Hall, so as to make a circular walk, the present moand being levelled, the w.II to , S tokey-street removed, and an ornamental palisade on atone ba.s in lieu thereof." lie did not think the committee {Vert. justified at the present Ulna in incurring any duel, ex- , pense as would be entailed. Councillor PLarr seconded the amendment; he did not think they were at present called upon to spend money in improving a place that was very nice as it was. Councillor BURGESS said that he thought it would be a great improvement and he should vote for the minutes. He thought it would relieve the difficulty of the crowded state of Sankey-street. Councillor Bovrow said that he should oppose it on the ground that there were no estimates in. Councillors CALD WELL and GREENING also supported the amendment.

The MAYOR explained that all that was asked for was a plan and estimate that would be submitted to the committee and to the Council, and pointed out that the Council would not by accepting the resolution be committing themselves to any expense. Alderman HOLMES observed that if the committee wished to get plans and so forth they intended to proceed with the matter in the long run. _ _

Councillor CR—OSFIELD thought that the Borough Sur- veyor's time could be better occupied. Alderman WEBSTER and Alderman BURGESS also sup- ported the amendment. Alderman PICEMERE : I think with such a concensus of opinion on this question we had better withdraw it. The MAYOR: Certainly the wall that exists at present is exquisitely pretty. It is quite festhetic. (Laughter.) I will at once proceed to put the amendment. The amendment was then carried, the remainder of the business of the committee being confirmed.
