div.head: EGYPT AND TIIE SOUDAN. REPORTED SURRENDER OF BERBER
div.p: EGYPT AND TIIE SOUDAN. REPORTED SURRENDER OF BERBER

Canto, Mow Dear.—l have heard to-day from private sources that Berber was surrendered last week to two Wekeels, or repreeentatives of the Mandi. One of these was the Sheikh Bonago, who it may be remembered, accom- panied Hicks Pasha to Kordofan, and was wounded and taken prisoner at the time of Hicks's disastrous defeat. The other of the Mandi's lieutenants was Zazuli Bey, the late Sub-Governor of Khartoum, who, on being dismissed by General Gordon, joined the Mandi at Obeid. Col. Fraser, of the Egyptian areal., left for England to-day to confer with the home authorities as to the fature of that force. The Egyptian Government are making strenuous efforts to raise a small loan to meet their immediate needs, and have applied to the Anglo-Egyptian Bank, but the securities offered are not solid enough, and the bank is indisposed to lend.— ...Standard. CAIRO, MOM:MT.—Colonel Stuart Wortley and Majors Kitchener and Rundle, of the Egyptian army, who have been ordered to proceed up the Nile on a reconnoitering ex- pedition, will be escorted along the banks by several Bedeuin Sheikhs and their tribes, in order to keep communications open between Assouan and Dongola. Assonme, SUNDA.Y.—NearIy 2,000 refugees have already reached this place from Kerosko, and more are daily ar- riving. The evacuation is proceeding satisfactorily under the control of Colonel Duncan, of the Egyptian Army. Those who left Khartoum prior to the investment by the MandPs followers are very shortly expected to reach Egypt proper. NEW PROPOSAL TO RELIEVE GENERAL GORDON. PARIS, WiDRRSDAY.—The Gatelois of to-day mentions a report that, in consequence of a request received from Eng- land. the Belgian Government is disposed to use the re- sources of the African Association for the relief of General Gordon; and it is farther reported that the-Government will instruct Mr. Stanley to proceed with a strong force by way of the Congo to meet the General, and that he will advance as far as the vicinity of Gondokoro. CAIRO, WEDNESDAY NionT.—An officer lately arrived from Assouan reports that the natives there are very uneasy on account of the unsettled state of the English policy. They consider that if the English troops be not sent they will not be sufficiently secure to remain with Egyptian troops only in the garrison, as they regard the latter as utterly unreli- I able. An employe of a merchant has arrived here to-day from Khartoum. He was twenty-five days en route. He Says that General Gordon has cut a trench between the Government residency and the town. The disaffected re- main in the latter.—Daily News.

THE PROPOSED CONFERENCE. PARIS, SATURDAY. The Journal dei Debuts publishes an article approving M. Ferry's attitude in regard to the British proposal for a Conference, and says it was difficult not to accept the principle of the proposal a priori, " for the English, our friends of yesterday, will also be our friends to-morrow; but it is essential that all misunderstanding should be removed beforehand. If a result is to be obtained everything should be settled between the interested parties, and the Conference should only haveto confirm the arrange- ments previously agreed upon in general terms. It is, therefore, necessary that England should make known all her intentions." ATHENS, PIIESDAY EvEsmeo —lntelligenco received here from Constantinople states that the Porte has not vet re- plied to Lord Dufferin's comrannication concerning the pro- posed Conference, and that great uncertainty prevails in the Turkish capital regarding the attitude of France, Russia, and Turkey in the question. VARNA, WEDNESDAY.—The Turkish Council of Ministers met on Sunday to consider the action of the Porte in refer- ence to the Egyptian Conference. It was decided that as nearly all the other Powers had agreed to England's pro- posal it would be expedient for Turkey to accept it in prin- ciple. It was resolved, however, to add, as conditions, that the Sultan's political and territorial rights should be reserved, and that no question of a proctectorate or annexation by any Power alone or with other Powers should he entered upon. A report in this sense was sent to the Palace, and awaits confirmation by the Sultan. Probably this will be obtained and a reply sent lathe above terms.

THE UNITED STATES. NEW Your, Skrunnev.—The Norwegian ship Alantine, of Drammen, has been wrecked off Magdalen Island. Nme- teen persons perished, the second mate being the only sur- vivor. Forest fires have occurred in the States of New York, New Jersey, and Pennsylvania. A great fire is raging fiercely in the Pennsylvania coal district. The town of Brishin has been entirely destroyed, and three thousand people have been rendered homeless. Several persons have perished. NEW YORK, SENDAY.—An explosion has occurred on board the steamship Gouverneur in this port, causing the death of five men.
TILE NEVADA-ROMANO COLLISION IN .THE
ATLANTIC.

The latest accounts received at New York regarding the collision between the Nevada and the Romano are conflict- ing as regards the date of the disaster. It appears. how- ever, that the collision occurred at noon, in latitude 42°, longitude 47°, the Nevada striking the Romano on the port side, abaft midships, and bursting into her engine room. The Romano sank in less than an hour. Calm weather pre- vailed at the time of the disaster. The Nevada sustained considerable damage by the collision. One cmipartment was fell of water, and her bows were stove in from the forefoot to the deck. She fell in with the St. Laurent last Sunday. The Nevada had on board four saloon, five inter- mediate, and fifteen steerage passengers. Mr. Seow, one of the passengers by the Raman°, remained on board ths Nevada.

div.head: CONVICTION OF AMERICAN DYNAMITERS.
div.p: CONVICTION OF AMERICAN DYNAMITERS.

. - - HALIFAX, WEDNESDAY.—Two Americans, whe were ar- rested here eight months ago with dynamite and infernal machines in their luggage, have been tried and found guilty of having dangerous explosives in their possession. To-day they were sentenced to six months' imprisenment. They pretended to be miners, but gave ne satisfactory ac- count of themselves. When they were arrested there were a number of British war vessels in the harbour, including the Canada, with Prince George on board. It was thought they had designs on them. RUSSIA.—NIHILIST ARRESTS. Manus. MONDAY.—Notwithstanding the present unusual quietude of the Revolutionary party in Russia. Nihilist ar- rests continue to be of frequent occurrence. Many arrests were made by the police in several towns at the end of last month, among them being four artillery officers at Nov- gorod, who, after their apprehension, were taken to St. Petersburg, and imprisoned in the fortress. The numerous arrests lately made among the artillery officers are connected with the murder of Colonel Soudaikin, the assassin Degaieff having formerly belonged to that arm of the service. Several more stuednts have been arrested at Moscow, on which oc- casion the police discovered the first number of a new So- cialist paper, bearing the title of Studentcheski Sbnornik, printed by hectograph at St. Petersburgh. Important ar- rests have been made in the persons of the Secretary of the Board of Justices of the Peace, in whose possession many compromising papers were found, and of a Polish lady, one of the mistresses of the Bestusheff Educational Establish- ment for Women. RUSSIA AND CHINA.

ST. PETIMSBI7IIG, WEDNESDAV.—The Turkestan Gazette states that the Chinese authorities in Kashgar are prevent- ing Russian Massulmans from trading in any of the towns of Eastern Turkestan except Kashgar, in violation of the existing Russo-Chinese Treaty. It is expected that the Russian Minister of Foreign Affairs- will make representa- tions on the subject. ZULULAND.
DURBAN, MONDAY.—A strong force of Usutas, sent by Unanyamana against Obam, has been defeated by the latter with heavy loss.
'.THE CAPE MINISTRY.
CAPE Tows, WEDNESDAY —The Ministry have resigned, in consequence of their recent defeat in the Rouse of Assembly. GERMANY.—SERIOUS ILLNESS OF TEIE

div.head: EMPRESS.
div.p: EMPRESS.

BERLIN, MONDAY.—The Boursen Courier says that de- spite the semi-official reports, the condition of the Empress has undergone a change for the worse, and gives occasion for grave apprehension. Yesterday prayers were off red up ía the Domkirche for Her Majesty's recovery. FRANCE AND CHINA. SHANGHAI, Tourasney.—Li Hung Chang has been in- vested with fall powers to deal with the whole Aunam ques- tion. Shut Sing Chen has been appointed Minister to France, and Ma Kien Chung Vice-Minister.

div.head: SERIOUS PANIC IN A CHURCH.
div.p: SERIOUS PANIC IN A CHURCH.

TRIESTE, THURSDAY—WhiIe the special devotions for the month of May were being celebrated yesterday evening in the chapel of St. Anthony, in this city, the decorations of the altar caught fire, causing a terrible panic among the female portion of the congregation. In the rush for the doors which ensued, several persons were seriously injured. A MANIFESTO BY PRINCE NAPOLEON. PARIS, THURSDAL—Prince Napoleon has written a letter in reply to several of his partisans, who have requested him to put an end to any misunderstanding on the subject of Prince Victor's position. The Prince states that his son having already declared his feelings of respect and submis- sisn towards him, it is superfluous to interrogate the young Prince any further on the subject. Prince Napoleon coun- sels his partisans to treat with contempt the allegations of adversaries, and states that his name does not represent one I form of Government exclusively.

div.head: CROFT.
div.p: CROFT.

A REMARKABLE DIICK.—Mr. Charles Wild, farmer, of Heath-lane, Croft, has an Irish duck which laid an egg every morning for a month, and than desired to sit. Eleven duck eggs were placed under her, out of which she hatched eleven ducklings. When they were a week old she com- menced laying again, and bas now been laying over a fort- night without retssing a single day. SUDDEN DEATH.—A man named Peter Hankinson, aged 69 years, a fustian cutter residing at Stone* Platt Cottages, Croft, died rather suddenly on Wednesday morning, about eight o'clock. It appears that the deceased bad been un- well since the Thursday previous, but would not consent to have a doctor. It seems that he had been up in the early part of Wednesday morniug, and had gone to bed again. A little before oi.zht o'clock he got out of bed to give his wife some money, as she was going to fetch 3 doctor. when he ei denly fell on the room floor, and expired. The coroner lad,l been communicated with.

div.head: An honest man's the noblest work of God.
div.p: An honest man's the noblest work of God.

He (the Mayor) believed their old friend, Mr. Woolfall, was an honest man, for he did not think hie integrity was as- sailable, and he did not think that he (the deceased) could have been bribed to swerve in the least degree from what he believed to be the truth. As a public man Mr. Woolfall was always ready and willing to perform any duty that was put upon him, some of them only incidental to his office and duties, which woull have had few attractions for any of them. As auditor of their municipal accounts be was in- valuable. As they knew, he spardd no pains to effectually discharge the duties of auditor, and in that respect he was almost indispensable. He (the Mayor) hoped he should not lay himself open to a charge of undue lev;ty if hesaid that be I did not think the adventurous gold digger was ever more I delighted to discover Ja valuable nugget than was their friend, Mr. Woolfall, to discover an inaccuracy, and in that respect it was of no moment who committed the error so long as be succeeded in discovering it. He (the Mayor) thought Dryden said in one of his prologues— Errors like straws upon the surface flow, He who would search for pearls must dive below. He (the Mayor) thought the very worst of their poor friend lay upon the surface, whilst in the depths, so to speak, there was a whole heart with plenty of sympathy. loyalty, and devotion towards those who had the tact to win his friendship and secure his confidence, and as for those who did not—amongst whom he (the Mayor) was afraid he must class himself—it was their duty to remember, and if their Christianity was werthy the name, it should teach them that the grave should bury every error, cover every defect, and extinguish ever particle of ill-feeling. He then moved the resolution—" That this Council receives with deep re- gret the announcement of the death of Mr. John Woolfall, one of the Councillors for this borough, which took place on the 9th April, and desires to express its appreciation of the valuable services rendered by him to the borough during a period of thirteen years." The resolution was unanimously carried. THE VOTES OF CONDOLENCE.

The MAYOR reported that be had received letters from the Secretary of State and Mr. Collins, acknowledging the re- ceipt of the addresses of condolence to Her Majesty and the Duchess of Albany, on the occasion of the death of His Royal Highness Prince Leopold. SANITARY COIDd ITTEE.—THE DEPOT AT LONGFORD.

Alderman BURGESS moved the adoption of the minutes of this committee. There were, he said, two or three matters referred to in the minutes which were of considerable im- portance, and he asked the serious attention of the Council to them. The first was the minute that referred to the purchase of a plot of land in Winwick-road, in front of the land that the Corporation now owned, and on which the manure depot was erected, for the sum of £3OO. The land would be required for the purpose of constructing an eleva- ted roadway to the works and, inasmuch as Mr. Broadhurst, to whom the land belonged, was in a delicate state of health, the committee thought it wise to take the matter in hand ' while Mr. Broadhurst could deal with it. The committee were of opinion that Mr. Broadhurst had met them in a proper manner, and that the price asked was a very reason- able one when it was considered that the land was a piece that fronted the road, and which would probably be of con- siderable value some day. Another serious consideration, if they desired to build upon the land, was that the road was already made, and the committee thought it would be to the interests of the town that it should be acquired. The Council would also have observed that deputations had been to Belvedere for the purpose of watching the experi- mental draining of material that was sent from Longford, in a pan or pot belonging to Mr. Johnson, of Belvedere. The reason why the committee took this course was simply from the fact that while they were satisfied themselves that their process of evaporation was correct, they were desirous of finding some process by which the stove, which would form a part of the new arrangement should be got rid of. At present the work was carried on through the instrumentality of a vacuum pan with a Firman's dryer, and in the proposed new works it was intended that there should be added to that what was called a stove, a heated chamber to which the material should be transferred, and there finish its Idraining process by the natural action of the heat within the heated chamber. They were satisfied that so far as the vacuum pan and the Firman's dryer were concerned that the material in its drying process could not escape into the atmosphere. But when the material had had say 70 per cent, perhaps of its moisture taken from it, there was yet a considerable per centage that had to be drained, and it was impossible hermetically to seal up a chamber such as he was speaking`of, and he himself had always had a misgiving as to what might be the consequence of the finishing in that stove. Their object in goieg to Belvedere was to see whether the arrangement of Mr. Johnson would enable them to dispense with the stove and adopt his plan in lieU of it, for so far as the finishing process was concerned they were satisfied that the stove might be and must be dispensed with, and that when the operation went on through the Firman's dryer into the Johnson's patent instead of into the stove, the finishing was done in a less space of time, and he believed at a less cost. They were perfectly satis- fied as a committee that this machine ef Mr. Johnson's would do the work that they required, so far as the finishing process was concerned, but it bad occurred to them that by having a machine on their own premises they could work on the experiments for them- selves. It was worth the effort to see If they could not conduct the whole operation through the instrumentality of the vacuum pan and from that transferred and finished by the Johnson's pan. If so, the plan would be simplified and the cost considefiblV re- duced. They thought that it would be wise to take a tenta- tive course and ask the Council to let them have this dryer, which was to cost £220, and if they could dispense with the Firman's dryer the cost would be considerably reduced. The cost of the scheme which was at first adopted, and he (Alderman Burgess) asked the Council to allow them to adopt, was £4,685. When he asked the Council to withdraw that he ventured to foreshadow the possibility from the further experieace that they had had in the working of the present plan, that they might reduce that amount, and the result of an inquiry into the matter was that an amended estimate was received, reducing the amount to £3 469. If the Council allowed them to have the machine he was speak- ing of there would be a very large reduction on that amount of £3,469. The question really amounted to this, that they we-e collecting material in Warrington and con- veying it to Longford, which, when evaporated and dried, would give them at least nine tons of powder in the week. They were selling that material with the utmost ease at from £6 to £7 a too. About £6 108 a ton uas the price that it was realising, and they had a demand greater than the supply. If they reckoned the number of tons at £6 10s per run it would give an income of nearly £3OOO a year, and he had not the slightest hesitation in saying that that would be their income from that material with the present population of Warrington, and with the growth of the popu- lation there would be a proportionate growth of the material that they had to build upon. They were not also without hope that as time went on and the demand increased they would get some slight advance. What the committee were i proposing to do would admit of a great deal more work being done than they had to do at the present time. The cost of the collection of the material—£4,ooo—was very heavy, but they would be surprised to find that in Birming- ham the cost of collecting on the old system was more than the cost in Warrington. Whatever system they had the removal must take place, and it could not be done without the expenditure of a lot of money, although he was not without hope that when the thing WAS got into working shape the cost of Collecting might be reduced. The only question was bow to deal with these matters with the most rigid economy. The committee asked that the machine should be perchased for £220, which, with carriage and fitting, would make about £250. They would have to have this pan if not for this purpose, and what the committee said was "let it come now, and the experiments we can make with it may lead to a reduction of the cost in other things." The question had occupied the Council and the committee to the prejudice of Other work that shotfid have received attention, and he hoped that they might now get the matter disposed of, and go on with other descriptions of work that urgently called for attention. If the Council had confidenee enough in the committee, who were satisfied that what they had before them did not require any further consideration, the com- mittee asked that the minutes should be confirmed. ,

Councillor -GREENING seconded.' Councillor FmkNoomn proposed an amendment to the minutes to the effect that the resolution making Councillor Greening the deputy-chairman of the committee should be deferred. He found that Councillor Broadbent had got a resolution on the minutes to make the chairmen and vice- chairmen of committees members of the General Purposesl Committee. Mr. Greening was already a vice-chairman of the Finance Committee, and therefore had got a seat on the committee, or would have one, and he (Mr. Francomb) found that Councillor Sutton had been a member of the Council since 1874, and Mr. Greening only since 1880. Mr. Sutton had also been a member of the Sanitary Committee for many years, and Mr. Greening only for a few months. He thought it was unfair to pass over time after time one who had saved so long as Mr. Sutton had.

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

The proceedings of the following committees, which con: tamed no items of interest to the public, were passed. :—Water Committee, on the motion of the Mayor, se- conded by Alderman Pickmere; Finance Committee, on the motion of Alderman Holmes, seconded by Councillor Green- ing; Street Improvement and Lighting Committee, on the motion of Councillor Platt, seconded by Councillor Barker; Paving and Sewerage Committee, on the motion of Alderman Kean, seconded by Councillor Taylor; School Attendance Committee, on the motion of Alderman Web- ster, seconded by Councillor Caldwell; Museum, Library, and Arts Committee, on the motion of Alderman Webster, seconded by Councillor Burgess; Cemetery Committee, on the motion of Alderman Kean, seconded by Councillor Hutchinson ; Markets Committee, on the motion of Alder- man Chandley, seconded by Councillor Taylor; Gas Com- mittee, on the motion of Alderman Holmes, seconded by Alderman Webster; Fire Engine Committee, on the motion of Alderman Pickmere, seconded by Councillor Burgess ; and General Purposes Committee, on the motion of the Mayor, seconded by Alderman Pickmere.
THE GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE AND ITS WORK.-A DEADLOCK. _ _

The MAYOR, in the absence of Mr. Broadbent, moved the following motion, of which Mr. Broadbent had given notice, namely:—" That the following resolution of the Council of the 9th November, 1883, be rescinded, namely: That the General Purposes Committee consist of the Mayor, Deputy-Mayor, every member of:the Council who has held the office of Mayor, and the chairman of the several com- mittees being members of the Council.' And that the fol- lowing resolution be substituted in lieu thereof:—' That the Mayor, Deputy-Mayor, every member of the Council who has held the office of Mayor, and the chairman and deputy- chairman of the several committees being members of the Council be appointed the General Purposes Committee for the purposes set forth in the minutes of the Council of the I 9th November, 1883.'" He (the Mayor) had great pleasure in moving that resolution becand experience had shown them that the present state of the General Purposes Com- mittee was lamentably defective. Alderman BURGESS thought it would be more expelient and more orderly to move the motion rescinding the reso- lution of the 9th November. 1883, first. Councillor Ptarr said he would second the proposal of the Mayor. Councillor BURGESS: In what respect is the General Pur- poses Committee lamentably defective ? The MAYOR: Because we can only get very poor attend- ances, and sometimes when very important questions come before the General Purposes Committee and there is only a small attendance there is a great relucLance to deal with such questions. . .

Councillor Bmanass moved as an amendment to the re- solution, that the last part of it read, "That the whole of the members of the Council be appointed the General Pur- poses Committee." (Hear. hear.) The Mayon: You cannot do it; you have given no notice of your intention. Councillor BURGESS said he should certainly vote against the resolution because he thought it was undesirable to have a committee which contained more than half the members of the Council unless this committee contained all the members. A committee that contained more than half the members could bring forward their minutes and the Council could discuss them but they were in the position that the members of the committee were almost sure to vote in favour of their minutes, and the other membera of the Council were not sufficiently numerous to reject these minutes.

Councillor FRANCOMB ihked, since the small committee composed of aldermen had refused to do what was expected of them, Why they should net have a committee of other members of the Council. Ile thought it would be a pity if the members of one committee should come into the Council and do what they liked. He did not see why they should make a hard and fast line as to the membership of that committee. He should certainly vote against the resolu- tion.

Councillor Dans said he should also vote against the reso- lution. All of them, be added, knew what was the result of having a committee containing more than half the members of the Council. The MAYOR then intimated that he would move the first part of the above resolution separately, namely that the resolution of the 9th November be rescinded. Alderman Humus seconded. Councillor BURGESS objected to the two parts of the resolution being put separately, but the Town Clerk having stated that it was perfectly in order to do so, the first resolution was put and carried without opposition. On the second resolution, to re-appoint the General Purposes Com- mittee with the addition of the deputy-chairmen of the several committe-s being put, however, a considerable number of members stood up in opposition.

The MAYou declared that this part of the original motion had been negatived by four votes. Alderman BURGESS: Now you have no General Purposes Committee. (Laughter.) Councillor PLATT: What can von do without a General Purposes Committee? The MAYOU: We shall have to do the best we con. (Laughter.) We sholl have to call a special meeting to appoint a committee. WORK FOR THE NEW COUNCILLOR.
On the respective motions of the Mayor, Alderman Ghana- ley, and Alderman Holmes, Mr. Councillor Tinsley was appointed to be a reelpber of the Watch, the Markets, and the Finance Commi..
THE DEFUNCT COMMITTER.
The MAYOR intimated that the Town Clerk was of opinion that the re-appointment of a General Purposes Committee was one of those things which should be disposed of at that

_ Councillor Purr said that although the Mayor had ruled it to be in order that the Council then proceed to appoint a General Purposes Committee, he thought a matter of that importance ought not to be gone on with without notice. Mans' members had gone away not knowing anything ef that kind would come before the Council, and' he (Mr. Platt) thoaght it would be hardly fair to them or to the Council as a whole, that a portion of the Council should have the op- portunity of deciding upon that matter. He should very much prefer a special meeting of the Council to be held, as the Council was not there represented as a whole. The MILYOR did not think it was any excuse that gentle- men had left the Council before business was disposed of. They had nothing to complain of. Alderman BURGESS: But still this must be considered somewhat of a surprise after all. I think with Councillor Platt that nothing will be lost, and we may gain something by haying a special meeting. The M4YOR : Very well; I have no feeling in the matter. I only thought of saving you some trouble. Councillor DIXON thought that because other people had left the Council was no reason why they should not go on with that business. The MAYOR (leaving his chair): It is all over now. The meeting then ended.

He was a greater hoped the institution would go on and prosper, and that at some future time they would have a second cottage hospi- tal in some other part of the town. Plans and specifications had been prepared, and tenders were being obtained for the extension.—Mr. Laokland responded on behalf of the col- lectors.—" The clergy of all denominations "was proposed by Major Ogle, and was responded to by the Rev. div.head: 31ANCITESTER SHIP CANAL
div.p: THE 31ANCITESTER SHIP CANAL

On Monday, Mr. T. D. Hamby, chairman of the Mersey Dock Beard, was examined. Mr. Hornbv said the Dock estatl was administered solely in the interests of trade. He mentioned the reductiom in rates made in ruceut years, and expressed a hope that the Board would be able to make still farther reductions, all that they desired being to pay interest on the bonds and to make their creditors secure. He did not consider that the charges made were at all ex- orbitant. The Dock Board felt compelled to oppose the bill in order to protect the safety of Liverpool as a port, for the prosperity of Lancashire depended upon the ,maintenance of the Mersey. They thought that the safety of Liverpool ought not to be staked on the success of such an experi- ment as this. But for their fears as to the estuary, he did not suppose that the Dock Board would greatly dread the making of a Ship Canal: They had not, however, con- sidered the commercial question eutliciently for him to ex- press an opinion upon it—Captain Kennedy, who had been a master in the service of the Ininun Company for twenty years, and had crossed the Atlantic 540 times, was nest called to Bbow that the canal would not be navigable for large steamers, and would be dangerous for shipping generally. On Tuesday Captain Inglis, matine surveyor to the Cunard Steamship Company, was examined in support of the Liverpool case, and he declared himself oi opinion that the proposed channel would he dangerous to shipping. Captain French, one of the Board of Trade assessors, gave evidence in the same behalf. He said he believed that only paddle-boats of 250 tons would he able to navigate the chan- nel. The promoters might get an ocean-going steamer up the canal by way of exhibition, but they cuuld not carry on such navigation. Rear-Admiral Dancombe Grant and Com- mander Philips, R.N., were afterwards called by the Mersey Dock Board. The latter witnese, who was from 1873 to 1875 in command of the coastguard ship stationed in the Mersey. said an accident in the channel on a falling tide would be very serious, and the vessel would be almost certain to get across the walls and Po come to grief. The evidence of a Liverpool pilot closed the case of the Dock Board, and council for the Shropshire Union Reilway Com- pany then addressed the committee, and in doing, so ad- mitted that that company's opposition was really that of tbe London and North-Western Railway Company. On Wednesday, Mr. Dngdale, Q.C., continuing his address on behalf of the Shropshire Union Railway and Canal Com- pany, the owners of Ellesmere Port, submitted that the pro- moters in taking samples of the waters of the Mersey for the purpose of analysis had committed the mistake of deal- ing with the ebb instead of the flood, when the current was not on'y strong but largely impregnated with matter in sus- pension. The consequence was that their tables showed that more detritus was carried out than came in with the tide. The fact was that if a proper analysis had been made it would have been found that one-third more sand came in with the tide than went out. With regard to the capital proposed to be raised, he submitted that there was nis reasonable probability that it will be subscribed.—Mr. G. R. Jebb, C.E., who was then examined by Mr. Lankester, said be was the engineer to the Shropshire Union Railway and Canal Company. During the last 15 years he had made observations of the channels of the Mersey. Ira 1872, the level of the sand- banks opposite Ellesmere Port were nearly 15ft. above the level of the old dock sill at Liverpool. and at that time the channel was gradually changing its direction. If the pro- posed subsidiary channel now used by the Shropshire Union and Canal Company to silt lap, and thus interfere with the entrances to Ellesmere Port.—Mr. Vaughan, general manager of the 31illom Hematite Works, Cumberland, also gave evi- dence against the bill, stating that it was important in the interests of the iron trade that Ellesmere Port should be kept open.

On Thursday the evidence was given by Mr. Hale the traffic manager of the Shropshire Union Railway and Hale, Company, who in reply to Lord Loyal, admitted that it would be an advantage to have a broad channel at Elea- mere Port, but his company were afraid that the Ship Canal Company would be unable to maintain the channel, and that silting up would take place in the estaary.—Mr. T. H. Jackson, chairman of the Liverpool Steamship Owners' Aasociation, and a member of the Birkenhead Corporation, said there would be great risk of large vessels, navigating the proposed low water channel, getting on to the training walls. The risks would be great in calm weather, and very great in stormy weather and fogs. If the proposed estuary works silted up the entrance to the Birkenhead Docks, as had been suggested by the engineering evidence, Birkenhead would be ruined. If the canal were made, and one of his vessels was chartered with a cargo for Manchester, he would rather pay the railway freight from Liverpool to Manchester out of his own pocket than allow his vessel to try and navigate the canal.

A StrtiDAY Nionr's DISTunniNCE. At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday last; Robert Richardson, a farmer at Tarbock, was summoned for a breach of the peace at Tarbock, on the 20th April; and he was also summoned for assaulting George Brunt, Mary Boyne, and Mary Ann Beesley, on the same date.—The defendant, for whom Mr. Swift, of St. Helens appeared, pleaded not guilty in eack case.—From the evidence of P.C. Rutherford, it appeared that the defendant was interrupting several persons passing along the highway near Hough Green station, and he threatened to throw them over the hedge if it cost hint £3O. Witness spoke to the defendant about it, and the de- fendant said he was only doing it for a "joke."—The com- plainants in the various cases were then called, and thew deposed that the defendant had seizod them and threatened to throw them over the hedge.—Mr. Swift, on behalf of the defendant, submitted that the case was a trumpery squabble) between two or three persons who had two or three words, and to bring it there was a most farcicial proceediog.—Two witnesses were called, after which the defendant Richardson said as he was walking along the road the man Brunt pulled his (defendant's) coat acd told him to more along; whereupon he (defendant) simply said he would not be ordereel on by such a man as he (Brunt) adding that if he did it again he would throw him over the hedge. He denied that he had assaulted the complainants or that bewas. ia any 'my disorderly.—The Chairman said there was no doubt the defendant did net enjoy the best of chamfers in that neighbourhood, and he would be bound over to keep the peace for three months. The charges of assault would , be dismissed. Summons CHARACTERS AT TARBOCB RACES.—Before F: W. Earle and Captain Willis, at the Presc,ot Petty Sessions, on Inesday, Joseph Crook, a stranger, was brought up for attempting to pick pockets at Tarbock races on the 23rd ult.—On the date named George Malpass, a joiner, residing at Woolton, attended the races at Tarbock, and while them caught the prisoner's hand in his pocket. Malpass told the prisoner that he would give him into custody, whereupon he was "set upou " by a gang of roughs who severely struck him and kicked him. and the prisoner said be would "punch his -- out."—P C. Almond deposed that while he was on duty at Tarbock races he saw the prisoner kick the Prosecutor and he took him into custody, when be was told that be bad been attempting to pick nockets.—Superinten- dent Barker stated that the prisoner lived in one of the worst streets in Liverpool and was committed in 1883 with a number of others for breaking into a warehowse.—He was I now committed to prison for 21 days with hard labour.— Thomaslones, an elderly man, was charged with obtaining Money by false pretences on the 23rd nit—The evidence of P.C. Hudson and P.C. Crook showed tbat the prisoner vraa lit Tarbock races with a crowd of boys and young men round bim. He pretended to be selling 4mall bits of Dew,. pipers. and then gave to the purchaser a card which he alleged contained views of an obscene and indecent character. I Be told his hearers that ho dared not sell the cattle alone ias he would get slx months' hard labour if be was caugbt , doing so. The two constables named %Yore resent in plain clothes, and on apprehending the prisoner they found that ' the cards were entirely plain ard had no views at all oa them.—Tbe prisoner was committed for one month wick hard labour,

SATURDAY, MAY 10, 1884.

ANOTHER vote of censure l The Tories are disorganised—a flock of sheep without shep- herd an army without a leader, —or they would not struggle in this irregular fashion. It is not many weeks since they sought to pass a vote of censure on the Government, in relation to this self-same question of their policy in Egypt and the Soudan, but they were utterly routed, flying, as Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT said, like chaff before the wind, when the "sick lion" stretched forth its paw. The PRIME MllusTEß on that occasion literally pulverized Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE, whose followers incontinently left him to get out of the scrape he was in as best he could. It is no wonder that the right honourable baronet has on this occasion given place to Sir MICHAEL HICKS-BEACH who is to lead the attack on Monday night. The stalking-horse IS GORDON again—always GORDON; but we venture to say the Tories are much more interested in wasting the time of the House of Commons in the hope of prevent- ing the Franchise Bill becoming law than they are in the safety of the brave 'soldier who has his hands full at Khartoum. The cry has gone forth that General GORDON has been abandoned by the Government. and the most extravagant denunciation is beinz in- dulged in by people who have never taken the trouble to master the facts of the case. It is true that the latest telegrams from the General show that he is bitterly disappointed at there being no military expedition sent to support him; but very few of the telegrams transmitted by the Government have reached him, and he is speaking, therefore, with an imperfect knowledge of the situation. But granting that he is wroth with the War Office for not placing troops at his command, does it follow that he is in the right as to the best course to be pursued ? Who is to be held responsible for the policy of this coun- try with regard to the Soudan—General GOR- pox or Her Majesty's Ministers ? If we are to be committed to a war with the Soudanese, let us do so with our eyes open and know who we are to blame when disaster overtakes us. The present Government have made it known to the world that so far as they are concerned the Soudan is to be abandoned, and General GORDON concurred in this when consulted on the subject—going the length, in fact, of speaking of an attempt to re-establish Egyptian authority in that vast territory as something monstrous. But whilst the Soudan was to be abandoned it was desirable, with- out provoking war, to withdraw the various Egyptian garrisons, and General GORDON went to Khartoum to accomplish this object peacefully. He believed he could do every- thing by his own unaided authority, and dis- tinctly entered upon the task on the under- standing that he was not to be supported by a military expedition. He held it to be the wisest course to make his mission an essentially peaceful one. But what is the peculiar position now? He has found that his authority is not so great as it was formerly; the children of the desert are more or less under the control of the MAHDI ; they be; lieve in him, and are ready to fight for him, . and General GORDON has at length come to I

the conclusion that the best way out of the difficulty—to use his own expressive language —is to "smash up the MAHDI." Hence his demand for troops—troops, be it under- stood, not to enable him to retire peacefully and in safety from the Soudan, but to "smash up the MAHDI." It is for the Go- vernment to say as to this whether the cir- cumstances warrant the entire change of policy which is thus proposed; whether the peaceful mission is to be converted into a warlike one; whether we are to add to the grave responsibilities we have assumed' as to Egypt itself, the tremendous responsibility of entering upon a war with the MAHDI with the insane object of reconquering the Soudan—a country overrun with a fierce and fanatical race of people, and as large as France, Germany, and Great Britain put together! This is the issue which is at stake, and it is so great on the face of it that we venture to predict that the Opposition, on Monday night, will turn any way and every way rathcr than meet it. The question as to the personal safety of General GORDON is a smaller matter than that of a change of policy which may mean the sacrifice, for no just object, of thousands of lives and mil' lions of money. Not that the life of this heroic, if somewhat eccentric, man is to be rated as cheap as even he himself holds it 'The Government are pledged to make ever/ exertion to secure his safety, but, apart from any such pledge, we are quite sure that the members of the Cabine: are not the kind of men to abandon a gallant soldier to his fate. If they were actuated by no higher consi- deration, they may be supposed to have soine regard to their own safety as Cabinet Ministers, unless they are to be set down as lunatics, for no Government could keep its place for a, week which, while having it in itS, power to do so, declined to succour a Genera' reduced to the last extremity in the service, and his country. But this is not Genera' GORDON'S position; he is not in the las; extremity; for it is not long since he saio that, for two months, he was as safe •at Khartoum as he would be at Cairo; while io, the last telegram from him he says he will hold on as long as he can, and try to "suP,; press the rebellion," failing which he wi" "retire to the Equator." This is not the language of a man who is in exiremis ; be knows his way out of Khartoum when he cares to leave; but what he wants now is not, merely to bring back the garrisons by peacefn means, but to "suppress the rebellion." Tbi,e, means fighting "the MAHDI and his Men, and we put it to the Tories who are loudest in condemning the Government whether :heY, are prepared to sanction an undertaking °' this kind. They will have the opportunitY on Monday of declaring what they would do. if the chance were given them, and it will be of some interc,st to note how they propose to deal with the question of an expedition r° • the Soudan. The failure of the Government, if it has failed, will be their opportunity' but they must be careful not to make it too evident that they are moved to their presen; course less by love of GORDON than by hatre° of GLADSTONE. They have made themselves ridiculousby one fiasco ; and it is to be hopedj after again " breathing threatenings an° slaughter," that something more than " many hours wasted" will be the outcome of second vote of censure in the first half 01 the Session. '

Indeed, he may be Oh' • to cling to it closer than ever now that McMiNsir.s has announced his intention ; leaving the representation of the borough ti.° a younger and stronger man, for Sir GILBO,: , is not the sort of person to perceive to' absurdity of an old man offering himself for a task which is being declined as too exact' ing and laborious by a man ten years his junior. Mr. iVIOIrriNiEs, we are glad to be able to say, is better in health than he was on ' his return from Spain, and it will be seen tot ' from our local columns that he is attending Bu his duties as member for Warrington. ' of he knows that he is advancing in years ; lo,ng tne night sittings tell on the health strongest of men, and he is too conscientious to occupy a post when there is a doubt of his being able 'to discharge its duties faithfully and well. The Conservative candidate has no such scruples; great brewers are not as a rule over-nice as to conscience; but the working-men of Warrington who have been invited to attend the Conservative Ward Meetings may be excused if they hesitate and honestly say—" Sir GILBERT has had his, day. and it has gone by; if he is capable 01 anything, he ought to be otherwise employ el than in seeking to represent the electors o Warrington." It is not sufficient for th,e Brewer of Wilderspool to mutter feeble plat!' tudes, as he did on Thursday night, about WS "desire to promote the interests of the working classes," They can best judge 0` his desires by his deeds, and, as he deliber- ately challenges his criticism, it may fairly he asked--What have been his deeds in the past? Flogging was, ° course, confined to men of the toiling clasS' Whoever heard of a Sir So-and-So bting. brought under the lash ? Can it be as these peculiar acts that he is losing III; memory, and concludes that other people ar' similarly affected, just as deaf people take everybody else to be deaf; or does he NO think that flogging is a boon to the working classes? If he does, he will perhaps tell ii what steps he intends to take—if by any till,: lucky chance he should find his way again r`i St. Stephen's—to procure the restoration this " blessing in disguise." A NBW INDUSTRY VOR RCNCORN.—A firm of fustian cutters have recently established a branch of their business in Runcorn, and are giving employment to about 50 girls. Commodious rooms have been fitted up fm the purpose at the Alexandria Building, Top Locks, and a rooin has tiled been engaged at tie Royal Hotel, while it is intended to extend the operation in a short time by the lake of pre- mises lately occupiei by Mr. Statham. builder, in Halton- road. The firm expect, if suitable buildingi can be pro- vided, to give employment to between 400 and .500 girls. A LONG LOST 'fame am WVDNES.—Peter Leonard, a labourer, was brought up at Widnes Police Court, on Mon- day, charged with stealing a coat, the property Of Michael Griffin, of Cromwell-street.; and also with being "drunk and disorderly. It appeared that some years ago the prisoner lodged with Griffin, but on the 2nd May, 1882, he decamped with a coat, and nothing had been heard or seen of him un- til Saturday night, when P.C. Cheers took him into custody on a charge of drunkenness. For being.drunk he was tined 5e and costs 5s ed, and for the theft he was sentenced to a month's hard labour. OBSTRUCTING THE MERSEY AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, no Wednesday, Edward 'Percy was charged with committing a breach of the Rivers' Navigation Act.— Mr. W. Pinfold, assistant dock solicitor (who was accom- panied by Lieut. F. 0. Simpson, R.N.. water bailiff, Liver- pool), stated the defendant had been summoned for throw- ing on the share at Widnes certain slag and rubbish, so as to become an obstruction to the navigation of the Mersey. Ke had agreed to withdraw the case on the payment of testa, £2 3s. 64, as the defendant had some excuse for his con- di:mt.—The costs were paid, and the caee eras withdrawn. ROBBERY OV A REEHIVIS AT WlDNES.—Yesterday, at the , Widnes Police Court, before Mr. li. Gaskel I. junr., John Taylor, a young man, was charged with stealing a hive of Imes, of the vaine of 304, the property of Mr. Thomas Bennett, :Upton, Widnes. —.lnspector Wood said the bees were seen safe at six o'clock on Wednesday night,laet, and on Thursday morning at eight o'clock they were tnissed. Information was given to the police, and Constable Bruce went to the house of the pri- soner's father at Bitten. On going into the back yard the constable found the prisoner beside the hive, butwhen he saw the officer he ran into the house, and concealed himself in the cellar. Re was taken into custody, and acknowledged that he had stolen the ive. VIOLENCE er •Roucoas.—Bridget Noon, a married woman, was summoned at the Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday. on a charge of assaulting Mary O'Hara —On the evening of the .20th ult. 0 tiara was standing in Back Brunswick-street with a young man, when the defendant came up to her, and after using most -filthy language to- wards her struck her on the body and almost knocked her down.—A due of 1.08 and costs wae impesed.—Ueorge Dean, a young man, was charged with assaulting John Kin- sey.—Kinseris foreman At a works where the defendant is employed, andmn theist inst, he found fault with something the defendant bad done. Next day the defendant knocked him to the ground with a blow on the face.—Defendant pleaded guilty.—The Tench characterieedi the asstult as an unwarrantable one,. and dned the defendant lOs and costs 9s 6d, or in default. 14 dayS' hard labour.

Isalary was settled at £so.—Mr. Speakman said this explana- tion was very satisfactory to him, and he thought would be satisfactory to the public.—Tne Coairmae, replying to the statement that the Library was established on the under- standing that it could be worked with a halfpenny rate, said Dr. McDougall did say that a halfpenny in the pound would do a great deal for the establishment of a Library in Run- corn, but he at the same tires propounded a scheme for a subscription reading room to go alopg with the Library. That, as they knew, came to nothing, and he did not think it would have been wise for it to have cotne to anything sol long teethe Act stated that the Library should be free in ' every partioular.—Mr. Meadowcroft said he distinctly heard a gentleman lay: if £9O a year will cover the expense of a Library, let us have one by all means.—The Chairman was of opinion they should gather a very good Library out of a penny rate.—The subject then.dropped. Tin READING Roust —On the motion of Mr. Meadow. croft, seconded by Mr. z•peakman, it was unanimously re- solved that the raiding room should be open every after- noon from 2 to 9-30, except Sunday, instead of three after- noons per week as at present, lansaataita REPOWT. The librarian reported that during April there had been borrowed from the lending library 1318 volumes, classified as follows :—theology, 23; philosophy, politicel sconomy, Stc., 8; history, travels, biography, 165; science and art, 57; poetry and the drama, 22; prose fiction, 998; miscellaneous, 63. Eighteen books were issued from the reference department. Tht-ro was no other business.

RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS. The monthly meeeting was held on Wednesday, under the presidency of Mr. J. Meadowcroft. There were pre- sent :—Dr. Steele, Messrs. T. Norman, It. Shaw, W. Whit- talv-r, P. Briscoe, J. Pritchard, P. Speaktnan, F. A. Lake, J. Williams, H. White, W. H. Linaker (law clerk), W. Brookes (secretary), and M. Barker (surveyor). PROPOWD ACCIDENT HOSPITAL—The Chairman had re- ceived a tter from Mr. Clarke Aspinall, coroner for the City of Liverpool, informing him that on the 9th ult., he held an inquest upon the body of a man named Thomas Burgess, who was injured on a canal boat near Runcorn, on the 5 h March, of which injuries he died in the Royal In- firmary, Liverpool. The jury desired him (the coroner) to call the Commissioners' attention to the desirability of some provision of hospital accommodation being made in Run- corn in view of saving sufferers from accident and injury the pain and risk of a somewhat long journey to a Liver- pool institution.—Dr. Steele observed theta committee, con- sisting of himself,' Mr. P. Speakman, and Mr. Lightburo, haa been appointed to consider the ways and means of ob- taining and maintaining an accident hospital, but owing toi the illness of Mr. Lightburn the committee had been unable to meet. He quite agreed that something should be done. —The Chairman said he had acknowledged the receipt of the letter. The committee was appointed to consider the matter in consequence of the case referred to in the letter. It would be quite competent for Dr. Steele to propose addr- Banal members for the committee at the end of the meeting. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.—The Medical Officer of Health (Dr. Mauritz) presented his monthly report, which stated that the number of deaths regietered in Runcorn during the past month amounted to 23,representing a death rate of 17 per 1,000 per annum. Of the above deaths 5 were due to phthisis, 4to diseases of the nervous system, 2 to bronchitis, 2to cardiac affections, 2 to senile decay, can- cer, whooping cough, premature birth, mesenteric disease, jaundice, exhaustion, scarlatina, and spinal disease accoun- ted for one each. Of the deaths 7 were children 5 yetis and under, and 5 below one year. The number of deaths in the corresponding period last year was 28. SANITARY SumacTs.—The Highway and Sanitary Com- mittee had instructed the surveyor to write to Mr. J. A. John- son drawing his attention to the unsanitary condition of his property in Back Cooper-street, and Messrs. Taylor, White, Williams, and Speakman were appointed to inspect the pro- perty and report thereon. It was,recommended that the applications of Mr. Peter Noon, Church-street ; Mr. G. Lee, Lowlands-road; Mr. J. Humphreys, and Mr. S. Spruce, High-street, for permission to allow their projecting sign- boards to remain, be granted, subject to their removal on a month's notice.—The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. Norman, seconded by Mr. Williams. -

THE ACTION AGAINST MR. Buctrzrr.—The Law Clerk reported that the action against Mr. Beckett was held on Tuesday, and the judge decided that the shed was properly erected for the purpose intended, and that the storm that occurred on the night of the 111th December as an extraor- dinary one and that.therefore Mi. Beckett was not respon- sible for what took place.—Mr. Shaw observed that the Commissioners now knew exactly what their position was In regard to these temporary erections. They would be able to give the surveyor such instructions that when tem- porary erections, such as the one in question were put up, that he should examine them and report thereon with a view to making them secure so far as life and property was concerned. It was quite clear that if the shed bad been blown away at the time when persons were passing they must have been mainesd or killed. Any builder whose at- tention was called to what the surveyor considered a wea% point in the structure that would prevent it standing ordin- ary and extraordinary storms, would place himself in an awkward position if anything occurred. To that extent the judges decision would be important.

CADISREAD WATER STIPPLT.—An agreement has been conclieled between ibe Corporation of Manchester and the Barton Rural Sanitary Authority whereby Irlam and Cadis- head soon be supplied with water from pipes in con- nection with the city mains. div.p: RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY. COMMITTEE.

-.- The monthly meetiegof this committee was held in the Commissionerie-Beard-room, on Thursday afteruoon. Mr. W. Handley presided, and there were present Messrs. John Simpson, P. Briscoe, J. Meadowcroft, epeakman, T. itilev, and 11. D. Joaes (librarian and secretary). CHARGES GE EXERATAOANCE: The COMMISSIONERS' CONsclENcEs.—+The Chairman informed the members that the income of the committee for the next 12 months Was estimated at £lO5, made up by th. id rate and £2O from the sale of catalogues,. fines, drc. The estimated expenditure was as follows :—Librarianes salary £5O, binding £25, ma- gazines £l5, printing, stationery, Jtc. Lie, rent,- eke. £35, new books 565, total:£4os.—Mr. Meadowcroft remarked that it had been said outside that the Library Committee had been somewhat extravagant in its expenditure during the past year. His attention had been drawn more than once to the covering of the-floor of the room where the books were, which be thocght caused an expenditure which ought not to have been incurred. He had no objection, to, thelleor in the secretary's roombeing covered. He had also been spoken to on several occasions with reference to the advance which had been made in the secretary's salary. -Mr. Hand- ley had, however, explained that to him in a light which gave a different colour to the matter, and he had :no:tided his opinion somewhat. Still, he thought they were paying ample, if not too much, for services rendered in connection with the library; but he did not mention the subject with a view to reducing the expenditure on that head—far from it. He simply named it because be thought it proper that the cenunittee-ohould'be acquainted with these views, as it was not desirable that an impression that the committee was extravagant eheuld go abroad while complaints were made that sufficient books temeet the wants of the public were not being obtained. elle wished to seethe library-useful, but at the same time be did not wish there to be any wasteful extragagence. The Chairman : Do you make a prepesitime in tegard to it, Mr. Meadowcroft ? Mr. Meadoweroft replied in the negative, and a short dis- cussion took place between the geatleraen with regard to the estimates.—be Chairman pointed Out that there was a balance from the library rate for the year 188243 of £4B 7s Id, and the rate foe 1883-84 produced £172 4s 7d, being a total amount to the credit of the Committee of ..£220 lie Bd. The total amounteeceived by the Committee, how- ever. amounted only to e£l4B, 7s id, the Commissioners hiving charged them.the following items for fitting up the library rooms :—Shetves„ Sm., £34 Os sd; gas pendant, £2 Ss 7d ; chairs, ifeele ; tables, £0 18s. In addition they had charged £1,.1.4c for the floorcloth that covered the old Commissioners' Board-room Li 5s for the chandelier from the same place; and,ios for the table in the secretary's room; making a tetal of. £54 19s; while the charges for ; rent, cleaning, &a, left a balance due to the Commissioners of £5 Sc 3d. ThreChairman said that while on the question of rent, he mightetate that he had not altered his opinion on the matter. Hew-acquits satisfied that the Commissioners +had no right and no pewer , whatever to charge rent. The keayment of rout supposed that there might be notice to:quit, ' which no Libraries Act recognised at all, except it was for rtae rent of a buildineeone, an entirely foreign patty. He wail not going to raise the question, but he did say that the Commissioners might have been it:little more lenient, and not have taxed the intelligence of the people of Runcorn to hale enormous extent out of the paltreeeurre they received. He tbought it Was a thing no Commissioner could look upon with any saticfaction to hie conscience. If the Commissioners bad , got the actual expenses they were out of necket be thought that would have been sufficient, and tbeettepayers would have been grateful for any little con- ceesiee that tbe Act ,of ,Earliament clearly allowed to be dame even outside the rate. When the ratepayers had taken, the whole of the money produced by the sale of the old building that they ,neeercontribeted a farthing to, and had feted up their preeent,premises„ as the ratepayers said in an ortravagant fashion, Abe thought they might have allowed the Library Committee a little share of extravagance instead of charging them tfor an old gee pendant and an old oitclettesreore than they woeld have.fet;lbed at an auction sale.—Mr. Meadttercroft thought the chairman's observa- tions with regard to Coe Commissioners deserved some remaree item hint as chairman of the Board. When the question of adoptiug the bibrary Acts ,was first mooted, it was urged that the expenditure .would not exceed more than a halfpenny in the £. The ratepayers on that occasion were not merely ,mislead by the statement, .tiat the Commis- sioners had-now someground foletbe course they had taken. .He thought the Commissioners were rather to be commended than otherwiae for asking the Library Committee to exercise Some economy in the management ef theirsdepartment. It might be thaLcorne pereons tkought the Commissioners had been extravagant in fitting Ali their rooms, but he main- tained that, in ,proportion, the roomy of the Commissioners -.bad not been nearly so extravagantly "welshed as the seems of the Library; and be thouglit it wac very unfor- tunate one department should be charging the other with extravagance ar mismanagement. Ile was azienated by no other feeling, and .he hoped none ,Of them had other than good feeling Mayer& and good wishes:ler the success of the library. (Hear, bear.) It was unierstood that when the Library wee removed to Waterloo House and opened a reading room that as the librarian's duties would be much increased, his salary should be raised and rs-erranged in accordance with the work done. Then the preparation of a new catalogue entailed a great,deal of extra work, and it was thought it 'would be better to include in Mr. Jones's salary a sum that would recoup him for the time and trouble he nad taken in the performanco of that work, rather than to pass a, special sum ass gratuity. div.head: •CUE 111311.122.
div.p: The Finance Committee recommended that in addition to the rent of £25 per annum to be charged to the Library Committee for the use of the suite of rooms occupied by them, a further sum of £lO per annum be charged for ' cleaning, heating, and lighting; that the library account be debited with the sum of £ll 19s. 4d. for rent, heating, lighting, and cleaning, to March 25th-; and £3 103. being value of floor-cloth and gas pendant in reading-room, and table in librarian's room, and that the balance from rate, amounting to £5 6s. 3d., be transferred to the committee. It was recommended that the list of irrecoverable rates for the past year, amoanting.to £153 15s. 11., be allowed.—The confirmation of the minutes having been proposed, Mr. Lake moved an amendment that the Library Committee be charged for the use of rooms the sum of £l5 per annum. He took it for granted that all the members of the Board, whatever theft feelings were at first, were now convinced that they aught to do their best to make the library a success. With the small income they had it was very evi- dent they could only make it a success by working it economically, and, therefore, if the Board could see its way to charge a lower rent, he thought it was their duty to do both in the interests of the ratepayers at large and of the library in particular. The rooms for which .£25 was re- commended when the report was submitted from the House Committee were those now occupied by the overseers, and not for the rooms which the Litaiary Committee occupied. If they put the rooms in the market, as a business &armee- lion between the Board and an outside body, he was satis- led that nobody would give £25 for the use of them. There was only , one place they could :is& a room, and that was the reading-room. The other had been used as a larder, aad the librarian'e room was in- tended for the housekeeper's sitting-room, so that the £25 I,as recommended should not stand in the way of the arrange- ment he had suggested. The expenses of the Library showed that it was impossible for it to be carried on on a I satisfactory footing if the committee were to pay rent and a sum for cleaning, heating, and lighting. Last year they I.spent £37 in new books, £3O in salaries—this year increased tof,so—magazines for the :quarter £5 odd, binding books ~£2O. stationery £l5 4s 6d, and miscellaneous £8 48 7d. This year the expenditure would be much increased, as the read- ing room would be open all the year, and if they had to pay the rent recommended there would only be £3O left for our- chasing new books, and the people would soon be dissatisfied ; if they did not get more of the new books that were creating 'a sensation in the literary world. He asked Dr. Steele to ,secood his amendment, as that gentleman had moved that ,the ,Library Committee have the Commissioners' Board- Ixoona in the old building.—Dr. Steele explained that he ' made that proposition because it would not cost anything, !but it was understood that the Library Committee should 141arepart of the rent at Waterloo House. They had no I right to-cause the ratepayers an expenditure of more than Iletin the p•und for Library purposes. He did not consider the rent recommended a high one. He should be sorry to restrict the operations of the Library, but they had a duty to the ratepayers as well as the Library.—Mr. Norman : I tnin,k this Library ought to be worked splendidly for a penny its the peund.—The Chairman pointed out that the rent would te reduced to £l5 when the overseers and School Board commenced to pay rent—Mr. Lake said he would alter hie resolution then that the rent of £25 should include cleaning, heating, and lighting.—Mr. Pritchard thought the committee might ha allowed a reduction of £lO in the rent , for the purchasing of new books.—Mr. Shaw contended that the Library Committee would have about £6O more this year than they had let, because the cost of fitting the rooms would not have to be borne again.—The Chairman thought the expenses of the Library Committee bad not been alto- gether Judicieus.—Mr. Lake: You are in the same.box as myeelf.--As Mr. Lake could not obtain a seconder for his motion he withdrew it, and the minutes were passed. THE RUNCORN BRIDGE TOLLS --Mr. Pritchard said he had obeerved from the local newspapers that a petition had been forwarded to the London and North-Western Railway Company asking for a reduction in the tolls for crossing Runcorn Bridge, There was no doubt that the public generally had for a long time past considered 3d for a return ticket. aed a shilling for a weekly`contract, excessive if not an exorbitant fare. He had beard many strangers say that it was the dearest bridge to cross. He suggested that a resolution should be passed expressing the hope that the London and North-Western Railway Co. would grant the petitioners request.—Mr. P. Speakman said be had no doubt that a unanimous vote of that Board would be appreciated br those who had get up the petition, and would have weight with the directors of the company in London.--Mr. Shaw suggested that a deputation should be sent, without recording anything. They were entirely in the hands of the company. If they approached the direc- tore without making any noise they would receive the mat- ter very much better, and be very likely to meet their wishes to some degree.—Mr. Norman observed that he presented the petition to Mr. Shaw, and it would receive the fullest

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

Iknowing ones having long been aware of the nokition of the bank. fhere follows tke usual and wholly illogical depre- ciation of other bank shares. Why, for example, should the Bank of Australasia shares hays gone down two or three pounds because the Oriental Bank has failed ? or why, for the same reason, should the shares in the Bank cf tic nth Australia decline in the market? The reason is twofold. Firet there are in all corporations a number of timid share- holders who when disaster overtakes one bank immediately throw upon the market their shares held in others, remote both geographically and in business connection& Beyond this is the organised effort of the bears who take advantage of the temporary panic to depreciate bank property which presentlythey will buy for themselves at the reduced prices. The failure of the Oriental Bank has hit very hard a class of military officers, clergymen, and widows. whose principal means of living goes with it. It is not only what they lose but what they are liable for that makes the case ruinous for people of small property. I heat of one gallant officer now on the retired list who, having bought his shares at £35 gave them away the day after the failure with a bonne of £lO each in cash, hoping thereby to clear himself from res- ponsibility. He has now learned that in accordance with the terms of the charter of the bank if the person to whom he sold them is net able to meet calls that my be made he will be liable.

I made a pilgrimage yesterday to the Agricultural Kati, attracted by the promise of an "Exhibition of Art Furni- ture." It is a very poor show, by no means coming up to its titular description. It is evident that principal cabinet makers have not thought it worth while to take stalls. Only one of the principal London firms is represented, and they certainly have a few good things at prices accordingly. One exhibitor displays a painful monstrosity in the term of a drawing-room suite, spindle-legged, and painted a bril- liant red. I suppose by-and-bye we shall come to this. The thin end of the wedge has already been inserte3 by the in- troduction at five o'clock tea of small tables of this striking colour. I saw one the other day blasting a pretty drawing- room. crrisvded with well-dressed women who had not done the hostess any harm. The picture by Mr. Frank lull, entitled "Did you ever kill anybody, father 2" in this year's Academy, was described a few days ago by a critic, who must evidently have been I overwhelmed by the "leagues of long Academy," as "a curious study of a little boy handling; his father's mod." Now it is a notable fact that the subjnt happens to ha little girl—Mr. Holl's own daughter, nine years of age— who has a sweet feminine face and long fair hair fringed her forehead. She sits on a red raz thrown over a sofa, and looks up with an enquiring, anxious gaze. Ir is rather a hazardous practice for critics to rely exclusively on their shorthand notes unless, like the late Mr. Torn Taylor, they can walk round a gallery, record its contents on the tablets of their memory, and write two or three columns about them when they get home. But lam not sure that even Mr. Torn Taylor did not occasionally attribute a picture to someone other than the man who painted it.
