POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
Boßoiilciu Poi= COURT.

SATinitro.Y.—Before Alderman Chandiey. BEGGING.—Thomas Haggaily. a boy. was c.hargad with begging In Thynne-street on the previous afternoon, when he was observed by P.C. 10 to be going from door to door. The oonstable heard him ask for bread, but the prisoner told him he was selling apers.—Mr. Hunt (chief cons(anle) gave the prisoner, who is a newspaper vendor, a very bad character. —He was ordered to receive twelve strokes with the birch rod —lames McGuinnesa was charged witn begging in Heath- lane on the previous evening —Hr. Hunt remarked that it was principally able-bodied people of the town who offended in this respect, and he was rather surprised at the public indiscrimi- nately relieving beggars •It was such men as the prisoner who disgraced the town.—Sent to prbon for seven day.. MeNDAT. Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), in the chair, Mr. John Fairciouzb, and Alderman Davies, DRUNK AND DISMIDEDIN,—EIizabeth Jackson. for being drunk and disorderly in Horsemarket-street on Saturfay after- noon was santenced to seven days' Imprisonment; she behaved very violently and had to be forcibly conducted to tiaa cells. —James Bently, for being drunk and creating a disturbance in Catherine-street on the 25th of April, was fined Is and costs only. it being his first offence.—Richard Buckley, a respec- table looking man, was summoned for being drunk and disor- derly in Greenall-street ; he pleaded net guilty and said that he was a wiredrawer and as be had gone to work during the strike he was continually shouted in the streets, which was what caused a disturbance.—Fined Is and costs.—Margaret Johnson, an old offender, was fined lOs and costs for being I drunk and disorderly in Winwick-street on the 23th of April. —Margaret Flannery was fined a I,lre amount for being drunk and disorderly in Hardy-Ares t on the 30th of April.--John Conway was fined 5$ and costs for being drunk and disorderly en Saturday evening in Hill-strest.--Miehasi Birmingham and John O'Keefe were charged with being drunk and disor- derly in Kinder's yard; the former WAS fined 59 and costs and the latter was fined ss, including costs. MAINTENANCE CASES—Samuel Stokes, farm labourer, was charged with leaving his child chargeab'e to the common fund of the Warrington Union on the 27th of March,—He was re- manded for a month to allow him the opportunity of paying the amour t due, 3Os and costs, in the meantime.—James Dagnall was similarly charged with respect to a child admitted on the 14th of April —He had been previously convicted for a similar offence and was now sentenced t twns months' hard labour.—Mr. Shearer, relieving officer pr/ved the cases. ScHooL ATTENDANCE.—The following persons were sum- moned by Mr. Riley, school attendance officer, for neglecting to send their children to school, viz. :—Lizzie Abrahams, lady help, Tilley-street, her boy proved to be a truant and was ordered to beflogged : James bee, f roman, Heath-side, his boy was ordered to be whipped. Matthew Statham smith, Latchford, fined 55; Charles Hayes. railwayman, Bank Quay, emit Ss •, John Birchall, forgeman, Hardy-street, fined 5s ; George Daniels, forgeman, . School-brow, adjourned • George Bishop, forgeman, Haydock-street, two cases, fined adjourned; ; Ben Ogden. forgeman. Napier-street, 'fined Os; James Backhouse, fergeman, Hardy-street, fined ss; Jotn Shepherd, General- street, adjourned. OBSCENE LANGIJAGE.—Jabez Stout, Bolton's-yard, labourer. was fined is and cots for using obscene and erofane language In Litton's-road. Wrianz Ternowirna,—Williarn Ward, a y .uth, was fined 23 6d, including costs, for throwing stones In Priestlev-street on the 27th ult.; and two boys named Lawrence and Patrick Hoarty were ordered to receive six strokes each with the birch rod for committing a similar offence. OnsTlencrion.—John Nichoisan, a boy, was summoned for wheeling a large skip on the footpath in Parker-street to the obstruction of passengers, and was fined 2s 64 including the costs. CHIMNEY ON FlRE.—Thomas Worthington was fined 2s 6d. Including costs, for allowing his chimney to be on fire on the 27th ult.. and Mary Grierson, for a sims.ar offence, was fined Le %winding costs. TUESDAY.— Before Captain Litton. _

DRUNK AND Dlsoltrolar..v.—Johri Culkeen, farm labourer, App:ewn. who was on Monday fined for being drunk and dis- erderly, was agenb/ ought up for a similar dfence, committed In Cairo-street on Monday evening. He was committed to bard labour for 14 days.--Thomas McNally, farm labourer, Stretton, was charged wit'd being drunk and disorderly In Bt. James's-street on Tuesday morning. He was allowed to go on promising to leave the town. AN ABSENTEE.—George Jones, 5, Watkin-street, was charged with being an absentee from the 4th Battalion S AUL Wales Borderers, was remalded pending the arrival of an escort. He had been arrested on Monday evening by P O. Neill. WEDNESDAY.—Be:ore Mr. John Palrclough. DRUNK AND D,SORDERLY.—Joeph Taorn, for being drunk and disorderly in St. Alban's Avenue on Tuesday afternoon, was fined 5s and costs or seven days.—Peter Banally was charged with being drunk tnd di=orde-ly in Welsh's-yard, Old- road, on Tuesday evening. The prisoner's wife appeared in court and said that her husband was in the habit of ill-treating her. She was" punished to death." he brought her no money. and she should be glad if the Bench could grant her some pro- tection. Prisoner was fined lOs and costs. or 14 days. A DESERTER.--Joshus Lee was charged with being a deserter from the 2nd battalion, 18th Regiment of Foot, stationed at Aldershot, and was remanded to Walton to await an escort. ' THIM!DAY.—Before Captain Litton.

DRUNK AND- DLORDIERLY.—PatiA Dolan. for being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket street, on Wednesday evening, was sentenced to 14 days' bard labour. FRIDAY —Before Captain Reynolds and Mr. John White. DRUNIC AND DI,ORDERLY.—John Noon, WI! lam Noon, and Thomas Moran were charged with being drunk and disorderly in Harsemarket-street on the evening of Thrusday.—The two is were fined IN and casts each, or 14 days, and Moran Ss and costs, or seven days. ASSAULT.—Swah Burke was summoned for assaulting Ellen Bailey, on the sth of May.—The parties are neighbours, and acccrding to the atm yof the complainant the defendant threw a poker and a pot ornament at her, Inflicting a wound on the head, because she (c nnp'ainant) would not allow her boy to fetch beer for the defendant and her husband.—John Bailey, husband of the complainant, was charred with doing damage to the extent of ss, to the door of Margaret Burke. another neighbour, during the progress of the quarrel.—Barah Burke was boind over to keel the peace f r six months, and Bailey was ordered to pay the damage and casts.
WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS.

WEDNESDAY.—Betore Mr P. Stubs and Mr. 8. DRTINY AND DISCIIIDERLY.—BamueI Terry, who did not ap- pear, was fined 51 and 9s costs, for being drunk and disorderly at Orford, on the leth ult. A BICYCLIST SUMMONED —Taxies Robinson was summoned for riding a bicycle on the highway at Sankey, on the 3rd inst. without haying alighted lamp attached.—P.C. 156 proved the case.—Defendant said that he had had his bicycle on a cricket ground in the rain, and on the return journey he lit the lamp four times, but it went out again. He walked the machine at Sankey, an did not ride until be was in the neighbourhood.— Considering the circumstances of the case. the Bench decided to dismiss the defendant. A CARELESS DRIVEIL—William Hampson was fined is and costs for riding without 'reins on the 24th alt.. in Liverpool - road, Sankey.

ST. HELENS —POLICE COURT. "MONDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison and Alderman Mcßryde. THE CHARGE OF WOUNDING A WlFE.—George Hayes, oharged on temand wih doing grievious bodily harm te his wife at Sutton, was further remanded till Monday next, bail being allowed. HIGHWAY ROMMEL—Thomas Molyneux was again brought up on remand for stealing EL ifis 41c1 from the person of George Dawson. colliery underlooker, on the 2nd April last,—Prisoner was further remanded until Monday next, bad (two sureties in £2O each) being accepted for his appearance. So4WITING ALMS FROM A Poracitmaw.—Barah Jane Williams was charged with solicit'ng alms from a police-constable in Market-street, on Barclay afternoon. Prisoner denied the oharge.—The plias-constable said he was on duty in Market- street, in plsin clothes, when the prisoner accosted him and asked for alms, and in corroboration of his statement that the accused was begging, he produced in mart a basket pretty-well supplied with edib!eA. which Williams had then in her pos- session.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for seven days. MclCHtsfsniti DOGS.—John Lowe, Ravenhead Farm, Sutton was summoned for keeping dogs without license.—lt was stated that the law allowed the defendant to keep two dogs to be used on the farm, exempt from duty, providing they were kept for attending to sheepPrily according to the Act, and defendant had rigned a paper to that effect; but the dogs were chained up and notnsed on the farm. He had therefore rendered him- sett liable to s penalty of £4O for making a false statement, and a penaltyof MO for keeping a dog without a license. Defen- dant said he was obliged to have the dons with so many cattle about.—The Inland Revenue Officer said ha saw the mastiff on the 28th of March chained in the yard to a box. Defendant admitted to him it was a very good yard dog, but no use for sheep at all. Mr. Murphy considered the case important in re- gard to the revenue —Defendant was fined 5s and costs 69 6d. —henry Clifton, Waterworks, Rainhil 4 was also summoned for keeping a dog without a license —ln defence he stated that he had been prevented taking one out owing to the illness of b4s wife.—Re also was fined 5s and costs. CHIMNEYS ON FlEE.—GeorgeDing was summoned for allow- ing the chimney of his dwelling-house, in Patrick-street, Parr. to be on fire on the 30th ult.—Pined 75 tncludin cost, Robert Dixon, Peter-street, was fined 7s Including costs for a similar offence. TinnewAy,—Before Alderman Harrison. Tire BEGOIAG NlllSANOg.—james -111cDermott,t a middle- aged man, was charged with begging in Baldwin-street, on the afternoon of the previous day.—The prisoner entered a grocer's shop and asked for bread. Because they met used to give him any he became very insolent and abuilve.—He was committed tto prison for seven days.

SAD FATALITY Ile A GLASS WORKS.—A sad fatality cc- -cured at Messrs. Pilkington's plate-glass works, Cowley Hill, on Tuesday evening, when a labourer, named James Bond, 14 years of aze, residing. with his parents at 66, Parr- street, .was instantaneously killed. It appears that the de- ceased was engaged at one of the sand machines and his spada fell between the buckets." He attempted to pick up t•le spade while the machinery was in motion, but his arm was caught and the poor lad was dragged round with the In ichinery. When extricated it was found that the lad's head had been smashed and mutilated in a shocking manner, death being instantaneous. An inquest on the body will be bald.

div.head: EARLESTOWN.
div.p: EARLESTOWN.

THE GOSPEL MISSION AT EAHLESTOWN.—An entertaia ment of a very enjoyable character was held in the Co- operative Hall, on Tuesday evening, in connection with the Earlestown Gospel Mission. There was a moderate attend- ance, and Mr. John Clarke presided. A programme of singing, reading, drc., was effectively cirried out by Mrs. Dillow, Miss M. Clarke, Mrs. Mellor, Mr. Pickett, and the Chairman. . . .

THE CO•OPERATIVE SOCIETY.—The quarterly meeting of the members of the above society was held in the Co-opera- tive Hall, Earlestown, on Monday evening. Mr. W. Davies (president) occupied the chair. The balance sheet for the quarter showed that the sales amounted to £1,392 Ss 31-d, which left a disposable profit of 2s 3d in the pound to Mem- bers and Is id to non-members, leaving a balance of £5 16s 4d to be added to the contingent fund. Messrs. White, Limond, and Seddon were elected to serve on the committee in the room of those retiring. THE EARLESTOWN CONSERVATIVE CLUB: BILLIARD BANLICAP.—For a week or two past the members of this club have been greatly interested in a billiard handicap which has been conducted on the new table recently opened by Messrs. James Fairclougla and Thomas Stone. The prize was a splendid cue given by the makers of the table, Messrs. Orme and Son, Manchester. The contest was brought to a close on Monday evening, when the final tie was played be- tween P. Bent and T. Owen. After a fairly exciting game, Bent proved the winner by nine points. EARLESTOWN GOOD TEC:MARS AT ASHTON.—On Wednes- day evening about 20 members of the Hope of Earlestewn Lodge of Good Tempters paid a fraternal visit to the Ash- ton Excelsior Lodge, holding its meetings in the British School. The visitors were warmly received, and were asked to " officer " the lodge for the evening. Brother George Clarke, D.M , presided, and the other parts were occupied by friends from Earlestown. After the transaction of several items of business, the visitors entertained their Ashton friends. Those taking part in the entertainment were Sisters Walker, Whittey, E. J. and M. Clarke, Mellor; Brothers John Bassett, Whittey, Walker, Barnard; George Warburton, Jun., and John Clarke. A very pleasant gathering was closed with a hearty vote of thanks to the visitors. TRESPASSING ON THE RAILWAY AT COLLINS GREEN.— IMPORTANT TO COLLIERS.—At the St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, before W. Pilkington and H. S. Hall, Earls., John Grimes, Wm. Conway, Richard Moody, Wm. Filling. ham, Wm. Hughes, Robert Hughes, an John Talland, all colliers, were summoned by the London and North-Western Railway Company for trespassing on the railway at Bold, on the 2nd April.—Mr. Preston, of the solicitors' depart- ment, Lime-street Station, Liverpool, appeared on behalf of the railway company, and stated that the defendants were charged with trespassing on the line between Collins Green and St. Helens Junction. Colliers passing to and from their work were greatly in the habit of trespassing along the line, making a short cat to their homes. So much did they do so that the railway company had had to get a special clause in their Act of Parliament last year, giving them the power to prosecute without the usual warning notices.—Evidence was then called, showing that the defendants were seen walking on the line between Collins Green and St. Helens Junction, and though au official of the company told them they were trespassing, and drew their attention to the "notice "board, they continued to trespass along the line.— The Chairman said that as that was the first case of the kind that had been brought before them they would deal leniently with it, but it was necessary for the railway com- pany to take some proceedings in order to put a stop to the trespassing. The two Hughes, who did not appear, would be fined ss. and costs each, and the other defendants 2s. 6d, and costs each. THE ALLEGED BURIAL SCANDAL AT NEWTON.: QUESTIONS me PARLIAMENT.—The reports of the alleged scandal at St. Peter's, Newton on the occasion of the recent interment of the remains Of the late Mr. Goldsworth, a prominent Wesleyan Methodist, evoked the greatest excitement, and the matter has formed one of the chief topics of conversation throughout the entire district. As will be seen from our re- port of the Newton Commissioners' meeting on Monday afternoon the matter was mentioned by Mr. Emmett, and Mr. Hunt (brother-in-law to the deceased) gave an explana- tion in regard to the affair.—ln the House of Commons on Tuesday evening Mr. Jesse Collings asked the Secretary of State for the Home Department if his attention had been called to a proceeding which took place on the occasion of the burial of a Nonconformist named Goldsworth, when the Vicar of St. Peter's, Newton, refused to allow the body to be carried into the church, but directed it to bo taken to the grave, where it was interred with the usual graveside service; whether he will state if the action of the Vicar in refusing to admit the body of Mr. Goldsworth into the church was legal; and whether he will cause inquiries to be made into all the circumstances of the case.—Sir W. Harcourt: This question relates to an ecclesiastical matter over which I have no jurisdiction.—Mr. Jesse Collings: Will the right . . -.

hon. gentleman inform use to whom I 'should address this question, or who is responsible? (Hear, hear.)—Sir W. Harcourt: This transaction is either according to law, or it is contrary to law. If it is not contrary to law my hon. friend could net apply to anybody. If is is contrary, the law no doubt provides an opportunity of redress. (Laughter.) EARLESTOWN GOOD TEMPLARS : QUARTERLY SESSION. —The quarterly session of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars was held in the Lodge Room, Bridge. Street, on Monday evening, when there was a good attend- ance of members. Brother John Taylor, W.C.T., presided. Several items of business were discussed, including arrange- ments for a picnic in connection with the lodge. The quarterly reports of the various officers were then received. The W.S. (Brother E. Newman) reported that a good work had been done during the quarter, and that the present number of good members on the books was 79.—The re- ports of the W.F.S. (Sisters J. E. Warburton and W.T. (Brother George Warburton, senior) showed that a balance remained in hand after the payment of expenses.—The W.M. (Brother James Nuttall) reported as to the property of the lodge; and Brother E. Newman (superintendent of the Juvenile Temple) reported that the temple was in a good condition, there being 49 good members on the books.— After a few comments the reports were adopted. The in- stallation of the officers for the new quarter was then per- formed by Brother John Warburton, assisted by Brother George Clarke, D.M., as follows : W.C.T., Brother George Warburton, junior; sr.v.T., Sister P. Walker; W.S., Brother E. Newman; W.F.S., Sister J. E. Warburton; W.T., Brother G. Warton, senior; W. Chaplain, Brother J. Barnard; W.M., Brother J. Walker; P.W.C.T., Brother John Taylor. After the appointment of the various com- mittees, the newly-elected W.C.T. briefly thanked the mem- bers for electing him, and promised to do all he could to further the interests of the club. He, however, would require the assistance of the members in making it success- ful, as he alone could not do it.—The proceedings then con- cluded.

div.head: EARLESTOWN CHURCH: ANOTHER SCENE.
div.p: EARLESTOWN CHURCH: ANOTHER SCENE.

Last Sunday's proceedings at St. John the Baptist, both inside and outside the church, showed that the people were sore as to the late trial. At the morning service on Sanday there was a moderately large congregation, and the choir occupied their accus- tomed seats in the church. Mr. Durman (the old organist) was also among them. The congregation evidenced a curiosity as to what the order of the service was to be, and this feeling was considerably increased when Mr. Pember- ton, the choirmaster and deputy organist of St Augukine's Church, Liverpool (who has previously attended the Earles- town Church at the request of the vicar), was observed to enter the church from the vestry and make his way to the organ with a number of music books in his possession. He opened the organ and had made every preparation for play- lag when the vicar (the Rev. T. R. Matthews) and the curate (the Rev. H. E. Smith) entered the church. The service was proceeded with as usual; the choir and a large part of the congregation not taking any part therein. When the canticles were reached the vicar paused for the organ to play, but as the instrument did not respond the vicar walked to Mr. Pemberton, and he was then informed that there was no one to "blow" the organ. On the vicar re- turning to the reading desk he proceeded with the service as usual. The responses, however, were but faint, and the organ remained silent throughout. When giving out the usual notices the vicar announced that the offertories that morning were to defray church expenses and in aid of the poor ; after which the curate preached all excellent ser- mon from the words "This do in remembrance of me "(Ist Corinthians, xi. chap, 24th verse). The vicar tl.en ad- vanced to the communion table for the purpose of reading the usual offertory sentences, but a number of persons rose in the church and created a commotion by leaving. Among those who left were the two or three sidesmen who had been present, and, as there was no one in attendance to make the collections, the vicar contented himself with read- ing one of the offertory sentences, after which he brought the service to a close in the usual manner. In the evening there was a slightly increased attendance, but it was a noticeable fact that many of the congregation were strangers, who had apparently come in the expectation of witnessing a" scene." The choir again gathered in their usual seats; but Mr. Durman' the organist, took a eeat in the body of the church. The Vicar's organist, Mr. Pember- ton, as in the morning, proceeded up to the organ, and be- fore the service commenced played a voluntary —the "blower "of the organ being the 'Vicar's son, as the usual blower refused to blow for Mr. Pemberton. The curdle first announced a hymn which was played by Mr. Pemberton, and a few persons sang, but the choir and the majority of the congregation took no part in doing so. Beyond evi- dently strained " coughs" when the Vicar read the lessons, the service was not interrupted until the Vicar entered the pulpit to preach, whereupon several persons, including a few members of the choir, left the edifice. The Vicar se- lected as his text the 11th verse of the 6th Ephesians," Put on the whole armour of God," but made no reference to the dispute. At the close of his remarks many more persons rose and left the church; and as neither wardens nor sides- men were present, (having gone out earlier), one or two friends of the Vicar. Mr. Atty, Mr. Barton, Mr. Henshaw, Fec., went round with the offertory "plates," but very few persons put anything in them. When the service was over the congregation waited outside the church, and as Mr. Bar- ton and Mr. Atty left they were derisively complimented for their services. As the Vicar and his organist left the vestry and made their way to the vicarage, they were hissed land hooted by the crowd. The people afterwards retired quietly to their homes. SETTLEMENT OF THE DISPUTE.

Since Sanla7, we are glad to be able to say, the position of affairs in connection with what has hitherto been known as the "Earlestewn Church Dispute" has undergone a marked change, and we are able to-day to announce that a

div.head: THF 'EXAMINER, SATITRUAY, MAY 10, 184.
div.p: THF 'EXAMINER, SATITRUAY, MAY 10, 184.

reconciliation between the contending parties has been effected and an amicable arrangement as to the control of the services has been come to. This welcome consummation has been brought about by the kindly interference of the Rev. Canon Hopwood, of Winwick, whose steps to ter- minate the squabble have met with the greatest success and merit the thanks of the parishioners generally as well as every peace-loving and law-abiding citizen in the district. Last week the wardens and sidesmen made a suggestion that the dispute should be referred to the arbitration of the Rev. Canon Hopwood, and they consulted that gentleman upon the matter. The Vicar (the Rev. T. R. Matthews), how- ever, would not consent to that course, and the result was a renewal of the "scenes," on Sunday last. The general opinion since then has been that the squabble was as far from settlement as ever, but on Thursday Mr. B. Corlett (late people's warden) received a note from the Rev. Canon Hopwood stating that the Rev. T. R. Matthews had been up to see him on the following day, and he would be glad to meet him (Mr. Corlett), along with Mr. Birkhead and Mr. Burchall that evening (Thursday), at half-past seven. At the time mentioned, Mr. Corlett, Mr. Birkhead, and Mr. Buchan proceeded to the residence of the Rev. Canon Hopwood, where they were ushered into the Library. A few minutes later the Rev. Canon Hopwood entered, and asked them if they had full confidence in him if he consented to act as arbitrator in the matter, and the gentlemen replied that they had. Canon Hopwood neat asked if they had any personal animosity or feeling against the vicar, Mr. Matthews, and on receiving a reply to the effect that they had not, he called Mr. Matthews (who had been in another apartment) into the room. The gentlemen present then talked the circumstances of the dispute over for a short time, after which the Rev. Canon Hopwood gave his decision as arbitrator upon the dispute. He stated that Mr. Matthews was to have full control over the organ, organist, and choir according to the law; but Mr. Dur- man was to take his seat at the organ as he was elected by the vestry. Whoever was elected organist at the next vestry meeting must be appointed conditionally upon a month's notice before leaving or being discharged ; and he (Canon Hopwood) strongly urged the vicar to con- sult the wardens upon any future dispute or squabble that might arise. The choir was to continue as formerly, and if they misconducted themselves in any way the matter was to be brought before the wardens'and the vicar, who would settle the difference between them. The Rev. Canon Hop- wood asked the vicar (the Rev. T. R. Matthew) if he agreed to those conditions, and the vicar replied " Yes ;" where upon Canon Hopwood said he hoped they would all shake hands and IA bygones be bygones. The Rev. T. R. Mat- thews then shook hands with Mr. Birkhead, Mr. Corlett, and Mr. Birchall, each of whom also stated that they agreed with the decision. Mr. Birkhead thanked Canon Hopwood for his kindness in taking the matter up; and Mr. Corlett stated be was only sorry they bad not had his ser- vices earlier. Canon Hopwood remarked that he did not want any thanks for what he had done, as he considered he had only done his duty, and he would consider himself ; well repaid if he could only settle the matter peaceably.— This brought the interview to a close. A considerable number of persons were waiting in Earles- town to learn the result of the "arbitration," and when it became known that a prospect of the scandalous scenes such as have recently been witnessed being events of the past, there was a satisfactory feeling manifested on all hands. The decision appears to meet with general favour among the parishioners.

NEWTON FAIR —The Law Clerk reported that the restric- tions by the county justices as to the holding of Newton fair had now been removed. THE MARKET TOLL Can.—Mr. Worsley reported that the case against Carney, a hawker, who refused to pay the market toll demanded from him, had been decided in the Board's favour, and he did not anticipate any further trouble in that direction. PRESCOT.

CATTLE FAIR—The last of these fortnightly fairs was held on Tuesday, when there was a supply of about seventy cattle and a few pigs. Business was brisk, and by mid-day the greater number of the animals was disposed of, the 3ellers obtaining good prices. NEW RATES—At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, the Bench signed a lighting rate of 3d in the pound, and a poor rate of 3s 6d in the pound for the next twelve months, for the township of Rainhill; and a poor rate of Is in the pound for Whiston, for the half-year. REIVING • LOCOMOTIVE DITRING,PLICHIIBITED Bonus.— At the Present Petty Sessions. on Tuesday, Frank Richards was charged with driving a locomotive along the highway at Prescot between the hours of sunset and sunrise on the -18th April.—P.S. Ball deposed that about eight o'clock on the night of the date name I he saw the defen- dant driving a locomotive engine along Derby-street, Prescot.—The defendant stated that he had been delayed on the road.—Re was fined 20s and costs.

THE SUPPORT OF AN AGED FATHDII.—At the Petty Ses- sions, on Tuesday, James Campbell and Henry Campbell were summoned to show cause why an order should not be made upon them for the support of their father, at present chargeable to the Prescot Union.—Mr. S. H. Hartley, clerk to the Board of Guardians, appeared to prosecute, and stated that the father of the defendants was an old and impotent person unable to work, and since the 21st March last he had been an inmate of the workhouse hospital. The sons were sufficiently able to partly maintain their father, and the Guardians had instructed him to ask for an order of 2s 6d per week. He understood that the son Henry had consented to pay that sum, while the son James was unmarried and being in receipt of 35s per week, he was well able to con-e tribute that amount.—The Bench made an order for 2s 6d per week upon each of the defendants. ASSAULTING A WlFE.—Thomas Lewis, a young man, was charged at the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, with assaulting his wife Ann, at Prescot, on the 28th April.— The defendant was represented by Mr. McKenzie, and pleaded not guilty.—The complainant alleged that about a fortnight previous her husband turned her out of the house, and sold up the furniture. On the 28th April she found him living at his sister's, and she went there. She said, "Where you are I have a right to be," but her husband said he would turn her out, and he did mo. He pushed her down four steps, and his t-ister stood over her with a " rolling pin," swearing what she would do to her.—Mr. McKenzie submitted that there was no assault proved, and that the wife had simply brought all the trouble upon herself by trespassing in the defendant's sister's house.—The Bench considered that the defendant committed an assault in the act of turning his wife out of the house, and fined hint lOs and costs,

THE RECENT LOCAL BOARD ELECTION : ALL2SED MALPRACIICES.—SeveraI cases of an important character were set down for hearing at the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday forenoon, the most important of which was one arising not of the recent Local Board election at Prescot. The magistrates en the Bench were Mr. F. W. Earle and Captain Willis. James Sergeant, a beerhouse keeper, re- siding in Kendal-street, Prescot; Edward Crawley, a watch- maker. Houghton-street, Prescot ; and John Makin, watch- maker, Warrington-road, Prescot, were summoned on the several charges of falsely assuming to act as voters, and , also fabricating voters. The informations in the case were laid by John Ford, potter, Kemble-street ; Terence Cray- mour and Thomas Craymour, of Smithy-wint, Prescot. On the cases being called, Mr. J. 0. Swift (St. Helens) said : 1 These are a batch of cases arising out of the recent Local Board election at Prescot, and I am instructed to prosecute. My friend Mr. Riley is instructed to represent the defen- dants, and as counsel are appearing for bcth parties they have, for their own convenience, agreed to an adjournment, with the consent of the Bench. I have therefore to ask your worships to allow the case to stand over for a fortnight_. The Chairman : The case is adjourned. HEARTLESS CONDUCT OF A PRESCOT HUSBAND. vv Chadwick, a bottle hand, was charged under a warrant at the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday last, with deserting his wife and child, whereby they became chargeable to the Prescot Union.—Mr. S. H. Hartley (clerk to the Board of Guardians), who prosecuted, stated ,that for some time the prisoner's wife had been an inmate of the Rainhill County Lunatic Asylum, and was there maintained at the cost of the ratepayers. Some few months ago she was discharged from that institution as recovered, and she was sent back to the workhouse, and from there to her husband. She then discevered that the husband—the prisoner—was living with another woman, and the poor wife who had just left the Asylum was compelled to stay in the house until ultimately her husband, and the woman he was living with, suddenly left, and the Union Authprities had considerable difficulty in ascertaining his whereabouts. They afterwards found I him at Manchester. An order had previously been made upon him to contribute 4s. per week towards the support of his wife while she was in the Asylum, and the sum of 1 £4 lie, was owing upon that order. The Guardians had instructed him to ask the Bench to deal with the prisoner as hard as they could, by inflictingthe highest possible penalty, —Mr. Stewart, relieving officer, gave evidence in support of this Statement; after which the chairman said it sunned to have been a deliberate attempt on the part of the D7isoner to get rid of his wife, and he had been cruel and hareh towards her. They would act up to the application of the clerk of the Guardians and would ememit the priaoner for three months with hard labour.

PRESCOT LOCAL BOARD. At the monthly meeting of this Board, held on Wednesday night, there were present—Messrs. C. Spenceley (chairman), T. P. McEgan, T. S. Preston, H. Whitfield, W. Hatton, T. P. Hewitt, W. Goldsworth (surveyor), H. Cross (clerk), and Dickenson (sanitary inspector). VITAL STATISTICS—The Registrar's report frit the month of April showed 9 deaths (Prescot 8 and Eccleston 1), and in the corresponding month last year 10 deaths (9 Prescot and 1 Eccleston). The rate was 16 82 of the estimated popu- lation as against 18.68 last year. The births were as fol- lows :—Prescot 17, Eccleston 1; corresponding month last year, Prescot 20, Eccleston I. MEDICAL OFFICEE'C. ANNIIA.L REPORT.—The annual re- port of the Medical Officer of Health was read by the Chair- man. It stated that the past year had been a very favour- able one, the deaths in all classes of disease having been fewer than they have been for some years. In the cases of disease of an infectious character everything was clone to prevent a recurrence of the disease. The health of the dis- trict at the end of the year was most satisfactory, ,no disease of an infeetions nature being present. The common lodging-houses in Prescot were under the care of the police, and 'as far as his in- spection went, with satisfactory results. The slaughter- houses were also in a much better condition than formerly, but some connections with the main sewers still remained to be done. Cottage property was in a much better state than formerly, and he did not think there was much over crowd- ing. The number of births rekistered during the year was 234 and the deaths 115. The death rate was a very low one for a town, viz., 17.8,,per 1,000 of the population. The zymotic death fate was also extremely low, viz., 07 per 1,000. The per centage of deaths also in children under five years was much less than usually, there being only forty per cent, of the whole deaths, or 15.8 per cent, on the total births. The total birth, rate was quite up to the average, viz., 36.4 per 1,000 of the population.—The Clerk asked if it was desirable that the report should be printed and circulated amongst the members.—Mr. Hewitt thought they. could not very well consider it without its being printed; and Mr. Preston expreased the opinion that it would be satisfactory if they had, a more definite repert as to the pro- perty, not specifiedywhich was said to be in an unsanitary, state.—The Chairman thought they ought to have the pro- perty specified.—The Surveyor observed that if the Board wished a special report on all the sanitary property in the , town it could be drawn up.—Mr- Preston thought it wouldi be a good thing to adopt the suggestion.—Mr. Hewitt again said he thought they ought to have the Medical Officer'sl report printed in order to give it due consideration—Mr.l McEgan :lam of the same opinion.—lt was ultimately re-- solved that the Medical Officer be asked to specify the in- sanitary property in the district —the report to be brought- before the next meeting.—The Surveyor and Sanitary- Inspector were afterwards instructed to inspect all ashpits and middens that were in an unsanitary condition, and re- port upon theca at the next meeting. There was no other business of interest.

div.head: NEWTON COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: NEWTON COMMISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on IVlonday afternoon; present Messrs. W. F. Gooch (in the chair), J. E. Pardey, J. W. Emmett, T. J. Gillespie, T. Forster, B. B. Glover, T. Stone, Thomas Hunt, James Fair- dough, J. E. Worsley (law clerk), and R. Rrierley (sur- veyor). MEDICAL OFFICER'S QUARTERLY REPORT.—DT. Watkins (medical officer of health) attended and read his report for the first quarter of the current year, which showed that there were registered :—Births, 52 males, 61 females, total 113; deaths. 17 males, 19 females, total 36; excess of births over deaths 35 males, 42 females, total 77. The birth-rate was 3939, and the death-rate 125 per thousand of the popula- tion. The infantile deaths were 27.77 per cent, and the deaths of persons above 60 years of age 33 35 per cent of the gross number. Of the latter group 5 were between 60 and 70, 5 between 70 and 80, and 2 were above 80 years of age. It would be observed that there was not in the whole three months a single death amongst the children from pulmo- nary disease. There were three inquests—two upon persons ' who died by accident (one of them a stranger in the place), I and theother upon a man whose last illness was supposed to be traceable to an accident some time previous.ly. Look- ing to these vital statistics, and especially regarding the comparatively low infantile death-rate and the high per centage of those who had attained the natural span of human life, it was his happiness to record the last quarter to have been one of unprecedented health. He regretted to state there had been a serious amount of sickness for some I time at the Reformatory. It had been of a severe febrile type, marked by persistent high temperatures and develop- ing in its course acute lung complicatiens. After exhausting the consideration of all probable causes of the special visi- tation of sickness and its continuance, it was his painful duty to state his belief that it was attributable to pollution of the atmosphere by sewage, and especially at the point of the influx of the Earlestown sewage into the Newton brook direct to windward, and at a very short distance from the Reformatory.—The report was referred to the Highway and Sanitary Committee. THE NEW CEMETERY —A meeting of the Highways, I Public Works, and sanitary Committee was held on the 21st ult. A letter was read from Mr. Roll, of the London and North-Western Railway Company Estate Department, asking for some steps to be taken to dispose of the sewage flowing into the canal from the west end of Earlestown, and it was ordered that Messrs. Gooch, Fairclough, Glover, Pardey, and Stone be a special committee to meet and confer 1 with Mr. Hull upon the subject generally.—The Surveyor I submitted specifications and quotations for the necessary team labour on the roads and to the gas works ; the same having been considered, it was resolved that the quotations of Mr. Richard Hunt be accepted for the ensuing three years.—Tenders for forming and sewering the site for the cemetery were read and examined, when it was ordered that I the tender of Mr. William Cunliffe, of Leigh, amounting I to £823 183 be accepted, subject to the usual agreement and bond being entered into.—The following plans were sub- mitted and approved :—Alterations to house in Park-road; *James Wright, three houses in Wargrave-road ; Gillespie and Mason, stabling in Wargrave New-road. The plan for the Primitive Methodist new schools was put back for more information; and those of James Starkie, alterations to premises in Market-street, were rejected as being too limited in the yard area.—The minutes were passed.
THE ALLEGED BURIAL SCANDAL AT NEWTON: IMPORTANT DISCUSSION.

After the minutes of the Highways Public Works, and Sanitary Committee had been confirmed, Mr. Emmett stated that a large number of the inhabitants ot,Earlestown were anxious that the cemetery should be pushed on and com- pleted as soon as possible,especiallv seeing what took place at St. Peter's Church about a week ago. The vicar there, he understood, refused to take the body of the late Mr. Goldsworthy into the church, and a part of the burial ser- vice was not read over it. That made the people of Earles- town very anxious that the cemetery should be pushed on with all possible speed, seeing that there was no knowing what might take place at one church or the other.—Mr. Pardey was exceedingly sorry that that should have been brought forward before the Board. He certainly knew, not only from the letter of the vicar about the matter, but had been told distinctly that the vicar of St. Peter's did not refuse in any way to take the body into the church, and he thought before such things were brought hefore the public the truth should be ascertained. He was pleased to see one gentleman present, a brother-in-law of the deceased, who attended the funeral, and he would like him to explain the case, so that they would know if there was any truth in what bad been stated.—Mr. Emmett: I may say I have got my information from the newspapers and some of the people that were attending the funeral Mr. Thomas Hunt said he thought he would be able to give them a little explanation of the matter with respect to the funeral not being taken into the church. The Vicar met the funeral at the church door, and said there was another funeral to take place, and it ought to have been up at the same time as theirs. But the other funeral had not come, and would not be up for ten minutes or a quarter of an hour. It would keep him there a long time, and if they would take the remains to the grave he would go on with that portion of the service' and if they would fellow him he would read the service. He (Mr. Hunt) remonstrated with the Vicar, and said that they would wait until the other funeral did come up, but he then said it would keep him all thy. He (Mr. Hunt) knew the Vicar was not well, and be had some sympathy for him, and did according to his request, taking the remains to the grave. The Vicar said, "We will return to the church, and the other funeral will then be up, awl the other portion of the service can be read for both." He (Mr. Hunt) must certainly confess it was an irregular way of doing the service, but they were agreeable to it ; and they did as the Vicar requested. He was sure the Vicar was much grieved when he saw it was announced in the papers that such a thin a had taken place, and he went to Airs. Goldsworthy in great trouble and wanted ber to write to the papers. She was sorry that such an a fliir should get into the papers, as it was contrary to what her husband wished. Her husband was really a churchman; having been baptized and brought up in the Church of Enedand,but he had a great liking for prayer meetings, and it was on ac- count of the prayer meetings that he getterally attended the Wesleyans. He thought there had really been a mistake, and out of sympathy for Mr. Monk he thought it was a matter of little moment, although he supposed many of the friends of the Dissenters had taken objection, and had blamed him (Mr. Hun* saying that he might to have con- sulted them first. Really he did not think there was any necessity for doing that. He was sorry it had got into the pipers, and he thought they bad no reason to think other- wise than that Mr. Monk was really doing what he thought was right—Mr. Pardey said he understood there was not a distinct refusal to take the body into the church.—Mr. Hunt replied that there was not a distinct refusal.—Mr. Glover thought the Vicar simply acted as he had done as a matter of convenience. If Mr. Goldsworthy had been the first dissenter Mr. Monk had had to bury then there might have been something in it, but when he bad buried them for years he 111 r. Glover) did not think Mr. Monk bad any in- tention of refusing to take the body into the church.—Mr. Emmett: Of course, I can quite understand Mr. Hunt put- ting the best construction upon the Vicar's actions that he possibly can. The Vicar, however, wrote a letter in answer to something that appeared in one of the Liverpool papers, but he did not deny that he refused to take the body into the church, and therefore I think it would have been better if the Vicar had stated distinctly that he did not refuse to al.

div.head: DYNAAIITE EXPLOSION IN SCOTLAND.
div.p: DYNAAIITE EXPLOSION IN SCOTLAND.
TEN LIVES LOST.

A terrific explosion of dynamite occurred on Thursday morning in one of the huts at Nobel's txplosive manufac- tory, Ayrshire, and four peepons were blown to pieces. The flames were speedily got under, but not before six, other girls bad been burned to death before the eves of their fel- lowemployde who could render no assistance. Of fifteen girls employed in the four huts ten were killed, two were so injured that they are not expected to recover, and only three escaped. The structural damage is very small, not extending beyond £BO. Another account says:—The buildings lay- scattered about, no two of them standing together. Employment was given to about 250 workpeople, men and women. Dynamite and other explosives are manufactured in large quantities, and owing to the dangerous nature of the substances every precaution is taken against accident. The explosion took place at about half-past eight o'clock in one of the huts where dynamite cartridges are made, and where there was about two hundred-weight and a hail of dynamite at the time. The report of the explosion, was heard many miles away, and tha force of the shock attending it wag so great that in the town of Irvice, three or four miles distant, doors and, windows were I shaken, and in soma of the shops articles were thrown off I the shelves. The hut in which the explosion, took place was of course smashed to atoms, and the body of one of thel g:rls employed in it was thrown outside the paliaade which forms one of the boundaries of the manufactory-. Four 1 girls were employed in the but at the time of the explo- sion. and all of them were killed, their bodies being dreadfully mutilated. Three huts immediately adjoining the one in which the explasien occurred took fire, and the dynamite in them' although it did not explode, burned fiercely. There' , were four giro in each hat, and co rapidly and completely I did the flames envelope the whole place that few of the girls could escape'. The scene was a truly shocklng one. Some of the men who happened to be employed in the vicinity rushed to the burning huts only to find that they were unable to render any as- sistance. They could see the girls in the fiery furnace, but could only stand helplees and gaze, horror-stricken. ?Rt. M`Roberts, the maaager of the works, at once took means to prevent the fire spreading to the other huts, 26 in num- ber, and in this he was quite successful. Half-an-hour after the exploslon the fire was completely extinguished, and it was then ascertained that ten girls had met their death and that four had been injured. The accident caused great excitement in the district, and even in Glasgevr, when the news became known.

ALLEGED FOWL STEALING AT ST. HELENS.-At St. Helens Police Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. J. C. Gamble and Dr. Gaskell, two middle-aged women named M.iv Murray and Catherine Connolly, was charged ,Ith staling a hen. worth 2s 6d, the property of Frank Keeney, Atlas-court, Parr.—lt was stated that on Monday =min.?' the ben was in Atlas-court, and that Murray threw some bread to it, and enticed it into her house. It was further alleged that the two prisoners out off its head with a hatchet, but no trace of the bird had been found. Both prisoners protested their innocence, and called witnesses who had been in tlaeir com- pany on Monday, and who stated they had not seen any trace of the hen,—Prisonera were discharged,

LOCAL BOARD MEETING. The monthly meeting of the members of the Huyton- with-Roby Local Board was held at the Local Board Offices, Elnyton, on Tuesday bight, when there were present— Messrs. Dobell (chairman), Siddeley, Banner, Brown, Par- ker, Dalzell, Cooper, Harrison, Swift (clerk.), and Worrall (surveyor).

• TEE' NUISANCES FROM WIDNES ALKALI, WORKS.—The Chairman remarked that be had recently bad- an interview with Messrs. Thornley and Cameron, solicitors, respecting the appointment of an additional inspector under the Alkali Act. He (the Chairman) found that they, as- well as the new inspector, would be exceedingly obliged to anyone who atoll smelled the nuisance from Widnes if they would drop him a line as to the date and about the hour. The inspec- tor was now making arrangements for night and "surprise " visits, and he would be obliged to any one who would render him any assistance. His address was Millhouse, Woolton, He (the Chairman) hoped the reporters would kindly men- tion the fact.

THD HIGHWAY AND SANITARY COMMITTEE.—At a meet- ing of the Highway and Sanitary Committee, held on the 29th ult, attention was drawn to the police station at Roby, which was reported to be in a very damp state, and the clerk read a letter, which he had forwarded to Mr. Hale (Lord Derby's steward) about the matter. Attention was also drawn to the condition of the road and footway in Dam House-lane. The surveyor was instructed to prepare an estimateof the cost of the required repairs. The estimate amounted to £.90 7s for the footpath, and £95 12s for the roadway. Mr. Brown moved that the work be done.—Mr. Brown now intimated that when be moved at the Commit- tee meeting that the work should be done he was under the impression that it would only cost £9o.—Mr. Banner said that the footway was in a good state of repair, and be thought the estimated cost of the repairs to the roadway was too great.—lt was ultimately decided that the minutes be confirmed with the exception of the one referring to the Dam House-lane, which was referred back to the committee. THE APPROACHES TO THE HUYTON RAILWAY STATION. —The Clerk stated that with reference to the approaches to the Huyton railway station he had again written to the au- thorities, and he had received a letter stating that the matter was still under the consideration of the directors, and his communica ion would be laid before them at their next meeting.
Pm/mom—At a meeting of the Finance Committee, held that day, accounts amounting to £l.ll ss, Si. were examined and passed for payment. —The •mieutes were passed.

MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.—The Chairman read the monthly report of the Medical Officer of Health (Dr. Hall) stating that during the month of April the deaths were—ln Huyton 3, Roby 1, Huyton Quarry 0, He believed the health of the township to be satisfactory. This was the only business of interest.

ASHTON. ASHTON LOCAL BOARDO An.ordinary meeting of this Board was held in the Board Room, Ashton, on Wednesday morning. rhere were preeent Messrs. Moubert (chairman), Gaskell, Goitrake, Lowe, Wrig'et, W. Latham, Painter, Roberts, C. Latham, Barton, Boardman, Simpkin, Laithwaite, Woods, Goldsworth (clerk), Hill (assistant clerk), Chambers (inspector). HIGHWAY AND SANITARY COMMITTER.,--IG was stated in the minutes of this committee that on the motion of Mr. W. Latham, seconded by Mr. Barton, Mr. Moubert had been unanimously elected chairman for the ensuing year.—The Esanuth: The estimate for the maintenance and improve- ment of the highways for the year ending 25th March, 1885, amounting to £1,408, and the estimate of the cost of scavenging amounting to £440 for the same period, had been considered, and on the motion of Mr. C Latham, seconded by Mr. Pimblett, the sums named were reootnniended for the approval of and adoption by the Finance Committee.— Rectihouyßridges : The Surveyor reported that he had written to Mr. Worthington, engineer to the London and Nerth-Western Railway Company, offering on the part of the Board to undertake the repairs of the railway approach roads for an annual payment of £15.-3Tagying Footpath in Gerrard-street: A letter was received from Mr. Thomas Barton asking the committee to reconsider their decision as 'to this work. It was resolved, on the motion of the Rev. IL Siddall, seconded by Mr. C. Latham, that as the offer to pay one-half the cost of -flagging the footpath as made at last meet was according to the usual arrangements in similar instances the committee could not vary, it in this case.— Sunitarylnspector's Report: The book kept by this officer showed that during the month eight nuisances bad been abated on verbal notice being given; ,in six other cases notices had been served, and in another instance notice had to be given.—New Plans : Plans of four new houses were submitted by Mr. Cunliffe, on behalf, of the Brynn Garswood Friendly Society. These houses were proposed tc be built in Rectorytroad. The Surveyor reported that the plans were in accordance with the bye-laws, except with respect to the absence of inspection shafts to the drains, and the committee resolved, on the motion of Mr. Barton, seconded by Mr. Pimblett, that the plans be sanctioned subject to the. omission being made good.—Tbese minntsa- were adopted. -

SERIOUS 01:172...11EA1E o Sa'ARLATINA.— Dr. N. Hannah (medical officer), reported to the ilighway and Sanitary Committee as follows :—I have to report that during the four weeks ending 26th instant, 20 deaths were registered, viz.: Measiell (Brynn Gate), erysipelas 1 (Nichol-lane), croup 1, scar:et fever 3 (Cross-lane. Downall Green 3, and Sims-lane-end 2), phthisis I, lung disease 3, other diseases 8, and accidents 2. The births for the same period were— males 17, females 22, total 39. With regard to the scarla- tina, I must further add that the disease is fast assuming an epidemic form, the wa-re passing over us from Wigan and Pemherton, The three deaths were registered last week, and on Monday I received a special return of another death from it at Factory Houses, Downall Green. During the past two months, 9 childrea in all have succumbed Left; all in Downall Green (N.-W.), division of the township. I have written copy letter to, be forwarded to all the schools, solici- ting the co-operation of the teachers by their exercising great care and caution iti re-admitting scholars after absence from ally cause, and possibly some good might result in uniting local medical men, as to treating cases by isolation in your temporary hospital. I yesterday advised• Mr. Golds- worth as to the necessity of issuing some handbills of "P&; precauticns for pelevouting its furtl.ot, spread." It is my duty to aclpaint the Local Government Board of this outbreak and I purpose doing so to-morrow. Two of the houses at Dowaall Green, between colliery and warehouse, ought to be provided at once with two new, closets, the old ones being entirely dilapidated and cause of nuisance. The same property also is void of through ventilation there being no hack doors-and the windows fast. I should suggest that the owner meet Mr. Goictsworth and myself with a view of improving their sanitary condition generally. I have been requested ta mention to your Board that many oomplaints have been :nada from Rosehill district in relation to the emptying of nightsoil, dm., the stench of course being more noticeabls and disagreeable in the day-time than its removal were at night, perhaps Mr. Chambers will endeavour to obviate the nuisance complained of.—After considering this report the committee agreed, on the motion of Mr. PimMett. seconded by Mr. Barton, that it be approved of and instructions given to carry out the suggestions made therein, and to serve the requisrte notices.—ln answer to a r_aestima with regard to the scarlatina, the Assistant Clerk stated that since the meeting of the Committee on the previous Wed- nesday, six more certificates of deaths had been sent in, THE NEW RATE.—In the minutes of the Finance Commit- tee it was stated that if the deficiency on the waterworks for 1884 and 1885 was provided for, the amount to be raised by general district rate would be £5,972 14s 9d. The cem- mittee had agreed to recommend the Board to lay a general district rate of 28 in the pound to meet expenditure to Sep- tember 25, 1884.—05. the motion of Mr. Grinske, seconded by Mr. Roberts, this recommendation was adopted UNPAID FOR WATER : FIR.E &MM.-4n the minutes of the Gas and Water Committee It was stated that Mr. Woods had mentioned a case of persons not having a water supply , using the Board's water without paying for it, and inquiry having been made if other similar instances were known, , the committee directed a list of all properties in the district not yet supplied with water to be made up and submitted to their next meeting. The minutes also stated that the ques- tion of purchasiug a Are engine had been fully considered

HINTON- by the committee, and it was agreed that the farther cog. Clunacit or ENGLAND TE2CPER.LNCE SOCIETT.—An ex- sideration of the subject be adjourned for six month These minutes ,a ere adopted morn. dis: cursion trip to Frodshani, under the auspices of the Huyton This was all the business of public interest. branch of the above society, was made on Monday. Between thirty and forty members, amongst whom were the Rev. Canon Penrhyn, Mrs. Penrhyn, Rev, H. d'a. Hubbard, Mr. and Mrs. Williams, Misses Willis and Guest, Mr. Rigby, and Mr. Webster formed the pic-nic party. They arrived at Frodsham about 10-30; and after enjoying rambles on the hills and various out-door games, sat down to a substantial re'past. Before leaving the party atten-led service at Frod- sham Parish Church; the Rev. Canon Penrhyn conducted the service. Home was reached about 10 o'clock. The trip was thoroughly enjoyed. 2ND LANCASHIRE ENGINEER VOLUNTEERS.—A full dress parade took place on Saturday, at their headquarters, Whit- field House, Roby. It was intended to have a march out, but owing to the inclemency of the weather this was post- poned. An inspection was made by Colonel Rothwell, of dress, accoutrements, and arms. There were also present Lieutenant Higgin, Adjutant Byrne, Drill-Instructor Goss, Sergeant-Major Bernard, Sergeants Edwards and Tomes, and about 30 rank and file. The Colonel complained of the men not attending drill. The band afterwards marched to Huy- ton. On the Monday following upwards of 70 members of the corps attended for drill, but for some reason or other there was no one to drill them. They satisfied themselves by recording their names as present for that purpose in ac- I leordance with their Colonel's command. A DRUNKEN LITERPOOL Dusvau.—Before Mr. Earle and Captain Willis, at the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday last, Joshua Hewitt, a young man, of Liverpool, was charged with being drunk in charge of a horse and trap at Huyton, on the 11th April.—The defendant pleaded guilty. —P.C. Crook deposed that on Good Friday afternoon he saw the horse and trap being driven furiously along the road, and when it came towards him he put up hie hand for the driver to stop. The defendant was in charge, and on reach- ing the officer he struck the latter across the neck with the whip. He (witness) caught hold of the conveyance and stOpped the horse' whereupon he found that the defendant was drunk.—The Bench said if the defendant could not behave himself with his tricks when he went out driving on the highway it would become a serious matter to him in time. He must pay a fine of 20s and costs, or, in default, one month's imprisonment. There were many complaints throughout all that district of furious driving about the I roads;

div.head: WRECK OF THE STATE OF FLORIDA-
div.p: WRECK OF THE STATE OF FLORIDA-

123 LIVES LOST. A telegram, which has been received from Father Point, Quebec, states that the steamer Titania, from Glasgow, which passed that station inward at a quarter to six on Tuesday morning, has en board 24 persons from the State of Florida, which it reports to have been sunk by collision with a barque in mid-ocean. The captain of the Titania states that out of 167 persons en board the State of Florida only 44 were saved. The remaining twenty are supposed to have escaped in another beat, and to have been picked LIP hY, a passing vessel. The name Jf the barque is unknown. Or her crew of fifteen men only the captain and three men were saved, the remaining twelve being lost. The survi` yore will probably be landed at Quebec. It is reported that none of those saved are women. The State Line Company, Glasgow, received the follow.' ing cablegram on Wednesday afternoon from their New York agents (Messrs. Austin, Baldwin, and Co) regarding the fate of the State of Florida The steamship Titania, just arrived at Quebec, landed part of the crew of the Florida—which had been in collision with a barque---24- hands in all; 20 others are supposed to have been picked 119 by another vessel ; 123 are lost."' The Titania is a Glasgow vessel, belonging to the firm of Donaldson Bros. Immediately on the receipt of the above cablegram the manager of the State Line, Mr. Murray, re- quested Messrs. Donaldson Bros. to cable their Montrea. agents for further details of the disaster, in particular for the names of those who have been saved. Messrs. Donald- ' son Bros. have done so. and it is expected that full 'Adieu' , lars wdl be received shortly. Another telegram states that the owners of the State of Florida have requested Messrs. Donaldson Bros., Glasgow'. owners of the steamship Titania, to cable at once to their agents in Montreal, instructing them to cable immediately I full list of persons saved. It is quite probable that the 20' others supposed to have been picked up by another veseel are those on board of the sailing ship which signalled on the. • 27th of April to-the steamship City of Rome. The Stat.' Line Steamship, Company are beeping :heir Glasgow officer open to late hours in anticipation of the receipt of further telegrams concerning the survivors. A Glasgow correspondent, later, says :—Up to 10 on iire4...l nesday night nothing further had reached the GlasgeW office of the State Line Steamship Company, although thd had expected that by that time an answer to their telegtal!X would have been received from Montreal. A large crevra of the relatives of. the crew and passengers are waiting at, the door of the office anxious to obtain the latest news, an° several of the wives of the crew who are waiting within the' office have difficulty in controlling their grief. The excite.", ment in Glasgow is very great, many years having elaPsett since a Glasgow-American liner has gone down. The State of Florida, a, was an iron screw barque-riggel.' , vessel of 3,153 tons gross, built in Gasgow in 1875, arr; I owned by the State Steamship Company (Limited). 87; was classed 109 A 1 at Lloyd's. She left New York 0" April 12, bound for the Clyde.

LIST OR SURVIVORS. A Quebec telegram received in Glasgow, on Thursde forenoon, says :—The survivors state that on the IStn, about midnight, the Pomona collided with the Florida, bog' sinking in fifteen minutes. Four boats were launchen• After forty hours' exposure they were picked up by o_B barque Theresa, boned for Quebec. Among the sarvivor° are—James Allan, Andrew Steel, Wiliam Armstrong, Francis Graham, David Walker David Clunie, Alex. obeli, James Thomas, William Walker, George Forrester, Nei' M'Kellar, James M'Kenzie, Robert Young, John M‘Dottaldr John Sanstran, John M•Gaw, Adam M‘Farlane, Win. Miller, James Bennett, W. 11PFarlane, David Struther, Jarnel Patience, Jonah Hale, and Eliza Churchonse. Those re" maining with the Theresa are—James Thompson Barr, John Smith (boatswM-ra), Peter Paterson, Henry Anderson, Johp Silverblade, John Miller, John Smith, Charles Love, Georg! Armour, John Beard, Wm. Lawson, WM. Hislop, Edwarcl Boyle, John M‘Dowell, Jane MTarlane, Hugh Morgan, Peter Kenning, Martin Paterson, and Francis Watson.

LATEST DETAILS. QUEBEC, WEDNESDAY EVENING,—The et eam er State of Florida collided with the barque Ponema of Chatham, Nal/ Brunswick. on the 18th of April. The cight was clear, but there was no :moon at the time of the collision. Both vas' eels sank. The survivors were picked up by the Norwegian barque Theresa, bound for Quebec, and 24 of their number were transferred on the 22ud to the barque Louisa, f?t. Quebec, and afterwards were taken on board the steamshiP, Titania on May sth. Captain Heplarnlind two seamen 0` the Ponema are also on the Theresa. QUEBEC, 7EURSDAY.—Mr. Allan, third officer of the State of Florida", reports that the survivors were thirty-00 hours in the boats without food or water. Toe sea at On time of the collision was smooth. 04 eight boats carded by the State of Florida four were lowered, two having been previously smashed by the collision. Soon after the boat!' were lowered the State of Florida heeled to port and sank stern foremost. Mr. Allan thought the disaster occurred in 49 N. latitude, and 34 W. longitude. Everybody on decks • including the ctptain, was washed overboard. The resulted men present a pitiable spectacle, several of them wearing , only their nightdresses when saved, The women absolute / refused to leave the ship or many of them could have bee° saved. Jane Macfarlane, the stewardeso, was the only wool° saved. Mr. 4ames Bennett is the only first class passene saved. nugeon Steele has expressed the opinion that Wet real cause of the disaster will never be known on accann of its extreme suddenness.

„ A Liverpool correspondent writes :—ft has been 00'; tamed that the vessel which collided with the State a' Florida and afterwards sank was the Panama, hound frail ' Liverpool to Miramichi. She was a, wooden barque of 7t14 tons register, and left the Mersey on the 10th of April ballast for Miramichi. The agents say the number of ber crew as stated in the newspapers—M all told—is quite cor- • rect, but tbe name of the captain appears to be inaccla rately given. The master's name is. Heyburn. The Ponelaa has been employed for some,considerable time in the timber carrying trade between Canada and Liverpool. She was te property 0 Messrs. J. and T. Jardine, of Hichibuote, a , was built there in 1875.
