RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
RUNCORN COUNTY COURT. TuEsnsi.—Before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoalkee. Judge.
LANAGES AGAINST • RIINCOB- N CAB PROPRIETOR. -
Birtlea, of Crewe, claimed from Jame Peck, cab

proprietor, Runcorn, the sant of £5O damages for personal injuries sustained by ,the plaintiff in consequence of the negligence of the defendant's servant. Mr. J. Pickford, barrister-at-law, Liderpool (instructed •by Mr. Hill, of Crewe), appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. A. Fletcher, of ICorthwich, appeared for the defendant. A jury had been empanelled to hear the case, Mr. T. S. Carr being foreman. The other members were Messrs. S. Coventry, John Coxhill, William Owley, and William Craddock.—Mr. Pickford, in addressing the jury, said the accident happened on the 30thl October last just outside the Runcorn railway station while the verandah over the footpath at the entrance to the station was being painted by the defendant and a boy named Hard- ing. In order to do this they had an erection of this kind. They had two ladders which were interlocked with each other at the pavement. The top of one of the ladders Was resting against the wall of the station and the top of the other against the overhanging part of the verandah. Between the ladder there was a plank resting upon the rungs. Upon this plank the two men were standing, and for two hours land a half until half-past nine they worked upon it safely, and there was no indications of danger. The length of the ladder was about 14 feet, and the plank was about 10 .11letallAVe- the-grotual, go that there would be plenty of 'room for any vehicle to be drawn up to the station properly to take passengers. About half-past nine a cab which had been standing at the entrance to the station drove away, and another passenger appearing came up, and the defendant's son who was in charge of a one-horse omni- bus, which, he believed, though it was of no importance, had been standing on the wrong side, drew up. The height of the vehicle would be about six feet six inches. Hard- ing seeing the omnibus coming, and seeing also that there would not be sufficient room for it to pees between the parapet and a trap that was standing there, and that possibly the omnibus might come in contact with the ladder, he shouted out to the cabman to stop. The cabman did not alter his course in the least, and the result was exactly as Harding had anticipated. The wheel of the omnibus ran upon the footpath and the top of the omnibus struck the ladder, and the scaffolding fell. The cabman was on the farthest side of his horse from the station, and was backing the vehicle. If he showed that these were the facts of the case, he thought under the direction of his Honour, the jury would come to the conclusion that careless and improper manage- ment of the vehicle had caused the injury to the plaintiff, and the defendant, whose son was his servant, must pay such damages as the plaintiff had suffered. The plaintiff and Harding fell with the scaffolding, the former, alighting upon the ground, a ladder and the plank dropped upon him, The plaintiff was taken up in a senseless condition, and was attended by Dr. McDougall, and then removed to the Infirmary provided by the railway at Crewe. It was there found that some of his ribs were broken and that he had been otherwise injured. For 12 weeks he was entirely pre- vented from working, and his wages for that period would amount to about £l5. In addition to that he had incurred £5 expenses for extra care and nourishment, so that he had suffered in a pecuniary sense about £2O. But he was en- titled to such damages as the jury thought proper and rea- sonable for the pain of mind and body that he had suffered by the defendant's negligence. Harding did not suffer Mich injury, be fell upon the top of the 'bus.—The plain- tiff was called and confirmed his advocate's statement. He was facing the station wall, and therefore did not see the accident. The scaffolding was sufficiently high to allow any vehicle to pass underneath it without touching it. He had not felt so well in health since the accident as he did before, and never would. He was a widower with three children, two of whom supported them- selves.—ln cross-examination by Mr. Fletcher, wit- nes stated that the plank would be between nine and ten feet from the pavement. He never warned any- body about the ladders, as he saw no necessity for it.— Samuel Harding, of Middlewich-street, Crewe, said he was working with the last witness when the accident occurred. He believed the plank projected a little over the roadway, but he could not say how far. The 'bus struck the ladder. —By Mr. Fletcher : A very little touch did it. The driver was proceeding slowly and cautiously.—Wm. Davenport, foreman painter in the employ of the London and North- Western Railway Company, deposed that the way the scaf- folding was erected was safe, and when he saw it 20 minutes before the accident a carriage could pass under it without harm if it had kept in the roadway. There were marks on the parapet where the wheels of the omnibus had been.— Mr. Christopher Henry Wentworth Bennett, pupil to Dr. Atkinson, surgeon at the London and North-Western Hos- pital, Crewe, described the injuries of the plaintiff. The two lower ribs of the left side were broken, and his spine was Injured; while he had a cut on the back of his head an Inch and a half long. The plaintiff was three weeks in the hospital, and witness attended him subsequently seven weeks at his home. He was not fit to work during that period. The plaintiff would not be in his usual health until Septem- ber.—This completed the evidence for the plaintiff.—Alder- man Joseph Harrison, Mayor of Warrington, was the first witness called for the defence. He said that on the morn- ing of the accident he arrived at Runcorn by train, and , went to the entrance of the station to look for a 'bus or Cab. Immediately Peck's boy saw him he drew his convey- ance to the footpath. As he was approaching he believed the top of the 'bus came into contact with the projecting plank. The 'bus certainly did not touch the ladder; but with the upper portion of the scaffold, and down came this unfortunate man. The other man deliberatley jumped on the top of the 'bus, and so saved himself. The upper por- tion of the scaffold projected over the roadway. The wheels of the 'bus did not come on the footpath. He was positive about that: He never heard any intimation given to the boy to stop.—James Bell, coachman to Captain C. W. Hazlehurst, deposed that the scaffold projected over the channel, and the iron round the top of the 'bus caught the plank. The ladders slipped along, and Harding then shouted out "stop," and young Peck at once stopped the vehicle. The scaffold and men fell. The wheels of the 'bus never left the channel. —John Peck, the driver of the 'bus, made a similar state- ment. He was leading the horse by the head, walking backwards.—Thomas Caygill, joiner and cabinet maker, Church-street, Runcorn, stated that the verandah was 13 feet 6 inches high to the eaves. From the station wall to edge of the verandah was 10 feet 9 ihches, and the breadth of the parapet was 7 feet 6 inches, showing a projection of 3 feet 3 inches.—The plaintiff was called and proved that the height of his 'bus was 7 feet 4 inches.—Mr. Fletcher then addressed the jury, contending that the plaintiff bad contributed to the accident by the flimsy construction of the scaffold and also that there was no person there to warn people who were going to the station in the ordinary dis- charge of their duties that the scaffold was there, and they must exercise more than ordinary care in approaching the station. The very movement of the men upon the plank must have been almost calculated to bring such a scaffold as that described to the ground, and the slightest touch of the 'bus caused it to fall. He asked the jury whether to erect a scaffold like that in a place where vehicles were constantly coming to and fro was not very negligent? If that were so the plaintiff was not entitled to any compensation whatever.—Mr. Pickford dissented from Mr. Fletcher's doctrine of contributory negligence. The doctrine was—and his Honour would cor- rect hint if he were wrong—that although the plaintiff might not have done all he might have done, still if the defendant, by the exercise of ordinary and reasonable care could have avoided injuring him, but dces not do so, he was liable : and the plaintiff was entitled to a verdict in this case, even if they accepted every word the defendant's wit- nesses had said.—His Honour, in summing up, said he differed with Mr. Flether as to what constitutes contribu- tory negligence. Supposing the scaffold was ever so weak and flimsy, if it was -sufficient for the work the men were performing and would hold them, that was sufficient. The men were not liable to make it strong enough to resist an elephant if such an animal ran against it. There was no evidence to show that the scaffold was not sufficient to hold the men. It ,was immaterial whether the 'bus struck the ladder or the plank; it was admitted that the vehicle caused the structure to fall; and the question for the jury was whether young Peak exercised the ordinary care and prudence required on thie occasion. If not the jury would find a verdict for the plaintiff, and consider what damages he was entitled to.—The jury, after a consultation in pri- vate, returned a verdict for the plaintiff, damages £lo. On the application of Mr. Pickford, his Honour granted costs on the higher scale.—Mr. Pickford said he might think it right to move for a new trial on the ground that the damages were insufficient—there was absolutely no con- tradiction of the loss of £26. When could he do so2—lt was decided that he could do se at the next court held at Runcorn.

ACTION BY Tag Rl:mecum COMMISSIONERS.—The Run- corn Board of Improvement Commissioners sought to re- cover from Mr. B. Beckett, builder and contractor, of Hart- ford, the Bum of £2 18s 8t for damages sustained by them by reason of the negligence of the de- fendant in the erection of a wooden shed at the site of the Church of St. Michael and Allangels, Runcorn.-- Mr. W. H. Linaker was for the plaintiffs, and Mr. A. Fletcher for the defendant.—Mr. Linaker said Mr. Beckett was the contractor for the erection of the church named upon a piece of land in Greenway-road, given by Major Orred. In Octhber and November last year Mr. Beckett put a wooden boarding round the site, and at the Greenway-road side erected a wooden shed with a sloping top and open an the side facing the enclosure. On the 12t1 December the top of the shed was blown away by a strong wind, and it came in contact with a lamp post belonging to the Commissioners, doing damage to the extent sued for. The question for his Honour to decide was whether the defendant took proper care and precaution in the construction of the abed so that in ordinary winds the property of no one should be damaged. —His Honour: You don't dispute the right to erect 2—Mr. Linsker said they did not raise any question of right.—Mr. M. Barker, surveyor to the Commissioners, described the hoarding and shed, which was in a very exposed position, especially to west winds. He did not see the lamp post broken, but from the position in whicn the debris from the shed was found the roof must have struck the poet in its cottisidS. ' fit Ofterwarde examined the shed. He considered the way in which the wall plate had been nailed to the up- right was not sufficient to hold it. It ought to have been bolted or strapped down.—By Mr. Fletcher: It was a very heavy storm, but he had known worse. Ile never made any complaint about the shed, the Board of Commissioners did not acknowledge them. The material was strong enough to resist anything it it had been properly put together.—BV

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.
MAY FESTIVITIES AT GOLBORNE.-CROWNING THE MAY QUEEN.

The village of Golborne was en fete on Saturday, when, notwithstanding the very unseasonable weather, the annual ceremony of crowning the "Queen of the May" was cele- brated amid great rejoicings. Though the custom has only been observed in Glolborne for the past half-dozen years, it has now become to be looked upon as 008 of the most im- portant events in the district, and thousands of persons flock from the neighbouring towns and villages to witness the in- teresting ceremony. The gathering on Saturday last was no exception to the rule, though as far as atmospherical condi- tions were concerned a more uncongenial state of things could scarcely have been imagined. Instead of being a re- minder of the gaiety and joyousness one is accustomed to associate with the advent of the "merriest month of the twelve "—the month of sunshine and of flowers—the bitterly cold wind, accompanied by lowering clouds and occasional heavy downpours of rain and hail brought vividly to one's memory the bleak and dismal days of December. As in former years the preparations for the gathering were of an extensive character, and the committees having charge of the arrangements actively bestirred themselves in order to make the affair as great a success and the festivities as en- joyable as possible, and there can be no doubt but that the inclement weather spoiled what would otherwise have been the most important May-day celebration ever held in the district. The selection of the May Queen has always evoked the greatest interest in the town, and the day for the balloting, by which the " Queen " is appointed, generally brings with. it eager curiosity. This year the happy chosen one has been Miss Annie Hayes, nine years of age, daughter of a bricklayer residing at Bank Heath, and she was fre- quently complimented by her friends when it became known that she was tha Queen elect for the next twelve months. As the day for the public coronation of "Her Majesty " drew near, preparations for the event were observable in many households. Characteristic dresses for the children were arranged with a neatness highly creditable, while more public preparations were made in a field near the Conserva- tive Club, which had been kindly lent by Mr. A. Caunce, grocer. There a massive " May-pole " was erected, at the foot of which the ceremony was to be per- formed. Stakes and ropes were also planted at a convenient distance in order to keep back the spectators, and evidently everything was done to ensure a most successful " commo- tion," and its attendant festivities. Unfortunately, however, the proverbial fickleness of the weather displayed itself in a marked degree, and as a consequence, what were expected to prove gay and joyous festivities, were turned into a some- what formal though still interesting ceremony.

Early on Saturday morning rain was falling very heavily and as it continued for some hours the spirits of those anxious for a fine afternoon were considerably damped. Be- fore noon, however, the weather "cleared up," and as the sun began to burst through the clouds, the hearts and hopes of thousands of persons in Golborne and the district rose higher and became lighter. Early in the afternoon large numbers of people were observed making their way towards the" royal" town, and hundreds of visitors from Earles- town, Newton, Ashton, Leigh, and other places were met with in Golborne. By half-past two, the time for the com- mencement of the proceedings, the village presented an ani- mated appearance—the streets being densely crowded by thousands of persons dressed in holiday attire. About this time, however, there was another heavy downpour of rain, and the "procession," the first item on the programme was delayed for nearly an hour. On the rain ceasing, the pro- cescion—a truly imposing one—issued from the " royal " grounds. In all nearly 600 persons took part, including "her Majesty," and her attendants, character representa- tions of almost every known branch of industry, and four brass bands. First came the Golborne brass band, and following was the carriage of Mr. Unsworth, containing the ex• Queen (Miss L. R. Yates) and her attendants. Then came a number of boys representing marines and rifle vol- unteers, who were succeeded by the open carriage of T. D. Grimke, Esq., is which rode the Queen-Elect (Miss Hayes) and her crown-bearer (Mies Mort.) This carriage was " the observed of all observers," and as the future Queen rode by in stately dignity-she commanded the respect of all behol- ders. She was attired in a splendidly. worked blue silk dress, made by Mies Yazaokerly, of Earlestowm and a white veil, gracefully thrown over her head and shoulders." Hr Majesty's" train-bearers followed and also a band et "May-pole" dancers. The St. Thomas's (Ashton) brass band was the next in order of the procession, and then were flower girls with baskets of flowers, girls characteristically dressed as Red Riding Hoods, milk maids with,wans and stools, and a van belonging to Mr. Molyneux, of Earlestown, Upon which was a massive loaf of bread I surrounded with a number of smaller loaves. Following the van were a number of gleaners carrying bunches of straw, weavers with their shuttles and brushes, flower girls, and a well got-up representation of a tribe of gipsies with their travelling tent. The "Old Folks," both male and fe- male, were excellently represented, and they were followed by other two of Mr. Molvnenx's vehicles, the last one being filled with sacks of flour. The lads representing " bakers " with their square-cornered paper caps and tins, were fol- lowed by the irrepressible "niggers "—a contrast in "-black and white—and next were the representatives of the " black- smiths," with their Lammers ; labourers, with their horls, spades, dtc.; the street newsboy with a bundle of papers; cricketers with their bats and stamps; miners with their lamps and picks; sailors, .ic.; the rear being brought rig by a "guard "of soldiers. The Edge Green and Low ton brass bands also occupied positions in the latter part of the procession.

The procession paraded the principal streets of the town, and the bands discoursed a selection of lively airs. Fortu- nately, during the greater portion of this tinge the rain held off, but on the coronation field being nearly reached another heavy downpour took place, and many expressions of fear aud sympathy for the children, many of whom were nixes- early but thinly clad, were heard. The ceremony was ' afterwards performed in fine weather; Miss Hayes on I mounting the temporary "throne" at the foot of the May- pole being warmly applauded. Mrs. W. H. Arnott stepped forward, and whilst placing a most beautiful floral crown upon the head of her Majesty, said that she had very great pleasure in crowning her Queen of the May. Sbe hoped she would be a very good girl at all times and be attentive to her parents at home as well as the teachers at school. Cheers followed the " crowning" ceremony, and the bands struck up "God save the Queen," which was heartily sung by the people present. Mrs. Arnett then presented the new queen with a workbox, and the proceedings concluded. A fine exhibition of " may-pole " dancing was afterwards given by a band of 22 girls, who bad been cirefully trained by Mr. T. Berrick. The excellent manner in which the per- formance was given drew forth deserved applause from the onlookers, who also manifested some interest in the evolu- tions and drills of the " marinee " and "soldiers." The bands afterwards played for dancing, which w with interest until dusk.

RUNCORN AND WIDNES. EXTRAORDINARY BOATING FATALITY. Considerable sensation was caused in Widnes, on Tuesday, I by a rumour that during the night a flat had sunk in the London and North-Western Railway Co.'s Dock, with a man and one or two women on board. The facts are these. About the latter end of laet week the flat Emma Styles, of Runcorn, arrived at Widnes Dock, and on Monday was loaded with a cargo of 63 toes of coal for Messrs. Heywood and Massey, glue manufacturers, near Frodsham. The cap- I tain of the craft, James Pickstock, of Frodshatn, ought to have superintended the loading of the cargo, but it is al- leged that instead of doing so be was 'kinking in the town all day, and about ten o'clock at night he was seen going towards his flat in a very intoxicated condition by a man named James Ford. He was then alone, but rumour bad it that he was accompanied by a female of bad character. Daring the night the flat, in consequence, it is supreesed, of , overloading and a leak, sunk, and next morning only the top of its mast was visible above the surface of the water. The "drags" were brought into requisition, but after consider- able labour there was only recovered a pair of trowsers and a shoe. It was therefore decided to run off the water in the dock, and in the evening this was done. A search revealed Pickstock lying in his bunk, dead, with a slight wound over the left eye, but no other human beings were to be found. Part of the cargo was removed, and the water pumped out, snd when the tide had again filled the dock the vessel floated. The deceased was 49 years of age. TILE INC),IIEST YESTERDAY, Mr. S. Brighouse, the county coroner, held the inquest upon the body at the Commercial Hotel, Old Marsh, yes- terday et noon.—CharlesPickstock, 1, Jordon-place, Jordan- street. Little Peter-street, Manchester, said the deceased was his father. and had lived at Frodsham Bridge, Frodsham. lie was 47 years of age.—William Ford said he lived at Widnes. and was a " tipper " of coal at the clocks. On Monday night last, at ten o'clock, be saAr Pickstock coming dewn Gossage's Bridge, on his way to the flat. He was drunk. Witness asked Pickstock where be was going, and he replied that he was going on board the flat. He left him standing against a cask.—Benjamin Blakemore said he was !ism) with his father on board a flat. While on his way to hie father's flat, about a quarter-past eleven on Monday night. he saw a flat in the dock that looked very low in the water. When he got "abreast of her " she sunk.—Thoreas Fyldes, of 49, David-street, WidC6l3, deposed that he helped to load the "Emma Styles" on Monday afternoon. Thomas Holland was with him. The craft was loaded with 63 tons of slack for Frodsham. There was nothing to prevent over- loading, but in his opinion he did not think the "Emmal Styles" was overloaded. lie thought the boat sunk in consequence of taking water in her upper planks, Formerly . the boat had carried carboys of vitroll, which was a light cargo, and the upper part of the boat would not have been immersed in the water for some time, and the seams would open. When the loading was completed at half-past five, the top of Ins boat was within eleven inches of the water, and he tried the pumps, but there was then no water in her.— Henry Urmston, 18, Bridge-street,Rancorn, said he was the owner of the flat, Emma Styles, but he had not seen it for nearly a month. The deceased had worked for him for , seven years. He was not an habitual drunkard, but occa- sionally he would break out. The shipping clerk had in- formed him that the boat had a cargo of 66 tons, which was too much. He had frequently warned the deceased never to take on more thin 60 tons, and 55 tons if he could manage it. The deceased, who was cap- tain, ought to ' have superintended the leading of the boat.—The Coroner said that if the captain had been at his post, instead of unfortunately drinking in the town, this ac- cident would not most likely have occurred. The deceased had brought aboat his death by his own neglect.—The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased came to his death accidentally through the overloading of the flat, and that no blame was attributable to anybody but the de- ceased for the said overloading.

lifflaway Boaan.—'The annual meeting et this Board Was held in the Board-room, Daresbury, on Thursday after- noon. 'There were present—Messrs. E. Greenall, J. Cooper, J. Mayer, W. Wilkinson, T. Massey. .1. Mclntyre, T. J. Rigby, T. Clarke, P. Percival, J. W. Haddock, J. Parr, T. Bennett, A. Kenworthy, S. Rigby H. Hayes, D. Darby- shire, H. Houghton, P. Tickle, D. Rigby, C. T. Whitley, T. Bates, W. Turner, T. Handley, J. Barber, and W. Long Election of Chairman and Vice• Chairman: As that was the annual meeting, Mr. T. Bennett said he begged leave to propose their old chairman• (Mr. E. Greenall) to be again chairman of the Board. As he bad said, the chairman, Mr. Greenall, suited them very well. He was a business man ; he was very courteous ; and before they changed they should look for a better man, who would be very difficult to find. (Hear, bear.) Mr. Mclntyre seconded this proposal, which was carried unanimously., Mr. Greenall, on taking the chair, retu-ned thanks for the compliment they had paid him, and expressed the hope that their business would bares amicably conducted in the future as hitherto. He then pro- posed the re-election of Mr. Cliff as vice-chairman. This proposal was seconded by Mr. Bsrber ; it was also carried unanimously.—Cogshall Brook: Mr. Mclntyre moved that a bridge be built over Cogshall brook, and that a sum not to exceed £2OO be allowed by that Board towards the cost of the bridge. He (Mr. Mclntyre) estimated that the total cost of the bridge would be about £3OO, and he thought if the Board allowed £2oCrtlre other £lOO might be raised by subscription amongst the lacel owners and occupiers. Mr. Rigby seconded the proposal, which was opposed by Mr. T. Bennet, who said that the local owners and occupiers ought to take steps towards raising the money required, but when they had been asked only one of them was willing to do anything. He would like to know what Cogshall township would contribute towards the £2OO, and he was sure the township he represented would have to pay five times as much. The Clerk said Cogshall township would contribute 355. (Laughter.) Mr. Bonnet: I thought so. The Rev. A. Eenworttry also opposed the proposal. If they contributed towards this bridge, he said, they would have seven other ap- plications before it was done. In fact they would always have to be making bridges, and would very likely have to raise their rates to such an extent that, like the Warrington • ieople' they should groan underneath their burden. On fr. Mclntyre's proposal being put to the meeting, only nine In embers voted for it and fifteen against it. It was come- , qu nay lost.—This was all the business of public interest. ‘

div.head: G 'HURCH DISPUTE AT STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: G 'HURCH DISPUTE AT STOCKTON HEATH.

The relations betweea the vicar of Bt. Thomas's, Stockton 11,,ath (the Rev. T. S. Tofts) and a large portion of his parisbic n.ers are, we believe, at the present time in a some- what str. 'tined condition, owing to the notices of dismissal from Mat + posts of master at the National Schools, and organists t the church, whicla have been given to Mr. J. R. Timson. During th,e five or six years which he has held hi s present appointment in the parish, Mr. Timson seems to ha ye won the esteem and good will of almost the whole of h. '5 fell" residetits <in Stockton Heath and its I neighbourho ad, and consequently the somewhat unexpected 1 notices of die missal which have been served upon him have given almost general dissatisfaction. Whether rightly or wrongly we unot say, bat the opinion appears to be popu- larlyCa held that they are not die in any way to any unfitness , in Mr. Timson 1 or the posts he occupies, but rather to a dif- ference which to ok place between him and the vicar a few months ago on , a trivial matter in connection with the USa of the schoolroom for a conceit in aid of a local class, a use which the vicar in ',expectedly and peremptorily forbade. At all events, in the, course of the past two or three weeks a petition protesting a tgainst the dismissal of Mr Timson has been sent round, am, 1, we niolerstand, had appended to it in a comparatively short time the. names of over 500 persons, which, considering t he. small size of the parish, seems te argue an unusual Milli aumty of feeling. This list of persons it is said, includes tht 1 whole, or almost the whole, of the • parents who send theii children to the school of which Mr. Timson is master, the a embers of the choir, the sidemen, and nearly all the conk regation. A copy of this petition ' bee been sent to the vical , and to each of the trustees of the • school. It is perhaps nat orally thought by the promoters of OP petition that as thoss t who send their children to the school acd pay the school Pence, are aided by the Govern- ment grant. practically the . main supporters of the school, this emphatic expression 01 their satisfaction with the ser- vices of MY. Timsen as schoolmaster may have its due weight; while the unanimity of the choir speaks with equal force as to his suitability as so. -ganist and choirmaster. How- ever this may be, there seem stobe no doubt that the dis- pute has evoked considerabh, s feeling. That it will be speedily and amicably settled fa ight to be a matter of course. All that is wanted to secure i hat end is a little common . t charity and the absence of arrogi n self-assertion, and, con- sidesiug the character and posit ton of those chiefly con- corned, it is hard to think that thee se qualities will be wholly wanting.

In Imo, he said, the Liberals got into power by a large majority by promising better trade and wages, and now there were hun- dreds and thonsands of bard-working men and their wives and families starving. No one had confidence in the Government. There were members in the House of Com- mons who were desirous of being called Liberals who had declared that they were not in favour of the policy that the Government was pursuing. He hoped that they would never have to witness such a thing in regard to a Conserva- tive Government. From examination of the past they could find that the Conservatives had always been united, and the action of the present Government had made the working-men Conservatives more than ever united. He be- lieved that the wire drawers were told that if they com- menced work on the terms of the employers they would be able to get almost as much money as they had before. Well, perhaps they would with some improved machinery, but if the machine was made to go quicker, the responsibility of the man was increased, and he would want some recompense for that res- ponsibility, but he did not see that the wire- drawers were offered that. If the wire manufacturers of Warrington had all been Tories, they would have been branded as grinding the workmen to death. He was glad to say that where Conservative capital WAS invested the peo- ple were getting good money. He had no fear but that a Conservative Government would be returned at the next election. CLAIM FOR DAMAGES FOR ASSAI7LT.—OG Thursday afternoon, before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, judge, and a jury, a claim for damages for an assault brought by Margaret Skidmore, wife of Jeremiah Skidmore, of 10, Nicholson-atreet, against Edward Pritchard and Frances, his wife, and Samuel Henry Turner Williams, was heard.— Mr. Davies, solicitbr, Warrington, appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Swift, solicitor, St. Helens, represented the defen- danie. The plaintiff and the defendants Mrs. Pritchard and Williams are brothers and sisters, and the alleged assault took place in Nicholson-street, where all parties to the action were then residing.—Mr. Davies said that this was a case in which the plaintiff claimed damages against the defendants for personal injuries resulting frcm an assault which was committed upon her by the defendants Frances Pritchard and Samuel Henry Turner Williams. It seemed that some few weeks ago the plaintiff brought an action in the County Court against the defendant Pritchard and his wife, for the detention of certain articles which belonged to her whilst she was living with her mother-in-law and sisters. Those articles were of comparatively small value, but it was irnpertant that he should relate the facts in order to show how the parties to the action came together on the date on which the assault was committed. On Thursday, the 10th April, the plaintiff, Mrs. Skidmore, brought an action against the defendants for detaining these articles, and the defendants brought a counter-claim against the plaintiff for lodgings and also for other payments on her behalf, which amounted in all to £2l. His client, Mrs. Skidmore, whom he appeared for on that occasion, satisfied his Honour that her claim was a bona fide and proper one, and his Honour ruled that the goods should be returned to her, except one article which was in pawn, and the damages were for the full amount of the claim, £4 15s 51, that amount to be reduced to 83 10d on the return of the goods. The next point in the case was that the Judge ruled that the goods should be returned to the plaintiff, and that the parties to return the goods were the defendants in the present action—Mr. and Mrs. Prit- chard. The counter claim brought by the defendants in the original action was characterised by his Honour as a dis- honest one.—Mr. Swift : I think that is going rather too far.—His Honour: I think you must not import my re- marks into the case.—Mr. Davies, proceeding, said that it was the duty of the defendants to return the goods as ordered, but instead at doing so in a quiet and proper man- ner, on Friday, the 18th April, at about 1-30, a chair was brought out of the defendants' house and placed in front of the plaintiff's house, and on the chair were placed some of the articles which his Honour bad ordered to be returned, a dolly tub and dolly being placed by the chair. The articles were: —One ladies dress, value LI 103; a large wool- len shawl, value is 4d; one turnover, value 23 3d; one dolly tub, value 23 6d; a peg, value is 8d; and a watch, which was in pawn. All these articles, with the exception of the watch, were ranged on and near the chair in front of the plaintiff's house. The plaintiff had prepared a receipt for the goods, which she was willing to give up on their de- livery. Mrs. Skidmore, seeing the articles in front of the house, went to examine them, and sea that they were all there, when the defendant, Mrs. Pritchard, put her hands on the things and said, "Leave these things alone until you have given me the receipt." The plaintiff said that she was only examining the goods, and would not give no the receipt until she got their into the house. Plaintiff then took some of the things into the house, and was taking bold of the turnover to remove it when the defendants, Williams and Pritchard, threw her down on the parapet of the street, and Williams put his knee on her chest and held her down whilst Pritchard snatched the receipt from her, and then took the dolly tub and the turnover back into her own house. Mrs. Pritchard then returned to Williams, who had his knee still on the chest of the plaintiff, and was kicking her on toe legs, and they both then dragged her (plaintiff) along the ground, which caused her great pain, her condition also at the time being such as to make it a very dangerous thing for them to do. Whilst doing this the defendants called plaintiff foul and filthy names. In consequence of the assault the plaintiff fainted several times on the after- noon of the sameday, and on the Saturday she again fainted several times. She had suffered considerably ever sine* and was yet in a very nervous and weak state. Since the assault the defendants had repeatedly been to the house of the plaintiff and called her foul names. She was examined by Dr.,Joseph on the 24th April, and he would tell them in what state he found her. He (Mr. Davies) should ask the jury, after hearing the evidence, to give his client such damages as they thought would meet the case.—The plain- tiff having given evidence bearing out the opening state- ment of Mr. Davies, Dr. Joseph was called, and spoke to examining the plaintiff for her injuries, which he described. The attack was such, he said, that the results might have been serious, although he did not think that they had actually been so. Cross-examined, witness said that he did sot think that a mere struggle for a hankerchief, coupled with a fall, would have made the defendant so weak and nervous.—For the defence, Mr. Swift called Mrs. Pritchard, Leicester-street, formerly of 12 Nicholson-street, one of the defendants, who said that she took the articles to the plain- tiff, who was her sister, and said, " Mrs. Skidmore, I have returned your things with thanks," whereupon Mrs. Skid- more threw the things into the lobby, and gave witness the receipt. The defendant Williams claimed the dolly tab and turnover, and the plaintiff then tried to snatch the receipt from witness. Williams put the turnover under his coat, and the plaintiff rushed at him, burst the buttons off his coat, and broke his watch chain. The two etruggled for possession of the turnover, and the plaintiff fell on her left side, sustaining what. in- juries she had received in that manner.—Other witnesses were called, and Mr. Swift, for the defence, stigmatised the case as a trivial and paltry one. It was, he said, ex- tremely unfortunate that these two sisters ehould have got ' to loggerheads over a few trifling articles and that, after I Mrs. Pritchard had given up the things and paid some £5 or £6 for expenses, they could not be satisSed without again com- ing to wash their dirty linen in court. It seemed to him to be one of those ordinary cases that frequently came before I the Borough Bench and were more satisfactorily disposed of • by each party Mrig bound over to keep the peace. How- - ever, as the case was now before the jury they Must make • the best of it. No questions of law were involved, and the • only questions were those of facts for men of the world and I of common sense to decide. As regarded Mrs. Pritchard, he contended that there we no evidence to show that she

cninmitted any assault, and, that in the case of Williams it was simply a struggle between him and the plaintiff for the possession of a shawl, and could not properly be character- is•'d al as assault —His Honour informed the jury that where serious assaults were committed it was often proper that they shonld be heard in a County Court so that the 'person assaulted might get that compensation which was not obtainable in a Criminal Court, Ftrd even in a c Ise of trivial assault where much publicity was given to it. it was right that the case should be heard to vindicate the 'character of the aggrieved party. In this case the evidence of fliedamage was of the slightest possible character. In point of figures there had really been nothing proved, and it rested with the jury, If they thought an assault had been committed, to r give such an amount as they thought was a sort of senti- -1 mental satisfaction for the assault. It was true that the plaintiff at the time was in a delicate state, but the doctor

Snocarse DRUNKENNESS.—Mary Ellen Wilkinson, 21 years of age, an old offender, was charged at the Warrington County Sessions, on Wednesday, before Messrs. P. Stubs and S. Rigby, with sleeping out at Sankey without visible means of subsistence, and with drunkenness.—Superintend- ent Jackson said that the ptisoner got so helplessly drunk that a doctor had to be sent for, and she had afterwards to be taken to the Workhouse. The doctor was so much afraid of her condition that he would not allow her to be taken to the Workhouse in an open cart—The Clerk (Mr. Buck- ton) : She had nearly drunk herself to death.—Superin- tendent Jackson said that the prisoner had been in conmpany with two labouring men from Burtonwoed at Sankey drink- ing whiskey —Mr. Stubs asked if the prisoner was the same girl mho had been imiore them so many times.—SopPrin- tendent J.'ckson said that she had been up for all kind' of offences.—Mr. Rigby: We appear to have tried everything. The Clerk thought that.the penitentiary would be the beet place for her.—Prisoner: Ido not care what you do with me, I am really tired of my life.—Mr. Rigby thought that she should be tired of such a life as she had been leading. —She was sentenced to a month's hard labour.

div.head: PUDDLERS' WAGES.
div.p: PUDDLERS' WAGES.

Sir,—A letter appeared in the Birmingham Daily Post, en Monday, the sth inst., containing the astounding infor- mation that the puddlers at the Ilorsehay Ironworks (Shrop- shire) had commenced working at the extraordinary low rate of es per ton, which is is ed per ton below the trade price. It appears the men were told that if they did not accept the terms offered the works would be closed, an alternative which, in my opinion, and which I believe will be the opinion of the great majority of the ironworking community, it would have been more heroic and more con- ducive to the interest of trade generally for the men and masters to have faced. What gives a special interest to the above painful intelligence is the fact that a local ironmaster, and prominent Liberal, and one who has always professed to take a deep interest in the welfare of workingmen, is the managing director of the works in question, bir, it is be, l'fond my comprehension how any Man who profeseeS to have a park of generosity in his nature, and who has anything like a practical or theoretical knowledge of puddling, can satisfy his conscience by paying a puddler es per ton for his labour, for a business more destructive to health and life there does not exist. Trusting you will insert these few lines in your valuable paper, I am, yours truly, May 7th, 1884. AN EX-PUDDLER. [We have made room for our Correspondent's letter, although we have reason to know that the gentleman referred to had nothing whatever to do with settling the wages ques- tion, and, further, that the amount named is incorrect.— En. Examiner.]

I should like this fact kept well to the front, and in writing to you / am but the mouth-piece of scores of people in the parish of Earles- town. No one need be happier in his parish than Mr. Matthews. Here we have a beautiful church, a splendid organ—both of which have been raised by public subscription—a beauti- ful house to live in, an efficient organist, a voluntary choir —which, I am certain, cannot be excelled within a radius of 20 miles—and a compact parish of intelligent people. What more does he want? And yet he can insult his parishioners by saving, "What have the people of Earlestown ever done for me ?" Are we to sit down and quietly submit to his high hand without raising our voices? Are the parishioners and wardens to be alike treated as nonentities without a voice in anything? Are the people to be deprived of their tights—rites of worship—for a mere whim of his? He would perhaps like it so, but I appeal to my courmyman and women to say if it is right.—Faithfully youre, Earlestown, May Ist, IP4. A.B.C.
THE SURVIVORS OF THE STATE OF _FLORIDA.

MONTRE&L, FRIDAY—The steamship Titania has landed here the twenty-four survivors from the State of Florida, which were transferred to her on the 22nd ult, from the barque Louisa. FIGHTING BETWEEN SPANIARDS AND BRITISH. NEW YORK, FRlDAY.—Advices from Bonacca (Hondu- ras) report a riot on the 6th inst., between Spaniards and British. The •former having trespassed on some land grants were ordered off, whereupon they attacked the British, and I a conflict ensued in which two persons were killed and four wounded.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.

The HOMO WI at four o'clock. , THE PIGEON SHOOTING BILL—Lord Betroun, of Bur- leigh. moved the second reading of the Cruelty to Animals Acts Amendment Bill, intended to render the shooting of pigeons from traps illegal.—After a debate, the House divided, and the second reading was lost by 78 to 48 votes. Other orders of the day being disposed of, the House ad- journed. HOUSE OF COMMONS.

The House met at four o'clock. QUESTIONS, &c.—Sir H. MAXWELL gave notice that in ' consequence of the withdrawal of the motion of Mr. A. Brown, and the falling to the ground of the amendment of Mr. Stagg, he should, that day month, call attention to the treaty with Portugal regarding the Congo. and move a resolution.—Mr. TRETELYAN, replying to Lord A. Hill, justified the appointment of Mr. John Hamill to the com- mission of peace for Louth, he being properly qualified for the office.—Lord HARTINGTON, replying to Earl Percy, said it was intended to cancel the last examination of officers for promotion in the army in consequence ef a typographical error in the papers, and officers would be allowed another trial.—Mr. GransTofirsl, replying to questions as to the safety of General Gordon, said he adhered to the statements he had already made. The general question could be better raised next Monday. Replying to a question of Sir W. Bartellot relative to the Conference, he said the place of meeting had not been fixed. It would be open to the powers to raise othra: question to that contained in the invitation, but if any new question was raised it would be tantamont to a new Conference. I CORRUPT PRACTICES AT AIUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.—The [ adjourned debate on the motion for the second reading of the Municipal Elections Corrupt and Illegal Practices Bill I was resumed.—Mr. WARTON opposed and moved that the I Bill be read a second time that day six months.—Mr. BIGGAR seconded its rejection, believing it entirely useless. —Mr. Dawson and other Irish members objected to the Bill applying to Ireland.—Sir H. GrFFonn thought some limita- tion of expenditure was necessary to the Bill. If that was not done, he thought the measure would create the very evil they had legislated to prevent as regarded Darliam,n- tary elections.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL said he had foand insertion of a general schedule of maximum expenditure an impossibility. He believed he had done all that was ne•

cessary on that subject in prohibiting paid canvassers, mes- vangers, and committee rooms, If it was the opinion of a majority in committee that Ireland should be exempted from the Bill he should not object—The Bill was read a second time without a division on the motion that it be referred to a Standing Committee.--Sir K. CROSS opposed and moved as an amendment that it be referred to A com- mittee of the whole House. The Bill contained Important points, which, he contended, could only be satisfactorily disposed of in a committee of the whole House.—Mr. J. LOWTHEIk also objected to the Bill going to a Grand Committee.—Mr. GLADSTONE contended, that nothing had been said to prove that the Bill was not ail suitable one for reference to a Grand Committee. What had been said went to prove that the Grand Committe.ea were not advisable things to have at all.—Mr. RAISES mid what hebad to say against the Bill he should defer until the Bill was in committee.—Thia House divided, when the pro- posal that the Bill should be referred to the Grand Com- mittee on Law and Justice was carried by 206 to 14Ci LAW OF EVIDENCE IN CRIMINAL CASES.—The ATTOR• NEE-GENERAL moved that this Bill be referred to the Stand- ing Committee on Law,..lustice, and Legal Procedare.—Sir 24. BEACH opposed, and believed time would be saved by the Bill being considered in committee of the whole House. —A discussion ensued, during which the SOLICITOR- GENERAL for Scoratoro said in committee the Bill would be made applicable to Scotland ; and several members insisted' that the Bill was a most important one, Eventually the motion to refer the Bill to the Standing Committee was carried by 179 to 134.—The sitting wax then susßended. A Corner OUT.—The Speaker resumed the chair at nine, and the House was counted out. Forty members not being present tha House adjourned at three minutes past nine.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

The Glasgow Citizen states that a firm of Greeaock sugar boilers II ts suspended payments with liabilities estimated at zioa,ooo. Sir William Jenner saw Sir Bartle Frere yesterday, and reported that the patient continues to gain a little in strength. It bas been decided that Lord Dalhousie shall introduce the Deceased Wife's Sisters Bill in the House of Lords during the week after Ascot week. Lord Randolph Churchill telegraphed to Birmingham yes- terday that the report of his having withdrawn from his candidature for that borough is a malignant falsehood. James Smith, warehouseman, was committed for trial at Manchester, yesterday, on the charge. of attempting to murder an elderly woman named Jonas by cuttiny, ' her throat. A farmer named McKnight, whilst driving home from Newry op Thursday night was attacked by throe men and so brutally beaten that his dying depositions have been taken. Three arrests have been made. CHILD MIIRDER.—EmiIy Wilcox, a factory worker. only 21 years of age, was sentenced tc death at Taunton Assizes, yesterday, for the murder of her illegitimate child. The jury recommended her to mercy on account of her youth. STATUE TO EIER MAJESTT.—A statue of the Queen was unveiled in the Free Library, Birmingham, yesterday after- noon. The cost of the statue was subscribed twenty years ago, the delay being in consequence of the death of Foley, to 'whom the commission was originally given. THE CASE AGAINST LORD Sr. LEONARDS.—The Central News understands that an application in Chambers will immediately be made for the admission of Lord St. Leonards to bail on the ground that the nest sitting of the Central Criminal Court will not take Tdace until the 26th ins., Mr. J. P. Grain will be retained tor the defence.

THE MA:INCHESIIER SHIP CANAL BILL. At the sittitur, of the Select Committee on the Ship Canal Bill yesterday morning, Mr. Pember announced that the pro- moters had, as they had anticipated, agreed wirh the Bridge- water Navigation Cempany for the purchase of the under- taking upon term p that would be explained, and the com- mittee, therefore, would not be troubled with any opposition from that company.—Mr. James Beazley, managing director of the Be,tish Shipowners' Company, expressed the posi- tive OrAnion that extra freight would be charged for the con- Trance f goods along the canal to Manchester. Asked 1! nether trades would not have a tendency to settle OD the _ .
banks_ of the canal, the witness said there was no doubt. a

scramble for a living just now, and people would settle themselves wherever work ;was to be got.— Mr. F. B. Boyden, ex-mayor of Liverpool, who is largely engaged in shipbuilding and is a shipowner, did not think, chiefly on account of the narrowness of the waterway, that the'trade of shipbuilding would be attracted to the canal. With regard to the bridges over the canal, he had prepared a list of 115 steamers trading with the port of Liverpool. and found that owing to the height of their masts only two of them would be able to pass under the bridges.
